text: Crocodiles lie up in the flooded yard and leeches thicken the shallows. The Lujei road above is the only safe approach.
Lujei salvagers strip its roof timbers and pull reed bundles from the flooded yards. Little is left to take.
The minder's platform is rotted, but Lujei's ferry families still drop a token of thread into the water here when they pass at dusk. The tree it served is the Blackrose tree.
Sheh-Ara lost its people to rising lake water between Lujei and Blackrose. The last families left for Lujei's ferry landing after the 4E 48 catastrophe.
A ferryman's lost child's bead string is caught in the dead tree, and a Lujei elder wants the village's hatching register fetched from the minder's platform.
Black posts stand in a ring where a hall was, with a dead sapling tree on a mud spit and a rotting ladder going into the water. A ferry channel from Lujei runs close beside.
Sheh-Ara has two halls on leaning posts above a flooded yard. A ferry channel from Lujei runs close beside it.
Sheh-Ara has no residents. Lujei ferrymen cut across its channel, and a few salvagers sleep on the dry platform.
Two halls still stand on leaning posts above a flooded yard, and the tree-minder's platform has slipped to a lean toward the lake. Lujei boatmen pass without stopping.
Snake nests under the rotten platform and stinging midges at dusk, with silt that hides deep holes. A stranger is likelier to be hurt by the ground than by a person.
Farmers from Tei-Kur salvage planking and sow what rice will still take at the edges. Scavengers come for the old irrigation sluices.
The village tree-minder's platform has fallen in. Farmers from Tei-Kur leave a rice-sheaf at the dry corner each harvest, a small courtesy to the people who first cleared the ground.
Oru-Neel stood in the north-eastern farm country between Tei-Kur and Reedfall and was emptied by a spring flood that took its rice fields; its families moved to Tei-Kur.
A Tei-Kur farmer wants the old dyke survey stone found, and a half-buried granary may still hold sealed rice seed.
A ring of grey posts stands in an empty paddy, with a collapsed hall roof in the mud and sluice gates still hanging from the old dyke. Rice stalks come up wild around them.
Oru-Neel is a ring of grey posts in an empty paddy, with a tilted hall platform and sluice gates hanging from the old dyke. A spring flood took its rice fields.
Oru-Neel has no residents. Tei-Kur farmhands pass through to reach the far paddies, and none of them stays a night.
The raised platform of the hall is cracked and tilted, and brown water sits where the paddies were. Farm families from Reedfall use the dry corner to dry nets.
Rotten floors, swamp predators and the occasional ghost story.
It was a fishing village; now it offers salvage.
A Hist sapling's root-hut still stands; the families took the sap.
The people left in the years after 4E 48, some for Jarecai, some for the Hist; no record says why.
A sealed hall, a missing clan's heirloom, or a smuggler's drop.
Collapsed stilts, half-tilted halls, strangling vines and quiet water.
A village of tiered timber halls on stilts, empty and sagging.
Uninhabited; smugglers use it at times.
The village is unheld. Squatters and smugglers use it, and the Mine-Burners avoid it.
Predators and scavengers.
The village once housed the Old Goldseam crews and their families, and it fell with the mine after the uprisings; salvagers from Salaxul now pull timber from the empty halls.
The village's tree-minder is gone, and its shrine is a hollow stump with a ring of bird bones. Hunters from Salaxul touch it for luck.
Emptied after the 3E 427 uprisings.
A tree-minder's records; a family cache.
A ring of rotted halls in the trees.
Zeh-Orun is a ring of rotted halls in the trees. It housed the Old Goldseam crews and their families until the uprisings.
Zeh-Orun has no residents. Hunters from the Salaxul road pass through, and Old Goldseam scavengers sleep in its dry halls.
Rotted stilts.
Deep water hides the old lanes and house floors, and crocodiles lie among the roof peaks. Drowning is a greater danger than any person.
Mir-Xal salvagers wade in for roof timber and iron fittings, and eel-trappers set weirs between the posts. The salvage is nearly exhausted.
A fish-bone shrine to the Hist is set on the highest roof peak by Natai fishermen who still make the offering for luck at the trap lines. No minder tends it.
Zul-Etha stood in the southern washes between Mir-Xal and Natai until the 4E 48 catastrophe sent its families to the larger towns.
A Natai fisherman says a trap line came up with a dated brass tag from the drowned street, and a Mir-Xal factor will pay for a salvage count of the iron.
Three roof peaks stand out of green water, with a leaning platform and a line of stumps showing the lost lanes. The drowned posts show a straight street.
Zul-Etha stood between Mir-Xal and Natai. Three roof peaks and a leaning platform now show above green water, and Natai fishermen call it the drowned place.
Zul-Etha has no residents. Natai trappers set lines among the posts by day and go home before dark.
The village has fallen into the water: three roof peaks and a bent tree-minder's platform are all that shows. Natai fishermen call it the drowned place.
Sea-drakes and wreckers; storms off the Sea of Mists.
Fish, salt, small boats.

Acra-Tiin's Sithis shrine is a salt-white stone at the head of the landing, and the fishermen cast a fin or tail into the tide for it before a long set. The village sends its eggs the long way round the cape by boat to the Banujha tree, and a shell-ledger on the shrine wall records each journey.
Settled as a shore landing for the Soulrest port.
A smuggler's landing; a lost boat.
Low stilt houses, drying racks, a boat slip.
Acra-Tiin is a row of low stilt houses with drying racks and a boat slip. A reeve runs it for Soulrest's council.
Argonian fishers and salters.
Run by a reeve for the council, with little attention from the city.
D2: wildlife and the odd thief.
Once a road post on the Gideon-Stormhold way; now stripped.
None; an Imperial plinth.
Reasoned: an Imperial road fort of the Third Empire, abandoned when the Legions left.
A smuggler's cache under the tower; a ledger hidden in the wall.
A broken stone wall, a stump of a tower and an archway half-buried in mud.
Agia Nero is a Project Tamriel name. UESP has no page for it (searched 2026-11-08).
None resident; scavengers and smugglers shelter here.
Roofless walls, a tower stump and a yard of tall reeds; a scavenger camp in the corner.
Sea-drakes offshore, unlit coast at night, raiders from the delta channels.
Fish, rice swapped from the delta, small boats.

Amalaja's minder looks east: eggs go with the salt-and-rice boats toward the delta trees, and drowned fishermen are given back to the sea at the point. The Hist is honoured in a small rice-straw shrine above the tide line.
Settled from Blackrose as the delta recovered after 4E 48, and has leaned toward Lilmoth in trade since.
A rice-swap dispute, a lost boat or a message for Lilmoth's merchant council.
Reed houses on a sandy headland, rice sacks under tarps, a line of fishing boats on the beach.
A village on a headland at the sea edge, one of the stage points between the lake and the delta.
Argonian fishers, a few delta-born families.
Its elders pay little to the island core and trade freely with Lilmoth.
Bay pirates raid it at night; the watchers shoot first.
Customs levies, a signal fire and a fishing boat for supplies.
Sithis and a small Nine shrine kept from the old retreat.
Built in the Third Era as a retreat; it survived 4E 48 and was taken over by the Archwardens.
A ledger with a smuggler's name, a pilot with a price, or a pirate parley.
A white-washed house with a verandah on a hill, a signal-lantern and a stair of rough stone.
A belvedere built as a view-house for an Imperial governor; now a customs watch.
Argonian watchers of Archein families and a Bosmer pilot.
Six watchers log ships in and out of Topal Bay and signal Soulrest.
Safe inside the walls; the harbour is policed and the water is a public road. Pickpockets, drunk sailors and smugglers working the lower wharves are the usual trouble. Outside, the beaches are D1.

The legal trade of the south-east: cargo handling, pilotage, bonded storage, ship chandlery, customs and the chartered privateers who stand in for a navy. Rice and fish arrive from the bayou by lighter; clay and dye come down from Aroxhu.

Sithis and the Hist as everywhere, but the nearest Hist is a small landward tree that harbour families tend; Imperial-descended residents keep a little of the Nine. Sailors leave offerings at the water stairs for those lost at sea.

Founded as an Ayleid town by the Barsaebic exiles, on ground held earlier by the Lilmothiit and the Cantemiric Velothi. Its coast was full of pirates in the late First Era until General Lucinia Falco chartered them with letters of marque. The East Empire Company later ran its wharves, and the Shadowscales kept a school here that closed in 4E 187. Umbriel in 4E 48 never reached it.

The sealed Shadowscale facility, which the Dark Brotherhood wants reopened and the townspeople watch, with a very old ku-vastei living near it. Paperwork disputes between chartered privateers and customs. Underwater games that a visitor can join, which teach swimming.

A low harbour town of stone wharves and timber warehouses with Company brick at the waterfront, wooden stilt houses behind, and taverns whose balconies overlook the bay. Boats and swimmers fill the water; the sea smells of tar, salt and rotting weed.

A major port city on the eastern coast, marsh to the north and beaches to the south, beside an estuary that leads inland. It is the province's principal legal port and the south-east end of the Archon, Lilmoth, Soulrest and Tear trade line. Anyone arriving by sea or by the bayou channels passes through its harbour.

About four in five are Argonians, with a sizeable Dunmer minority from Tear a short sail away, a few Imperials and Khajiit, and a floating population of sailors. Pilots, wharfingers, ferrymen and the merchant council hold the real authority.
The harbour authority uses the old Company wharves, the bonded stores and the counting-houses, which still stand. The charter that built them lapsed long ago.
Safe; swamp predators raid the paddies at night.
Red-clay pottery, saltrice and a toll-free rest-house for Soulrest caravans.
Dibella charms are pressed into the pots; Sithis is thanked at the kiln-opening.
Armanias is a Project Tamriel name; the place is a Gideon-era farming village that survived 4E 48 and has been rebuilt since.
A missing kiln-master, a pot with a hidden message, or a clay seam that should not be there.
Round clay kilns smoking along the road, red mud, drying pots on racks, stilt houses beyond.
A small village of kilns and rice paddies on the coast road between Gideon and Soulrest. The red clay of the Onkobra delta makes its pots famous.
Lukiul potters and rice-growers, with an Argonian elder who keeps the kiln-fires.
About eleven people live in stilt-and-clay houses, fire pots twice a season and send the best to Gideon's market.
Inside the village it is calm. On the shore road to the north, mudcrab swarms and fleshflies are the daily trouble, and outlaws from Skeith Isle sometimes land in the dark to take boats.

Red clay, ochre and fired pots go out by boat; salt, dried fish and Thorn's saltrice come back. The tolls Arorha charges outsiders landing on its quay pay for the mound walls. Unfired clay is cheap here, finished glazed ware costs three times as much at Thorn.
The village's hatching-tree is at Aroxhu, three days' walk inland, and its eggs go there. A small clay shrine on the quay holds votive pots to the dead; broken ones are left for the tide.

The mounds were raised by the village's founders, a generation or two after the Knahaten Flu emptied the coast of Cantemiric Velothi, over ground the Velothi had left fallow. In the Third Era the East Empire Company's boats called here for clay; in 4E 201 the landing is the same and the buyers are Argonian.

The elder wants a lost kiln-load of ochre found: the boat that carried it was taken by Skeith smugglers. A broken Velothi ancestor-tablet from Virtluush has turned up in the clay-pits and an old Dunmer trader will pay to know where it came from.

A ring of low red mounds, each carrying two or three reed-thatched houses on stilts, stained rust-brown by the clay. Kilns smoke at the water's edge and the shore is crazed red mud. Gulls and swamp-herons crowd the quay at dawn.

Arorha is the north-eastern outlier of the Aroxhu clay-mound country, a village on the first raised ground south of Hatandros Bight where the road from Inoja meets the sea. It exists to move the confederacy's clay, dye and pottery onto coastal boats. UESP has no page for it.

About eleven Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel, mostly clay-diggers, potters and boatmen. The elder is a pot-painter who keeps the village's tally of kilns and boats. Two or three Dunmer traders from Thorn lodge here in the dry months.

A working village with a short stone-free quay of piled mud-brick and wattle where flat boats unload. Elders from Arorha sit on the Aroxhu council. The warden post at Marshgate Watch to the north takes a toll on goods bound for Thorn, and Arorha pays it.
The town is safe; the elders keep a quiet watch of spear-bearers. The road to Inoja is a D1, but Sarpa and Paatru bands raid the outlying mounds.
Pottery, red clay, ochre and madder dye go down the rivers to Archon and Thorn; Aroxhu takes salt, fish, metal tools and coin. The clay trade is the confederacy's wealth. The Archwardens envy it.

The Aroxhu Hist is a young tree grown on the central mound. The elders hold the hatching rite beneath it, and eggs are laid in warm clay-pits at its roots. The town's dead go into the mounds beneath their houses.

Raised over generations on a clay ridge above the flood plain; it never held a stone wall. After the Umbriel year it took in the Arorha and Inoja families whose lowland villages were ruined, and became the confederacy's centre.
A stolen clay-dye recipe has been sold to a Thorn guild and the council wants the thief found. Two villages dispute a mound boundary and the speaker needs a neutral go-between.

A hill of terraced red mounds topped with a great gnarled Hist, reed-thatched houses on each terrace, kilns with long streamers of smoke, drying racks of cloth in madder red and ochre yellow, and a clay-paved moot-ground at the foot of the tree.

The seat of the Oxhu-Teeleel confederacy, a mound-town of red clay with a Hist at its centre, 40-odd people at the map's small-city tier. UESP has no page for Aroxhu; the people, the confederacy and the council are ours, built on canon's many unnamed tribes.

About thirty-eight Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel: a council of seven elders (each from one village, with a speaker chosen yearly), potters, dyers, mound-farmers and boatmen and a few visiting Agaceph traders.
A busy mound-town: the council meets each new moon under the Hist, the potters' quarter fires day and night, and the Archwardens must bargain for any road or toll in Oxhu country.
D1: wildcats and the odd thief on the road.
Quarried stone and fish, sold to Thorn's builders; Ayiin buys grain and metal tools.
A cairn takes the place of a tree; the elder reports dreams to Tsonac.
Founded as the Stone-Sleepers took the quarries of the east mesa after the Archeins' time.
A quarry cart stuck in the ford with a locked chest on it, and an elder asking who has been leaving shells at Balormaak's gate.
Squared stone houses with reed roofs on a riverbank, a stone jetty, mesa cliffs behind.
A hamlet in the Stone-Sleepers' eastern reach, on a river by the mesa. UESP has no page; the name and the people are ours.
Stone-Sleeper families, a gang of quarrymen and an elder who counts the carts that pass to Thorn.
Eight live there, working the Kalaxo Cut quarry upstream and fishing the river.
Undead guardians in the arch and snakes in the reed edge. At D3 the lower rooms are flooded and the track is the only safe place.
It was a small Ayleid hall. Relic-hunters from Slough Point now come to it, with the odd Fort Rustmoth soldier looking for white stone.
A cracked Ayleid shrine-stone stands at the top of the mound with Veesa-Teeleel ward-stakes ringed at its foot, leaning in.

Orimel is a small Barsaebic Ayleid hall on high ground north-west of Slough Point, one of the settlements left by the Ayleids after 1E 198. The map labels it an outpost; we read it as a ruin. Nothing is recorded of it.
A Vel-Sapha hunter has a rubbing from the shrine-stone he cannot read, and a Fort Rustmoth sergeant wants the mound's ward-stakes counted.
White arches rise from the reeds on the high ground, with vines over the fallen columns and black water in the lower rooms. The Rustmoth track runs below.
The map labels Orimel [Outpost] at (-15,-69), north-west of Slough Point; we read it as a ruin and named it in the Ayleid manner. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
Orimel has no residents. Hunters from Vel-Sapha Stand and the Fort Rustmoth garrison patrol the track below it. Neither side goes up.
The mound is dry in the cool months and flooded in the wet; Vel-Sapha Stand's people watch it from the track and the Veesa-Teeleel call it sick ground.
D3: undead guardians and giant snakes.
Once an Ayleid hall.
Fragments of a shrine.
Barsaebic Ayleids reached Blackwood after 1E 198.
A map to a vault.
White arches half-covered in vine; black water.
A Barsaebic Ayleid ruin at (-18,-71), named by us. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
Anutasil has no residents. Umpholo reed-cutters see its arches from their flats and keep clear, and the odd Meliton-bound traveller sleeps in its dry corner.
Half-flooded and avoided.
Giant snakes in the reeds and undead guardians below the arch. At D3 the stairs are drowned and the wardens do not cross to the island.
It was a minor hall of the Ayleid settlement. Scavengers and relic-hunters now come from Jal-Veesa by the Teel-Fen creek.
A worn Ayleid altar sits under a vine on the island's crown, ringed by Veesa-Teeleel ward-stakes set facing in.
Mirasel is a small Barsaebic Ayleid hall on a sedge island east of Loriasel, from the settlement that grew in the region after 1E 198. Nothing is recorded of it; its name is a map label.
A Jal-Veesa relic-seller will pay for a rubbing of the altar, and a Teel-Fen warden says a ward-stake on the west side has been pulled.
White arches stand in sedge with a fallen column lying across a black pool; the undercroft stairs go down into the water.
A Barsaebic Ayleid ruin marked on the map at (-8,-65); named by us in the Ayleid manner. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
Mirasel has no residents. Weir-wardens from Reed-Sill and Teel-Fen see its white arches on their rounds and have never seen a visitor stay.
The island is half-flooded and the Veesa-Teeleel of Reed-Sill Weir, a few cells to the north-east, will not go onto it and tell visitors it is sick ground.
D1. Slaughterfish and the odd predator in the inlet.
Red-clay pottery, dyes and pigments, saltrice; sold down the river to Archon and Thorn.
They bury and hatch at Aroxhu's Hist; the village keeps clay figures of ancestors on the mound crest.
Settled by mound-builders from the confederacy of Aroxhu, who found the clay banks of the inlet; the village's mounds raise it above the flood.
A potter's missing master-glaze; a dye vat spoiled by something in the water; a dispute with Aroxhu over clay rights.
A ring of raised red-clay mounds with thatched halls on top, kilns and clay pits, drying racks of dyed cloth, and a landing on the inlet.
A village of the Clay-Mound people at the north edge of the Nushara Bayou, where the east road meets the Okuwun-Rahei clay country.
Oxhu-Teeleel Argonians, with Three Waters traders and Archon dye-buyers as visitors.
About twelve households farm the mound slopes, fire pots and dye cloth; a council of elders speaks to the Aroxhu elders and to Three Waters traders.
Ghosts and skeletons in the halls, cliff-nesting hackwings outside and a tide that can trap anyone who goes in on the ebb and stays past it.
Once a fortified holding that taxed coastal boats. Now it draws scavengers: Velothi bronze, ash-glass and carved ancestor tablets sell at Thorn to Dunmer buyers.

The Velothi who came south followed the Mephala-led exile and kept ancestor veneration. Tablets and altar niches remain in the upper halls; the Argonians who pass by say the place is sick and do not leave offerings.

Cantemiric Velothi, Dunmer dissidents who settled the eastern seaboard, held this coast until the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560 killed them all. Nobody has lived here since. Chimeri myth says Mephala led a third of the Velothi into Black Marsh.
A Dunmer relic-seller in Thorn will pay for a particular ancestor tablet carved with the family sign of the holding's last lord. The lowest hall has a sealed door that only the ghosts can open.

Grey basalt and black volcanic stone in heavy, battered Velothi courses, half drowned at the base and crusted with barnacles and salt. A broken tower stands on the rock with a causeway that only shows at low tide.

A ruined Velothi hold on the rock off the Thorn coast, the nearest of the Hatandros Bight ruins to the city. It has no UESP page; its name is the map's, and its Velothi character follows from the Cantemiric Velothi's canon range between Archon, Arnesia and Thorn.
No living inhabitants. Ancestor ghosts of the Velothi walk the halls, for the Velothi buried their dead beneath their houses and the flu killed whole families at once.
Empty except for the dead. Thorn's slavers and, later, the Warden Marches' toll men both avoided it. The Argonians of the coast call it sick ground. The tide floods the lowest hall twice a day.
D3: undead in the cellars, snakes and flooding.
Once a farming and stone town; now a store of old ironwork and clay goods for scavengers.
The Velothi followed Mephala; Ayiin's people call the ground sick and leave a shell at its gate.
A Velothi settlement dead of the Knahaten Flu in 2E 560-603; Ayiin's people use its dressed stone and tell children it is empty of ghosts.
Ayiin's hunters want a child's lost egg-charm retrieved from a cellar, and a Thorn merchant wants a Velothi ledger.
Dunmer stone houses with scalloped roofs and a standing bell-tower stump, wrapped in vines.
A Cantemiric Velothi ruin of the east coast. UESP has no page for Balormaak; the Velothi settlement of this country is canon.
No residents; Ayiin's hunters pass it by day and look for strays among the ruins.
Broken walls and open cellars under vine, half-full of silt from the rains; scavengers visit from Thorn.
D2: the platform is safe; below it lie sea-drakes, drowning and the deep.
Salvage from the spires: bronze, vakka stones, jewellery, brass; the state takes its share, and Lilmoth merchants pay for licence.
Divers pray to the Hist and the drowned before descent; none carry Hist amulets, for the tree cannot hear them here.
Built after Lilmoth's drowned Imperial villas showed how much lay under the water; the successor state licensed salvage and set a station to take its share.
A diver who failed to come up; a clerk asked to hide a find; a bell that rises with something clinging to it.
A timber platform on pilings with winches, copper bells hanging on chains, drying diving gear, bunks in a hut and a lantern mast.
A working platform at sea, east of Lilmoth, whose diving bells reach the drowned spires. It is the only permanent human presence in Benthic Yobesh.
Argonian bell-divers, Archein-line clerks and a few hired Khajiit and Imperial specialists.
Eight crew live on the platform: bell-tenders, divers, a winch-master and a clerk who records every find for the state's share.
Inside, guarded and watchful; the lake margins hold gar and crocodilians; the boardwalks' feuds are real. The marsh around has rebel earthworks, Lilmothiit dens and Rose-bred outlaws on the roads.
Tolls and transit at the three-river confluence, lake commerce by canoe, fish and reeds and whatever comes out of the Rose by water or by raft.
Hist drowned in the lake, with the island core controlling hatching and naming; Sithis shrines on the boardwalks; a Lilmothiit-era sense of the ground as owned by the dead.

Built by the Lilmothiit; Kothringi and Yespest lived nearby. Red Bramman's bandit kingdom stood here around 1E 1033. The Imperial rebuild followed 1E 2837; the 2E rumoured it ruined; the city raised an army against the Third Empire and was broken by the battlemage Welloc's vampiric cloud.

Lilmothiit foundations under the island core, the drowned Hist's dive, the quarrel with the Rose, Welloc's vampiric cloud and what the rebel army left behind, and a smuggler contact for Bramman's river.

A walled island core of stone, most of the city over the lake on stilt and boardwalk districts raised above flood level, shore quarters at the feeder mouths, canoes everywhere, mist off the water at dawn.
A major city in a lake in south-central Black Marsh where three rivers converge. The Rose lies off in the marsh and is not the city's, though outsiders assume it is.
Argonian-majority, with prison staff families, ex-prisoners, deserters, refugees and coerced migrants. Distrust of battlemages and of the Rose runs through all of them.

Functioning but diminished, with ruined and rebuilt quarters of several ages and old siege earthworks in the marsh from Welloc's campaign. The island core holds the toll and the hatching. Its Hist lies drowned in the lake, reached only by boat and dive.
Blackguard bands above, Naga and undead below, and a sanctum path left open to test challengers.
Highway tolls and robbery, stripping the old Imperial settlements around it, smuggling through Blackrose's channels.
Sithis and a Naga raj-kaal's necromantic rites; the old Hist tradition is absent behind these walls.

Raised by Pelladil Direnni with stone atronachs for Potentate Versidue-Shaie, abandoned in the Second Empire's fall, held by the inmates' descendants, reclaimed by the Third Empire, and broken in 3E 432. After 4E 48 the cycle ran a third time.
A quest to break in, to bargain with the raj-kaal, to find what Jagar Tharn's last associates left, or to learn why the Rose is not the city's.
A grey stone fortress of Lilmothiit rubble, part-flooded, with bastions the marsh has crept into and Blackguard banners and fires on the upper wall.
The canon Imperial prison, 'the Rose', a day's march from Blackrose city. It is a ruin reoccupied by the Blackguards' heirs.
Blackguards' heirs, escapees' descendants, exiles and outlaws, Naga allies and a few dozen hangers-on. They raid the roads and trade quietly with the lake villages.
Held by Blackguard families three generations deep and a Naga raj-kaal who resent the word prison. The upper walls are their stronghold. The lower levels are held by the undead.
Wild predators; scavengers from Toklea's rivals.
A source of salvage stone and metal for Toklea.
The Chime-Keepers' custom of hanging bead strings on the doorposts survives at Bucalos as rotting cord. Its minder moved to Toklea with the people, so the shrine here is left to the damp.
A Kothringi town before 2E 560, resettled by Argonians and left empty in the generations since.
Footings that hide a Kothringi cache; a ghostly chime-singer.
Stone footings, a half-fallen hall, rusted chimes and green moss.
Bucalos is a set of stone footings, a half-fallen hall and rusted chimes under green moss. Toklea's people quarry its stone.
Bucalos holds no residents, only Toklea fishermen who tie up at its landing in bad weather and a family of eel-trappers who camp on the southern platforms when the water drops.
Stone footings and a collapsed hall; Toklea's people quarry its stone.
D3: Sarpa archers and diving attackers at the mouth, and falling rock.
It serves as a larder and nest, with a little hoarded loot from raided travellers.
The Sarpa keep to the Hist of High-Flower, their own tree; eggs are carried there for the hatching.
A natural cave known for generations; the Sarpa claimed it as the mesa country was abandoned by Imperial prospectors.
A stolen clutch of eggs, a prospector's lost crate, a Sarpa elder who might trade if shown respect.
A wide crack in the mesa wall with bone heaps and feathers at the mouth, nests on its ledges.
An unlabelled cave in the west of the mesa, named Sahlpesh Cave in the Argonian style. UESP has no page for it; the Sarpa are canon, exclusive to Middle Argonia.
Sarpa Argonians, a winged breed hostile to outsiders, and their young.
Used by the Sarpa warband from the nearby camp as a cold store and a roost; it holds their kills and their eggs.
Smugglers will fight; the tide fills the cave.
A cache for moon-sugar and salvage.
A sailor's charm to the sea.
Natural; smugglers have used it since Red Bramman's day.
A stashed crate, a hidden chart or a smuggler captain.
A low black cave mouth hung with kelp, a rock ledge and a rope ladder.
A sea-cut cave on the island's eastern shore, wet at high tide.
Smugglers, often Khajiit and Argonian, who work Topal Bay.
A small crew of Bay smugglers stash cargo here.
Highwaymen on the Percar road, burn-scar gas east of the village.
Carting, salvage, inns for travellers, tolls.

Chasepoint's Sithis shrine is a plain stone slab beside the carters' yard where drivers pour a drop of oil before a night run. Its hatchlings go inland by cart each season to the Banujha tree, and the shrine keeper keeps the road ledger of who went.
A road stage of the Third Era timber trade; canon names it Soulrest's eastern neighbour.
A cart gone missing, a salvage dispute, a smuggler's drop for Bramman's river.
Timber and stone stilt houses on a spit, carts under sheds, a salvage yard of ship timber.
Chasepoint is a spit of timber and stone stilt houses with carts under sheds and a salvage yard of ship timber. Soulrest's merchant council rules it and takes its toll.
Argonian carters, wreck-salvagers and a few Imperial-descended clerks.
Under Soulrest's merchant council and its toll.
Crocodilians in the channel, outlaws on the road.
Fares and rice-freight.
A Sithis-token on the landing post.
Rebuilt after 4E 48 when Lilmoth recovered and the Blackrose road was reopened.
Smugglers hiding goods in rice sacks; a message to be carried.
A plank landing, a winch raft and a lamp post.
A ferry landing on the delta channel on the road to Lilmoth.
Argonian ferrymen and their families.
Licensed by Lilmoth's merchant council.
D4: sea-drakes, drowning, pressure and cold; sounds that draw divers over the edge.
It has no trade; it is the edge of what salvage can reach and the reason the spires are not yet stripped.
Argonians hold it as a place where the drowned dwell.
Probably the drowned edge of the land the Hist's domain lost to the Padomaic; Argonian legend says Murkmire was swallowed by the Southern Sea.
A diver who recorded the echo; a sealed spire at its bottom; a sea-drake lair on the rim.
A wall of black water on the sea floor, cold currents and sound returning from below.
A deep trench in the sea floor in the middle of Benthic Yobesh; its name is the Bell Station divers'.
No residents. Divers speak of voices; Argonian divers say it is the old Hist singing.
Divers avoid it; bell-tenders refuse to lower below the rim.

D1: the house guards and their dogs keep the paddies safe, and the dykes shelter slaughterfish and young crocodilians. Thieves and runaway bonded workers use the road that crosses the estate to Lilmoth.
Rice for Lilmoth's market and the lighters, with a small surplus of sugar-cane for rum.

The tenants walk the road into Lilmoth to hatch their young and give them names at the Hist tree there. The Dunhallow family keeps a prayer-post at the end of the great house's veranda, where it sets out rice-wine for the drowned of the first planters.
Founded in the late Third Era by Breton planters on the Hereguard model. The family survived Umbriel by hiding in a store-cellar and later married into the Lilmoth coast.
A drowned cellar of the old house with the family's pre-Slaughter ledgers; a quarrel over who owns the land.
A long plank house on posts with a tiled roof, paddies like green mirrors, a boat landing and a bell on a post.
A rice estate north of Lilmoth, held by one family that has outlasted the town's rebuilding.
Mixed-blood heirs with Argonian wives and husbands, a steward and about a dozen tenants and bonded workers.
Eight people live in the great house and workers' huts; paddies stretch toward the road.
D1: the barn is watched by hired guards and dogs, and the reed channels hide snapping turtles and slaughterfish. Thieves at night are the usual danger, since the north road is always busy.
Rice, reed and the hire of boats for the Lilmoth harbour.

Silt-Orrel's Argonian family hatches and names its children at Lilmoth's Hist tree, as do its tenants. A small post of woven reed by the reed-channel landing holds offerings to the water-spirits, left before every cutting.
The land passed from an Imperial claimant to the family in the first generation after Umbriel, who paid in salvage from the drowned quarter.
A salvage chest from the drowned quarter hidden in the cellar; an heir's unclaimed deed.
Low thatched halls on stilts, a large rice-barn and reed-lined channels.
A rice and reed estate on the road north of Lilmoth, bought outright by an Argonian family.
An Argonian landholder, his kin and tenant farmers.
Six people on the estate; the family hires out its boats to the town.

D1: sentries on the veranda and dogs keep the barn, while the shore dykes shelter crocodilians. Stragglers from Fort Reedmoth's garrison and smugglers using the landing at night are the likelier trouble.
Rice shipped by lighter; hire of oarsmen to the fort.

Mereweather's tenants sail to Lilmoth for hatching and naming rites at the Hist tree. The family, of Imperial descent, keeps a small shrine post by the landing, where the lighter crews touch wood before a crossing.
Run since before the Slaughter by an Imperial family; it paid the garrison for protection and kept its title through every change of government.
A steward who wants an audit kept quiet; a boat of rice that never arrived.
A square two-storey house of timber and brick with a veranda, a rice-barn, a landing and tall palms.
A rice estate on the south shore of the northern island, close to Fort Reedmoth.
A landholder family of Imperial descent now Argonian by marriage, a steward, a few tenants.
Six people in the house and quarters.
D1: sea-drakes offshore, storm surges.
Roots, gourds, fowl and eggs for Karketa.
The family hatches and buries at Lilmoth's tree, a long boat journey north, and sees the Hist rarely. By the door a post hung with shells remembers the sailors drowned on the southern shoals.

Ixa-Ruu was cleared in the generations after 4E 48, when families spread back to the southern tip of the island. It sits close to Southwatch Keep, which has kept the shore watched for as long as the farm has stood.
A hawker who offers odd things from wrecks; a lost fowl that wandered into a den.
A thatched stilt house, a garden of gourds on a rise and chicken coops.
A family of three keeps Ixa-Ruu, a thatched stilt house with a gourd garden on a rise and chicken coops. Southwatch Keep's patrols are welcomed at the door.
A family of three keeps the farm.
The family sells roots and eggs at Karketa and mends its own thatch after each storm. Strangers from the keep's patrols are welcomed at the door; others are watched from the garden rise.
D1: predators that steal guar.
Guar meat and hide, reed-roots, sold at Lilmoth.
Seeku's family goes to Lilmoth's tree for hatchings and burials, an easy walk east. A post of reed beside the paddock gate holds the knotted cords of animals that were killed by predators.

Seeku was cleared in the generations after 4E 48, on the firm ground west of Lilmoth that the town's rebuilders left to smallholders. The guar stock came from the first family's marsh-guar, bred up over several seasons.
A guar that has not come back; a stranger who asks to rent a barn.
A low house, a guar paddock with a stockade and fences of reed.
A family of four keeps Seeku: a low house, a stockaded guar paddock and a vegetable plot, a short walk from Lilmoth's tree.
A family of four keeps guar and a vegetable plot.

The family keeps the guar paddock stockade in repair and drives animals to Lilmoth's market in the dry months. They know their neighbours on the road and keep watch for anyone who loiters near the pens.
D1: slaughterfish in the pond, wasps.
Fruit, pond fish and honey from a few hives.
The family carries its eggs and its dead to Lilmoth's tree. At the pool's edge a driftwood post with a fish-bone string marks the water-spirit they thank before netting.

Wattle-Pool was cleared in the generations after 4E 48, on the island's firm centre where a spring-fed pool made fishing and fruit possible. The wattle ring round the pool is the work of the first couple, who kept slaughterfish out of the shallows.
Honey with an odd taste; a stranger who sleeps in the shed.
A small stilt house, fruit trees and a pond ringed with wattle.
A couple and a child keep Wattle-Pool, a small stilt house among fruit trees beside a pond ringed with wattle. They sell honey and fruit at the nearest village.
A couple and a child keep the farm.
The couple tend the fruit trees and hives and net the pool in rotation. They sell honey and fruit at the nearest village, and a stranger who sleeps in their shed is made to leave by morning.
D1: road bandits, soldiers.
Rice and eggs for the fort.

Tal-Neesh sends its newborn to Lilmoth's tree and buries at Sal-Axan's moot ground when the road is clear. A post by the door is hung with scraps of soldiers' cloth, left for travellers who died on the road.
Tal-Neesh was cleared in the generations after 4E 48, on the island road between Sal-Axan and Fort Reedmoth. It grew by supplying the garrison's mess, and the family has outlasted three commanders.
A soldier who wants rice on credit; a bandit's note left in the barn.
A low plain house, a rice-paddy and a woodpile.
A family of three keeps Tal-Neesh, a low plain house with a rice-paddy and a woodpile. It sells rice and eggs to the quartermaster of Fort Reedmoth.
A family of three, who sell to the garrison.
The family sells rice and eggs to the fort's quartermaster and keeps its door barred at night against the road. Soldiers pass and trade on credit; the family tallies every sack.
Mudcrabs, fleshflies and the odd smuggler passing on the road.
Sea-salt boiled in clay pans, sedge for roofing and hardy marsh vegetables. The family sells to Seafalls.
They go to Seafalls for the death-dances and keep a painted shell at the door.
Cleared by a Seafalls family who wanted ground for growing food that the sea does not provide.
The family's youngest has found a smuggler's cache in the pans and is afraid to tell anyone.
Flat grey salt-pans, stacked sedge, a single reed house on a mound, drying racks, a boiling shed with a stack.
A farm on the salt flats inland of Seafalls. The name is ours; no UESP page.
Three Argonians, a mother and two grown children.
A working holding that sells salt and sedge to Seafalls.
Crocodiles in the paddy, marsh predators for the herd, and smuggler thieves.
Guar-hide, milk and rice, sold at Seafalls. A little of the herd goes to Archon on the pilots' boats.
They keep a clay figure of a guar at the door and do not trouble the sea-spirits.
Founded by a Seafalls family who had fallen out with the pilot-elder and wanted their own ground.
A guar has been taken and a foot-print leads toward the Vicrium mine. The family has an old grudge with the pilot-elder.
A green meadow with guar, a rice paddy, a reed house on a low mound, a clay fence and salt wind.
A guar farm on the meadow between Seafalls and the Khiar road. The name is ours; no UESP page.
Four Argonians, two adults and two hatchlings.
A small guar herd and a rice paddy, with a path to Seafalls.
Marsh predators.
Rice, reeds and fish.
A household shrine to Sithis; hatchlings go to the Lilmoth tree.
Cleared from marsh after 4E 48.
A failing paddy, missing boat.
A stilted house, paddies, a rice shed.
A farm on the channel bank, named Reedfall after its reed falls on the water.
An Argonian farming family.
Run by one family.
D1: crocodiles in the ditch and the odd thief; nothing worse.
Saltrice and eels sold to Stormhold on the causeway; a share goes to the Vicecanon's reeve.
Ancestor stones by the door and a Hist shoot in a clay pot, the family's one concession to both.
Reasoned: a smallholding on raised ground since the Dunmer colonial period; the family stayed when the Dunmer withdrew.
A missing son who went to the Silyanorn tunnels for crystal; a stranger who asks to rent the barn for a week.
A long stone barn and a two-storey mud-plaster house on a mound ringed by paddy dikes and a stone causeway.
An unlabelled farm on the Stormhold causeway country, named by us in the Stormhold manner (Dunmer family name, farm). UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
Dunmer-descended farmer, his Argonian wife and children; seasonal Argonian field labour.
One household and two hired hands work a few flooded fields and a stone barn on a mound.
D1: wildlife.
Saltrice and eels to Stormhold.
Ancestor stones and a Hist shoot.
Reasoned: a smallholding on raised ground.
A traveller asks to rent the barn.
A stone barn and house on a mound.
An unlabelled farm placed by us, named in the Stormhold manner. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
A Dunmer-descended farmer and Argonian wife.
One household works a few flooded fields.
D1: kept by the garrison; Sarpa raids come to its western approach.
Tolls and a share of the chalk the pit sends to Thorn.
No Hist; the garrison goes to Noota Nara's tree for hatching and burial.
The Empire built it to guard a chalk and limestone working; garrisons left after 4E 48 and Argonians took it over in the secession.
A garrison captain wants a patrol to find a missing chalk cart, and rumour says the fort's cellar opens into an older chamber.
Pale grey stone walls dusted white with chalk, a gatehouse and a square watch tower on a mesa shoulder.
An Imperial fort named in the Legion's '-moth' style, in 4E 201 a toll and watch post across the mesa. UESP has no page for it; it is a Project Tamriel name.
Argonian garrison families of old Archein lines, with a Dunmer quartermaster.
A dozen at most man it; they tax the chalk carts and watch the Sarpa to the west.
A fortified post is safe inside; outside lies open water and boat-robbers; the chain and the garrison's tempers are the usual hazards.
A toll on lake boats and a levy on grain; the garrison buys food from Yalugo and fish from Luntoc.
The fort has no Hist, so the garrison goes home to a village tree to hatch and bury; a small stone chapel of the Nine, empty but swept, is kept out of habit.
Built by the Empire as a lake post on the interior boat road; the Legion left after the Imperial presence ended and Archein families took the keys and kept the toll, as they did at the other forts.
The toll ledger shows a boat that never left; a cellar under the keep is sealed; the Truowa council would pay to see the garrison replaced.
A squat stone keep and curtain wall on an islet, mossed and re-roofed in reed, a toll chain across the channel and a signal lantern on the tower.
Fort Gysilla is a small stone fort on an islet at the lake's southern end, one of the Empire's old posts now held by the successor state. UESP has no page for it; it is a Project Tamriel name.
About ten, Argonian Archein families who still keep Imperial-style ranks and paperwork, a few freed-labourer's grandchildren as boatmen and one clerk.
A garrison of about ten keeps the toll and watch for the Archwardens, who barely supervise it. It is cool with Truowa's council and in a standing quarrel with Yalugo over the price of grain.
D2: the garrison are hostile to smugglers, and the marsh around is wild.
Tolls on road and strait; fish and rice bought from Sal-Axan.
Imperial forts carry no Hist; the garrison goes to Lilmoth to hatch, name and bury its dead.
An Imperial fort with a '-moth' name; the Empire is absent after 4E 48 and the successor state now keeps it.
A smuggler's tip about a night crossing; a dispute over tolls with the Three Waters.
A low square fort of stone and timber with a tower, a toll chain across the channel, and a moss-grown wall.
A stone fort held as a toll station and watch on the east end of the northern island, facing Archon's coast across the strait.
Argonian garrison families, some Archein-line officers, no Imperials.
Ten men of Archein descent keep the gate, take tolls and check cargo for the customs service; paperwork is half Cyrodiilic.
D1: a guarded fort; wildlife and fleshflies outside.
Tolls on the Blackwood Road, a levy on goods bound for Gideon and Leyawiin, and fines on smugglers.
No Hist: Imperial foundation. The garrison hatch and bury at village trees.
Built by the Third Empire to command the Blackwood Road; rumoured emptied when the Legions were recalled at the Oblivion Crisis; not Imperial after 4E 48.
A captain who has been paid not to look at a cart; a ledger that does not agree with the barracks' stores.
A square stone keep with corner towers and a yard, the Imperial eagle over the gate, a moat that is now a reed pond.

Fort Rustmoth is a Project Tamriel name in the Legion's '-moth' series. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08). The register places the Third Empire's Fort Swampmoth on the same road between Slough Point and Gideon; Rustmoth fits that placement and may be its map name, which we leave open.
Argonian soldiers under an old Archein-lineage captain; clerks; a few Nibenese families in the kitchens.
Held, but not by the Empire: an Archwarden garrison charges tolls and keeps a customs ledger for the successor state, in the old Imperial style.
Bay pirates and storm surges.
Tolls and a ferry for the garrison.
Sithis and a small Nine shrine.
The Legion built it to guard the harbour; the Archwardens inherited it.
A smuggler in the lock-up, a missing log or a captain bribed.
Grey stone walls on the shore, a signal tower and a sea-gate.
A small stone fort at the mouth of Topal Bay near Soulrest, one of the '-moth' forts.
Argonian soldiers of Archein descent and a Khajiit pilot.
Eight soldiers log shipping and collect tolls; they co-operate with Soulrest's merchant council.
Safe on the road; the fort has been attacked by Naga raiders and bay pirates, and a wrong word with the captain closes the road.
Tolls, a fort farm of saltrice, and a barracks market that sells salt and iron to travellers.
Sithis in private, the Nine in old habit; there is a small Imperial shrine to Zenithar the quartermaster still kept.

The Legion built it as a road fort; the Empire's last garrison left after 4E 48. The old Archein families who staffed it stayed and changed their letterhead, so the fort still collects the same tolls under a different seal.
A toll dispute, a smuggler caught in the stockade, a captain with a secret about Gideon's records.
Grey stone walls and a tower at a road bend, moss on the parapet, a toll chain across the road, reeds all around and a flag of the successor state.
A small stone fort on the Gideon-Soulrest road, one of the '-moth' forts of the old Legion naming. In 4E 201 it is the Archwardens' toll post and river-watch at the southern approach to Gideon.
Argonian soldiers of Archein-descended families, led by a captain whose paperwork is half Cyrodiilic. The fort has no Hist; they go home to a village tree to hatch and bury.
Eight soldiers and clerks man it, collect a toll on traders and watch the coast for bay pirates. They are courteous to Gideon's merchants and wary of the Mine-Burners' caravans from the basin.
D2: a smugglers' watch, snakes and mud-crocodiles in the ruined lower rooms, and rot in the stairs.
It makes nothing. The stores of a dead garrison, a few rusted Imperial arms and a smugglers' cache are what draw people.
Imperial forts carry no Hist; a bare stone shrine to the Nine on the ground floor has long gone to moss.
Built by the Empire as a road fort in the '-moth' manner of Legion forts. No Imperial presence is recorded after 4E 48, so its garrison is long gone.
A cache of contraband waiting to be moved; a sealed cellar of the old garrison's pay chest; an Imperial banner waiting to be retrieved.
A square stone keep with a broken stair-tower, green with moss and vine, on a low rise in the reeds with a road paving fragment at the gate.
A stone keep outside the living garrison network, on firm ground on the road inland from Archon.
No garrison. Three Waters families shelter in floods and smugglers use it as a cache; an old ex-privateer keeps a room as his home.
The fort is unheld. Part of the roof has gone; the upper floor is dry enough for refugees. The Archwardens have not garrisoned it as they have Fort Reedmoth.
D1: the garrison keeps the road. Bribery and smuggled goods make the gate a place to be careful with money more than with a blade.
Tolls on carts, boats and travellers entering Thorn from the jungle and the south; a share goes to the Archwardens and the rest stays in the fort.
The fort has no Hist, so its people go home to the village tree to hatch and bury; a small Imperial shrine in the yard is kept up out of habit.

The Empire built it to protect Thorn and its saltrice trade; it kept Imperial garrisons until the Empire's presence in Black Marsh ended after 4E 48. Argonians took it over in the years of the secession.
A captain asking for an outsider to carry a message to Thorn without going through the gate, a toll ledger with a missing page, and a locked store room where the garrison keeps confiscated goods.

Square grey stone walls and a gatehouse on a low rise above the shore, with the Imperial banner gone and Argonian reed-cord pennants in its place; a toll bar across the road and a jetty for the watch boat.

A fort beside Thorn on the western approach, named in the Legion's '-moth' style. In 4E 201 it is a toll station, river watch and the south end of the frontier screen facing Morrowind. UESP has no page for it; it is a Project Tamriel name.

Argonian garrison families, mostly old Archein lines under new seals, led by a captain who answers to the Archwardens and is on friendly terms with Thorn's Vicecanons. A few Dunmer drivers and merchants wait at the gate.
A dozen at most man it: toll clerks, a watch captain and bonded labourers' descendants as guards. Records are still kept in Imperial form.
D1: a guarded post, with road-side wildlife and the odd thief outside the gate.
Tolls on the road and the river, a levy on Dunmer and Argonian goods crossing to Morrowind, and a small market of traders who camp outside the walls.
No Hist: Imperial forts carry none. The garrison go home to a village tree to hatch and bury.
Built by the Third Empire as a border fort beside Stormhold. Canon records no Imperial presence in Black Marsh after 4E 48; the garrison left or died, and the fort passed to the successor state.
A smuggled cargo held at the gate; a clerk selling false toll stamps; a tower watchman who reports fires in the Morrowind hills.
A squat grey Imperial stone fort with a gate, a yard and a watch-tower; moss climbs the walls and the old Imperial relief is still over the gate. A wooden jetty and toll-bar sit on the road outside.
Fort Willowmoth is one of the Legion's '-moth' forts, named in the same style as Swampmoth, Moonmoth and Frostmoth. UESP has no page for it (searched 2026-11-08); it is a Project Tamriel name.
Argonian soldiers and a handful of clerks from Archein families; the commander answers to the Vicecanons for customs and to the state for the screen.
A garrison of a few Archwarden soldiers collects river and road tolls and watches the crossing to Morrowind. The ranks and paperwork are half Cyrodiilic, kept by old Archein families.
D4: Fenlord undead and the library's wards.
Once a library and tomb; now a treasure for scholars and thieves.
Hermaeus Mora and the Fenlord's death-cult; the Veesa-Teeleel avoid it.
Built by a sorceress of Hermaeus Mora to attract books; the halls drew in The Lusty Argonian Maid and Ruminations on the Elder Scrolls. Zahra entered about 2E 582 to find the Crown of Ascension.
A book that should not exist in the library; the Fenlord's vault.
A half-sunk pale-stone ruin on a reed island among black water; shelf-lined halls in the dry part.
Gandranen is a Barsaebic Ayleid ruin in Shadowfen: a library of magical halls that draws books from any time, and a Fenlord's tomb crawling with undead slave-guardians.
None living; an occasional scholar.
The library still attracts volumes; its undead guards still serve the Fenlord.
Lake crocodiles, leeches in the shallows, and travellers from Yulca who arrive tricked by illusions.
Dried fish, eel-paste and rice go to Yulca and Aroxhu; Gaweja buys books and scrolls from the Agaceph, for the elder's sake.
Eggs go to Aroxhu. A fisher's shrine of woven reeds stands on the point with a cord for every boat lost.
The clay-mound people's furthest settlement toward Yulca; founded as a fishing post, it became the place Oxhu and Agaceph meet to trade.
An Agaceph scholar has gone missing on the lake and Gaweja's fishers found his raft empty. The lake bed has been dredged at night.
Stilted mounds along the lake edge, drying racks of eel, rice terraces with water-lilies, reed boats pulled up, a small stone cairn on the point.
A village on the lake edge on the western side of the mound country, the border village with the Agaceph. No UESP page for Gaweja.
About eleven Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel, fishers and rice-growers, with a few Agaceph visitors.
A quiet village. The elders keep good relations with Yulca, which is rare. A fair is held at the lake's edge each autumn.
D4: undead and monsters in flooded halls; the roof is unsafe.
Once the Conclave's vault; now a source of tablet fragments and relics for scavengers and the Conclave's agents.
The Conclave's faith in learning and Molag Bal's name in their title; the Veesa-Teeleel call the ground sick.
The vaults sank when an associate of the Conclave cast a powerful spell. In the Simulacrum the Eternal Champion was sent in to recover the tablet.
The tablet itself; a Conclave scholar who needs someone to find the lower archive.
A collapsed stone vault entrance in a slope of reeds; half-sunk columns, flooded halls and rune-marked walls.

UESP's Vaults of Gemin are a ruined structure in Stormhold's city-state that once belonged to the Conclave of Baal, kept the ancient tablet for deciphering the Elder Scrolls and divining Murkwood's place, and sank into the ground when a spell failed.
None live here; the Conclave pays treasure-seekers.
A sunk, half-flooded ruin; the Conclave of Baal still sits in Stormhold and still cannot locate Murkwood without the tablet.
The town is guarded and safe by day. The closed Ayleid sections, the Ruction Ring's cut-throats and the swamp at the gates (death hoppers, fleshflies, hackwings) are where visitors get hurt.

Hunting produce, herbs, red-clay pottery from the Onkobra delta, and the Leyawiin trade; the cooks serve outsiders swamp food that they can stomach. Rootworm traffic ends at Gideon in winter and brings Middle Argonian goods, and salt and iron go out to the river stations of the Naka-Desh.

Dibella is worshipped openly in the old Dorcia Martius manor, a devotion the Nibenese took from the Kothringi substrate; Sithis is honoured in private by the Argonians. The Hist garden holds a planted cutting whose ownership is disputed.

Barsaebic Ayleids founded it as Twyllbek; the Kothringi left a Dibella devotion in the soil; Imperial settlers built the mansion, the temple and Castle Giovesse beside it. The An-Xileel's weapon killed the Lukiul majority in 4E 48 and the undead host of Umbriel overran the town, yet Gideon's destruction was light and it stayed an active settlement.
A courthouse case that turns on a missing record, the disputed Hist cutting in the gardens, the closed Ayleid cellars, digs for Kothringi treasure and the Gideon-Soulrest rivalry all start here.

Imperial brick and timber along Blackwood Way, wet red clay underfoot, crooked alleys running off the causeway, and Ayleid white-stone stumps in the plaza and the southern gardens. Steam rises from the bathhouses and fog lies in the streets at dawn.

Gideon is the first settlement on the Blackwood Road from Leyawiin and the province's civic-and-records city: a governor's mansion, a courthouse, a Temple of Dibella, an arena and mud bathhouses in a labyrinth of cramped streets. Most buildings stand along Blackwood Way because it is the only dry ground through the town.

Majority Lukiul Argonians who speak Cyrodiilic, trade with outsiders and hold apart from Argonian philosophy, beside Nibenese-descended families two centuries settled. Archein families survive as landholders and clerks. About 90 people live in the walls; Khajiit and Bosmer traders pass through.

In 4E 201 the council still sits in the Governor's Mansion and the courthouse still hears cases, because Gideon has a long tradition of keeping paper records. The town denies the successor state's claim over it and trades with the Archwardens only for what it must. The Blackwood Road to Leyawiin carries traffic except in the worst of the monsoon.
Ghosts and restless dead haunt the ruin itself; the huts are safe enough, but the track north to the castle is not walked after dark.
Guiding, scavenged stone and iron from the castle walls, eels and herbs sold at Gideon's gate. The ruin once housed a lord and a prison. It now holds nothing of value.
They leave Dibella offerings at a roadside shrine for the dead of the castle, and keep Sithis's name for the nights when something moves on the rise.
Calvus Vanin was the first lord; Empress Tavia was held here from 1E 2899. The castle fell to ruin. By the modern era it is described as haunted. The name now belongs to the hamlet.
Empress Tavia's cell, a locked records room, a ghost that wants a name carved in the courthouse, and digging crews who go in and do not all come out.
Grey, root-split castle walls on a low mound, a dozen huts below on stilts, a plank causeway to Gideon's gate and lamps burning all night.
Castle Giovesse was the Imperial ducal seat above Gideon and the prison of Empress Tavia; the ruin stands on a rise, and a hamlet of a few families has grown at its foot.
Poor Lukiul Argonian families and a few Nibenese diggers, led by an old woman who keeps the ruin's door-keys from the days when it was closed.
About nine people live in lean-to huts on stilts, a few more in season. They sell guided walks to the ruin, tend small yam beds and pay Gideon a gate-toll for the right to shelter under its guard.
Safe in town; the roads are wild and Paatru camps lie west of the river.
Salt, iron and herbs for river fish and clay; a caravan yard; river boats for the Onkobra line.
A Dibella wayside shrine and a Naka-Desh chime post where riddle-games are played.
Gul-Tej is a Project Tamriel name with no canon page; it grew along the Onkobra line that canon runs east from Gideon, as the Gideon-side market for the river tribes.
A riddle contest with a prize, a trade dispute over salt, a caravan that has not come.
A plank market on a river fork, reed-thatched stalls, red mud, boats tied in rows and chimes on the eaves.
A town of stilt houses and a plank market on a river fork north-east of Gideon, the last settled stop before the Naka-Desh river stations. It is Gideon's eastern gate to the interior.
Lukiul traders, Naka-Desh fishers who trade osheeja gar for salt and iron, and a few Nibenese herb dealers.
About twenty people live here; a market council of traders settles disputes. The Archwardens' tax-farmers visit twice a year; Gideon's council is the real authority.
D2: the village is peaceful but the wilderness behind it is full of predators.
Sap, smoked fish, hides and feathers; they buy salt and cloth from Thorn.
They keep the Hist's word by custom: eggs are laid in a root hollow near the village and the dead returned to the roots.
The Root-Folk have kept stations at the edge of the jungle since before the Empire; the Archeins taxed it, and the Archwardens now ignore it.
A clutch of eggs that will not hatch and a headwoman who needs a tree-minder from Tsonac, and a smuggler's raft tied up in the reeds.
Reed-roofed stilt houses joined by rope bridges, drying racks, dugouts on the mud, and thick jungle behind.
A small Argonian stilt hamlet on the bay's southern shore, one of the Root-Folk's outposts at the eastern edge of the jungle. UESP has no page for Guxal.
Saxhleel Argonians, a headwoman and her kin; they have no quarrel with the sky-blue Stone-Sleepers and a mutual dislike of Thorn's field-owners.
Eight or so live there, hunting, tapping sap and tending a clutch of eggs; they sell to the Thorn market.

UESP calls the city's alleys both wonderful and dangerous and its guard reportedly dangerous. The danger is social: a levy that is not accountable to strangers, assembly politics and a sour-spring cycle that the assembly will not discuss. Past the city every approach is deep swamp.

Helstrom does not trade outward; it receives and redistributes, because the rivers all drain to it. Rootworm and raft traffic, the Panther River fork and pilgrimage to the Root Talk feed it, and its market sells Murkwood feathers, sap, eggs and river fish.

The Hist, above all. Helstrom's city tree and its tree-minders matter more than any office, and the Root Talk, the occasion at which the Hist's alignment becomes audible to all the tribes, is held here in the holy month Hist-Tsoko. Sithis is honoured quietly; the Nine have no temple.

Helstrom was already active in the late First Era, during the Blackwater War. After the defeat at the Battle of Argonia in 1E 2811 the native armies retreated here. The Empire refused to follow. It never besieged the city. In 1E 2836 the Argonians simply stopped fighting. In the Third Era it became an incorporated city-state. Settlements were built around it by the fourth century. The Umbriel storm of 4E 48 passed it by.

A stranger can be stranded here and rescued by an Agaceph raftsman; the assembly will not time its sour spring in open session; the Root Talk draws every naheesh in the interior; and the ring of drowned Third Era villages holds the first settlers' abandoned goods.

Stilt and root-hollow houses of reed, mud and living wood, with no stone and no outward wall, because the marsh is the wall. Black Heart-Mud pools between the roots, the air is thick and warm, and rafts and plank walks thread the districts.

Helstrom is one of Black Marsh's eight great cities, in the reputedly inhospitable middle of the province, and many call it the immortal capital of the Argonians. It is the formal seat of the Archwardens' successor state and the meeting place of the Root Talk, though it is run by its own people, not by any distant government.

Overwhelmingly Argonian, drawn from the interior's exclusive breeds: Agaceph on tail-poled rafts, with Paatru and Naga visitors, and a very small licensed outsider presence of perhaps a few dozen. The guard is a tribal levy answerable to the assembly, not to strangers.

In 4E 201 Helstrom is intact and the least Imperialised city in the province. The state's formal seat is lodged here and largely ignored. The assembly of naheesh and tree-minders decides by consensus. A half-swallowed ring of Third Era villages lies on its approaches.
D2: the hamlet is peaceful but its illusionists test strangers.
Books, illusion work, fish and rare reeds.
They follow the Hist but are scholars; they keep books taken from dead missions.
A hamlet founded as the Agaceph spread along the mesa's rivers.
An Agaceph reader wants a book from a drowned mission, and a spell-frozen traveller stands in a doorway.
Stilt houses on slender posts, raft racks, bright painted shutters and a shelf of salvaged books.
A hamlet of the Agaceph, the canon Middle Argonian breed that is not a camp people. UESP has no page for Hirecan.
Agaceph with rainbow scales, readers and illusionists, wary of strangers and quick to freeze an intruder with a spell.
Eight Agaceph live there; they ride their thin rafts to Icalca and Yulca.
Fleshflies and death hoppers in the reeds; the road north is closed in monsoon; strangers are watched, though not harmed.
Ferrying, reed-thatch, smoked eel and a trade in herbs for Gideon's dealers; caravan drivers pay for the one dry sleeping platform on the road.
A small Sithis shrine on a raft that moves with the village; Dibella charms hang from the ferry post.

The Argonian Account mentions Hixinoag on the northern road in the Imperial era. The village outlasted the Empire, since its rafts moved and collectors seldom found it. After 4E 48 it took in survivors from the plantation country.
A raft that has drifted off its mooring with a passenger aboard, a caravan with a sealed crate, or a feud over the same channel claimed by two clans.
Tiered stilt huts, reed rafts roped end to end, black water, crows on the roof-poles and a long causeway of laid planks running out to the road.

A village of stilt houses and tethered rafts on the northern caravan road above Gideon. Canon calls it a drifting village; the community moves house-rafts along the channels as the flood rises and falls.
Lukiul and Naka-Desh families, headed by a river-headwoman who judges disputes over rafts and channel rights.

About ten people keep a ferry and a rest-house for caravans. They bargain with the Archein landholders for reed rights and with Gideon for salt. They ignore the Archwardens' collectors, who seldom find the village in the same place twice.
Surf, crabs and smugglers who sometimes land on the shingle at night.
Nets, rope and cord of coast-grass, sold at Seafalls.
They hang votive cords on the fence, one for every wreck.
Built by a net-mender who preferred quiet to the village.
The old net-mender once wove a net for a smuggler and knows his boat; she will tell a friend.
A single stilt house at the tide line, nets spread on the fence, a tarred boat on the shingle.
A solitary house above the shore between the farms and the sea. The name is ours; no UESP page.
Two Argonians, an old net-mender and her niece.
A quiet house; the household sells nets and rope to Seafalls.
Illusions that freeze, confuse or misdirect strangers; lake crocodiles and the bandits Icalca keeps out.
Books, scrolls and illusion-work are sold or swapped. Fish and lake-grain keep the hamlet fed.
They hold a weak respect for the Hist. They read the Maran books for amusement.
In canon the Agaceph looted the dead Maran monastery at Umpholo for its books. Their hamlets hold such books. Icalca keeps a shelf of them.
The hamlet needs a book returned that a Gaweja fisher took. A Maran monastery tract in Icalca's shelf names a ruin that has not been found.
Raft-houses lashed together on a blue-green lake, reed screens painted in bright scale-colours, long thin rafts hauled onto mats.
An Agaceph hamlet on a lake in Okuwun-Rahei's west. No UESP page for Icalca; the Agaceph are canon in Middle Argonia.
About eight Agaceph with rainbow scales, needle-faced, riding razor-thin rafts; the eldest reads three languages.
A hamlet of raft-houses and stilts, bounded by reed screens. The Agaceph keep to their lake and sell books and illusions to those who ask politely.
D2: the flooded cellar is the main risk, with snakes in the wall-gaps and a squatters' lookout on the north wall. Rotten floor timbers give way without warning near the old armoury.

The Legion built it as a road post between Karketa and Lilmoth, with a toll bar and a signal brazier, and its toll roll is long lost. Salvagers now strip the iron fittings and the brick for the village huts.
No Hist grows here, and the chapel niche in the east wall is empty of its Nine icon, though candle stubs show someone still lights it. The squatters call the yard unlucky and do not sleep inside.
Built by the Legion as a road post; abandoned when the Empire's hold failed and the garrison fled.
A flooded armoury with something left in a locked cage; a squatter who wants a letter delivered.
A low square fort of stone and brick, the wall broken at one corner, green with vines.
Fort Sallowmoth is a low square fort of stone and brick, its wall broken at one corner and green with vines. Squatters hold the roofless yard.
Fort Sallowmoth has no residents, but squatters keep a watch from the roofless yard and smugglers pass through. Karketa's villagers know the faces and say little to strangers.
Roofless; the walls stand, the cellar is flooded; squatters use the yard.
D2: the sea-cave floods on the tide and traps the unwary, while snakes nest in the tower rubble. Smugglers who guard the cache attack strangers without warning.
The Company built it to tax coasting vessels and signal storms to Lilmoth, with a shed for bonded goods. Scavengers now carry off the lamp brackets and brick, and smugglers keep their cache below.
There is no Hist and no shrine, only a rusted iron ring in the shed wall where the customs men hung a charm to Julianos. Fishers touch it as they shelter.
Built to tax coasting vessels, abandoned when the Company left.
A smugglers' cache in the sea-cave beneath; a ledger of old duties.
A low brick shed, a toppled signal tower, a rusted iron lamp bracket.
Brackwater Waystation is a low brick shed with a toppled signal tower beside it and a sea-cave beneath. Smugglers use the cave.
Brackwater Waystation has no residents, but smugglers use the sea-cave and fishers from Nundi stop in the shed during squalls. Both groups know the sea-cave and do not discuss it.
The tower has fallen; the shed's walls stand, with a sea-cave beneath.
Outlaws, marsh predators and flooded cellars.
A source of salvage; once a toll station.
None surviving.
Built by the Empire as a road post, abandoned after 4E 48; no garrison since.
A hidden Imperial strongbox; a smugglers' meeting.
A broken stone tower and wall on a mud rise, creepers over its Imperial crest.
A tumbled Imperial waystation whose name follows the Legion's '-moth' naming.
Passing outlaws.
Empty; outlaws and scavengers use it.
D3: bandits with a leader and a lookout hold the shell, and the burnt floors fall away underfoot. The garrison's patrols avoid it, so the approach along the island road is unwatched.
Built as an outlier to Fort Reedmoth, it once held a small customs post and a stockpile of signal fuel. Now the bandits sell what they find in the char to dealers on the island road.
The burnt shrine of the Nine is only blackened stone on a plinth, and the bandits spit on it for luck. Reedmoth's garrison calls the ruin cursed and will not patrol its walls.
Built as the Reedmoth's outlier; burnt out in the last years of the Empire's hold.
A bandit leader with a price on his head; the burnt records room.
A burnt shell of a fort, charred timbers, stone footings.
Fort Lowmoth is a burnt shell of charred timbers and stone footings, built as an outlier of Fort Reedmoth. Road bandits hold it.
Fort Lowmoth has no residents, but the bandits who use it as a lair post watchers on the island road. Villagers from Sal-Axan and the Tal-Neesh farm pay them in rice and do not argue.
Black with old fire, collapsed, used by road bandits as a lair.
Smugglers and sea-birds.
It was a south-shore watch post and signal tower for the Imperial coast, left when the Empire fell; it now draws scavengers after worked stone and brass, and the odd smuggler.
A chipped Imperial Divines' niche in the tower base holds a rain-filled bowl, and Xal-Tarek's men do not touch it.
Built as a coast watch; abandoned in the Fourth Era.
A smugglers' signal lamp; a hidden Imperial log.
A broken stone tower on a rise.
Mistwatch is a broken stone tower on a rise, with a chipped Divines' niche at its base. Smugglers use it.
Mistwatch has no residents. Xal-Tarek's patrols pass by, and sea-wreckers sometimes light a fire in the tower stump.
Empty; smugglers use it.
D2: wildlife.
Once a border watch; now stripped.
A small shrine niche of the Divines is cut into the tower base, empty now. The Hutan-Tzel do not touch it.
Reasoned: built by the Third Empire to watch the border.
A courier's satchel in the rubble.
A broken tower and wall in a thicket.
An unnamed Imperial ruin named by us. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
Aldanus Watchtower has no residents. Hutan-Veel scouts climb it for the view and sleep rough in its yard when they range south.
A stump of a tower and a wall in a thicket.
Bandits hold it, with archers on the tower top who watch the road. The granary floor is rotten and the cellar hides traps set by smugglers.
A waystation for couriers and carts, with a granary to feed them. Now it earns a living only for the bandits who rob the road below, and for scavengers after the iron nails of its door.
The waystation kept a small shrine to the Nine in the tower's lowest room, and a statue of Zenithar stood by the granary. Both are broken, though a Gideon traveller sometimes leaves a coin.

Nine Reeds Waystation was built in the late Third Era on the road north of Gideon, a stone tower with a granary and a signal-fire platform for travellers and couriers. The Imperial officers who held it left after 4E 48 and no one replaced them.
A legion pay-chest, a forged road-pass or a bandit leader holding the tower.
A square stone tower with a fallen roof, a granary block at its foot and a hearth platform on the top where the signal fire stood. Nine tall reeds grow in a ring where the well was.
A ruined Imperial waystation in the Nha Enasa, on the road north of Gideon: a stone tower with a granary and a signal fire.
The tower is uninhabited. A band of road-bandits holds it by turns with a gang of smugglers. Gideon's guard looks in only when a caravan goes missing.
The tower is empty and open to the weather. Bandits who rob caravans on the Gideon road use it as a bolt-hole, and smugglers store goods in its dry cellar.
Outlaws and predators.
It was a fort on the north coast of the cape, guarding the Topal Bay road; its stone and timber now draw Naxan builders and scavengers after Legion iron.
A weathered Imperial standard-shrine at the gate has lost its image. Naxan fishermen leave a shell on the sill for the soldiers who died here.
A Legion '-moth' fort abandoned after the Empire's fall.
An Imperial strongroom; outlaws' stash.
Stone walls grown over with creepers.
Wrackmoth is a flooded fort of stone walls grown over with creepers. It once guarded the Topal Bay road.
Wrackmoth has no residents. Naxan fishermen shelter in its gate on stormy nights, and scavengers camp in its yard.
Empty and flooded.
Smugglers armed with crossbows watch the pier, and the tower's lean makes its stair dangerous. Crocodiles wait under the pier at the tide.
A watch on the delta approaches, paid for out of Gideon's harbour dues. Now it works as a mooring and drop-point for smugglers, and the iron of its door and grille is prised away for scrap.
The watch kept a small Akatosh candle-niche in the tower stair for the night watch. The niche is cold now. The garrison's Imperial altar is long gone.

Gideon South Watch was built in the Third Era on the mangrove edge south of Gideon, a watch tower to see boats approaching through the delta. It lost its garrison when the Empire pulled out of the province after 4E 48.
A watchman's ledger, a hidden cellar or Gideon's guard wanting it cleared.
A round stone watch-tower that leans on a mud bank, with a broken lantern room on top and green weed around its base. A rotted pier runs out into the channel.
A ruined Imperial watch tower in the Kotherra Mangroves, on the south side of Gideon, built to watch the delta approaches.
The tower is uninhabited. Smugglers meet their buyers at the tower's foot. Gideon's patrol boats come by now and then to move them on.
The tower is unheld and half sunk in mud. Smugglers who bring goods up through the delta channels moor beneath it, and a few bandits use its top room to watch for guard patrols.
Wind and a loose parapet make the climb risky. The smugglers will not welcome visitors, and bay crabs and sea-birds crowd the rocks around its base.
A signal post for the bay's shipping, kept by Imperial dues. Today its main value is as a lookout for smugglers and a source of dressed stone for fishers' huts.
Sailors who wait out a storm on the isle leave a knot of rope on the tower door for Kynareth and for safe sailing.
Aphon Signal Tower stands on the high ground of Aphon Isle, paired with the Belvedere to give an unbroken fire-line along the bay. It was built in the Third Era, and after 4E 48 no one kept the lamp.
A signal lamp with a code, a pirate lookout or a lost message-chest.
A tall tower of grey stone on a bare rock crest, with the lamp-room blackened by old fires and a stair that winds up outside the wall. Gulls nest in its broken parapet.
A ruined Imperial signal tower on the high ground of Aphon Isle, paired with Aphon Belvedere to watch the bay.
The tower is uninhabited. Sea-smugglers keep a small band at the tower in the fishing season. Aphon's fishers pass it without a word.
The tower is unheld, a landmark for fishing boats rounding the isle. Smugglers who work the bay use its top as a lookout and keep a cache in the base.
D2: wildlife and the odd thief; fleshflies in the heat.
Once a waystation for the Legion's couriers; now stripped of any metal.
None; Imperial shrines had no Hist and left a plinth only.
Built by the Third Empire as a staging post on the road toward Morrowind; abandoned when the Legion withdrew.
A hoard hidden in the plinth by a Legion courier; a scavenger who wants a witness.
A low stone wall and arch in a field of reeds; a plinth with a worn Imperial eagle.
An unnamed Imperial ruin on the northern road, named by us in the Imperial manner. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
None resident; passing scavengers.
Roofless, with a standing gate arch and wall; scavengers sleep in its corners.
Safe by day. Slaughterfish and mud-crabs in the channel; high water closes the ferry for days.
Ferry fares in coin or goods, fish and a small trade in spare poles, rope and lamp oil. Passing cargo is quietly noted for the elder.
They tie a feather to the ferry rope at each crossing to ask the water for passage; hatching families walk to Uluo.
The hamlet grew around a raft crossing used by Cyrodiilic and Company traders; the Company's road is gone but the crossing is older than it. Records of it are oral.
Stranded travellers who need escorting round a flooded channel; a ferryman who knows who crossed unseen last night.
Six raft-houses on pole stilts either side of the channel, a long guide-rope between two stump posts, lanterns on poles and boats pulled onto mud.
A hamlet at the point where the road from Archon toward the north crosses a wide channel. The raft ferry here is the reason it exists.
Three Waters Argonians; the ferry-master is chosen by the elder at Uluo. Travellers from Archon, Aroxhu and the north pass daily.
Eight or so raft-families run the ferry in turns, tell travellers the state of the water, and keep a lamp lit for night crossings.
Safe in the town. Pickpockets, a few Naga road-robbers working alone on the river road, and floods that cut the crossing for days.
Clay, pottery and dye are sold in bulk; Inoja takes a market toll and runs the river ferry. Aroxhu's elders limit the prices.
Small clay shrines to the dead line the market; the Hist of Aroxhu is the town's tree, and its sap-gatherers walk there once a season.
