Grew from a ferry crossing at a river fork into the confederacy's market. The Aroxhu elders do not want strangers inside their mounds, and Inoja is a day's walk away.
A buyer from Thorn has paid for a barge of pots that never arrived. The river ferryman saw something at night but will only tell a friend.
Terraced mounds along the river, a broad market-ground with reed awnings and stacks of pots in red and brown, a rope ferry and stilted inns over the water.
A town of about twenty on the river fork where roads from Aroxhu, Arorha and the southern villages meet. It is where outsiders deal with the confederacy. No UESP page for Inoja exists.
About twenty-one Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel: factors, boatmen, ferrymen and inn-keepers, with a handful of visiting Dunmer and Khajiit.
A busy dry-season market. Dunmer clay-buyers from Thorn, Okuwun boatmen and now and then a Khajiit trader bargain here. The elders rule disputes between buyers and sellers.
D1: the town is quiet. Its own wardens patrol. Off the road, crocodiles in the weir channels, and looters and Naga brigands on the track toward the ruins.

Reed mats, rope, boats and dried fish sold to Stormhold; weir fees from the fish traps on the creeks. The town also guards the ruins of Gemin, Nenria and Loriasel against looters, paid in kind by Stormhold's guild halls.
A Hist tree in a pool at the heart of the town, tended by a tree-minder; hatchlings come here. The Veesa-Teeleel hold the Barsaebic ruins to be sick ground and teach children not to touch them.

No canon history. Reasoned: a Hist pool and sedge beds on high ground in an area ringed by Barsaebic ruins would have been settled early by Argonians; the Dunmer slave-raids of the Dres period came through this border country and are remembered here.

A looter caught with Ayleid goods and the elders' refusal to hand him to Stormhold; a weir warden who sees lights at Nenria at night; the Hist pool's tree-minder asking the player to carry a message to the Root-Folk.
Pale reed-thatched stilt houses on a ring of mud banks around a pool, boat-lanes between them cut through the sedge, mats drying on racks, fish racks smoking on the road side.

Jal-Veesa is the one town of the Veesa-Teeleel, the northern Argonians of the valleys between Stormhold and the Barsaebic ruins. UESP has no page for it (searched 2026-11-08); it is a Project Tamriel name, placed on the road west of Stormhold.
Veesa-Teeleel Argonians, courteous to Dunmer without trusting them. Elders and a tree-minder at the pool; a few Stormhold factors lodge in the market season.

A town of stilt houses and reed jetties on a Hist pool. The elders settle disputes themselves and refuse the Vicecanons' courts, but send men to the frontier screen for pay and trade every day with Stormhold.
Safe for the tribes' friends; strangers from the coast are questioned and sometimes held. Outlying posts are hostile.
Fishing, mine-metal salvage, a toll on every Soulrest Argonian who comes inland to hatch, name or bury and trade with Kharaxos.
Sithis and the nearest Hist to Soulrest, which the town guards; burning is a rite, and the burned mine-mouths are shrines.
The tribes of the basin burned the Imperial mines and timber concessions in 3E 427 and never reconciled to the coast. Jarecai grew as their council town; the name has no canon page.
A Soulrest Argonian who must hatch before the season ends, a mine-burning trial or the council's price for a pass.
Tiered timber halls on stilts, a palisade of burned stakes, black-scorched mine timbers used as posts, boats at every landing and smoke over the water.
A fortified town on stilts over the Banujha waters, the seat of the basin tribes. It is the political centre of the people who cut Soulrest off from its hinterland.
Mine-Burner Argonians, council elders and war-leaders; no Imperial-descended family lives here, and ex-Imperial administrators from Soulrest are unwelcome.
About 28 people live in tiered halls behind a palisade of stakes; the elders judge disputes, tax Soulrest's pilgrims and hold the hatching grounds as a lever on the port.
Pit collapses, crocodiles in the river mouth and Sarpa raiders from the west who come for tools.
Fine red clay dug in blocks and floated down the river to Inoja and Aroxhu. Joxhi clay fires to a deep brick-red that sells for double.
The village sends its eggs to Aroxhu. Diggers leave a clay figure in the pit for any lost to a collapse.
Its clay pit was found by a hatchling of the first Inoja families and has been dug for generations; the village is built on its own spoil.
A new seam of pale clay turned up in the pit that glows faintly at night; the elder wants to know what it is. An old Velothi tablet has come up in the spoil.
A village on stilted mounds beside a river bend, raw red pits edged by reed fencing, drying clay in blocks, an orange-stained river.
A village beside a river bend in the northern mounds, known for its pits. No UESP page for Joxhi.
About ten Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel, mostly diggers and carriers; the elder is a former potter who still tests every cart.
A working village, wary of the tribal camps to the west and of Thorn's buyers who offer too much.
A Naga band hunts the delta shallows; crocodiles in the braid; the ferry is the weak point.
Saltrice, a ferry toll across the braid, and small trade with Helstrom's outposts for sap and eggs.
Hist and Sithis at a little roadside tree; the Dunmer grandmother still tends a household Ancestor shrine.
Nothing is recorded. A Stormhold-style farm outpost this far inland is read as a settlement by families who left the northern river after 4E 48 and brought the habit of stone footings with them.
The ferry-rope has been cut twice; a cairn on the nearest firm bank has been opened; a salt trader's body washed up at the paddies.
Low stone footings with reed-and-mud walls, a causeway of laid stone out to the ferry post, flat rice paddies fenced with reed, and the lake's wide grey sheet beyond.
Julo is a hamlet of about six people at the delta where Helstrom's waters spread into the lake. It follows the Stormhold manner of raised stone footings and causeways; the name has no UESP page.
About six residents, Argonian farmers with one Dunmer-descended grandmother who keeps the ledgers.
In 4E 201 it holds a small saltrice patch and a ferry. It pays an annual tribute of rice to Helstrom's levy and keeps good terms with the Root-Folk outposts upstream.
Gar in the channel, bandit boats at night, and drowning under the stilts.
Fish traps, boat hulls and the channel toll.

Ka-Asei has no tree of its own, so its minder sends each clutch by lake barge to the Blackrose Hist and keeps a ledger of names on knotted cords under the longhouse eaves. Mourners tie a reed to a stilt for every death. The posts at the channel mouth are covered with reeds.
It grew from a fishing platform to a village as the Delta Ferry trade rose in the Fourth Era.
A stolen boat, a hidden cargo under the platforms, or a fisher's feud with Amalaja.
Houses on tall stilts joined by rope bridges, boats moored below, nets drying on the walkways.
A water-village on stilts in the channel southeast of the island core, on the route to Amalaja and the delta.
Argonian fishers and boat-builders.
It pays the island core a channel toll and takes its patrol boat's visits.
D3: flu-dead undead in the lower halls, loose stone and falling masonry.
Once a mason town; now a quarry of dressed stone for Tsonac and a source of Velothi goods.
Mephala is the god the Cantemiric Velothi followed by the Chimeri story; some shrine marks may stand.
Settled by Dunmer dissidents in the First or Second Era and emptied by the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560-603; the Hist have not claimed the ground.
A mason from Tsonac asks for a lost trowel-seal from the cellars; the hermit herbalist wants a patient brought to her.
Squared Dunmer stone, curved roof ribs under vine, a central well and a stair into the mesa.
A ruin of the Cantemiric Velothi, the Dunmer settlers of the eastern coast. UESP has no page for Kaochalit; the Velothi settlement of the country is canon.
No residents; travellers report a hermit Dunmer herbalist living in a tomb at its edge.
Roofless stone houses on the mesa edge, the dead in their halls; Tsonac's quarrymen take dressed stone from its outer wall.
D1: sea-drake sightings beyond the reef, storms and cutpurses on the Lilmoth road.
Fresh and salted fish, sea salt, boat repair and ferry service to the northern island.
They go to Lilmoth's third Hist for hatching and keep a small prayer-post for the drowned.
An old coast village on Lilmothiit ground, kept as the road to the Southwatch watch-tower grew; it lost nothing to Umbriel's storm but sent people to Lilmoth's rebuilding.
A boat lost beyond the reef with a villager's father aboard; a salt pan seized by a Lilmoth creditor.
Stilt houses on grey pilings facing the sea, drying racks, salt pans and a long jetty with a tower lamp.
A coastal village on the road between Lilmoth and Southwatch Keep, in the Lilmoth coast's orbit.
Argonians of the Lilmoth coast; the headwoman's family has kept the boats for generations.
Twelve households net, salt fish and keep boats, paying Lilmoth's council a tithe of the catch.
Safe in town; war-bands are heavily armed and the east road is wild.
Salvaged mine metal, fish and a river market.
Sithis and Hist; burned-timber posts mark graves.
The name is older than the tribes and was kept on the maps; the Mine-Burners did not bother to change it.
A metal dispute, a war-band muster or a Chime-Keeper wedding.
Dark timber halls on stilts, a black-scorched palisade, tin chimes from Oeneas on the market posts.
A fortified town of stilt halls on the basin's eastern shore, the tribes' gateway to the Chime-Keepers' towns toward Blackrose.
Mine-Burner Argonians and some Chime-Keeper traders from Oeneas.
About 22 people live here. It is a trade stop for metal and fish and a muster point for the basin's war-bands.
Marsh predators and a Blackguard watch post that has been seen at night.
What it was: a chime-maker's town on the Ka-Asei channel. Now its stone footings and metal draw scavengers.
The Chime-Keepers' tin and glass chimes still hang in the dead town's central tree, rung only by wind. The minder's shrine beneath them is dry. It has not been visited since the town emptied.
A Kothringi town before 2E 560; resettled by Argonians; emptied in the 4E 48 catastrophe.
Chimes that ring with no wind; a chime-maker's stash under the footings.
Stone footings under collapsed stilt houses, tin chimes rusting in the reeds.
Khariton is a dozen rotted stilt houses on stone footings, with tin chimes rusting in the reeds. It stood on the Ka-Asei channel.
Khariton is uninhabited. Brushmound hunters shelter under its few sound roofs in the dry season, and scavengers strip the last pegs from its stilt halls.
A dozen stilt houses on stone footings stand rotted, chimes still hung from some eaves.
D3: undead of the flu-dead, pit traps and scavenger crews who guard their finds; it is dark and cold below.
It was a settlement of masons and farmers; now it is a quarry of cut stone and a source of old Velothi goods for Thorn's markets.
Cantemiric Velothi followed Mephala, according to the Chimeri story; some shrine marks may remain. The Hist hold the ground to be sick.
The Velothi settled the coast between the First Era and the Second. The Knahaten Flu of 2E 560-603 killed every non-Argonian in the province, the Velothi among them.
A Thorn merchant's debtor says a plague chest is stored in the lower halls, and a scavenger crew has gone silent.
Dunmer-style stone houses with curved roof ribs, half buried in vine, a cracked central plaza and a stair down to the lower halls.
A ruin of the Cantemiric Velothi, the Dunmer dissident settlers of the eastern seaboard around Thorn, Archon and Arnesia. UESP has no page for Kharraluhl; the people are canon.
No residents. A scavenger crew camps among the walls at times, and a handful of Dunmer pilgrims leave offerings for ancestors they do not know.
Roofless, overgrown and picked over by Thorn's scavengers; the lower halls are cut into the slope and still hold what the scavengers have not reached.
Surf, crocodiles at the inlet, and Mazurath's ghosts on the headland.
Dried and salted fish, shell-fish and boat-timber; they trade fish for clay goods and for Seafalls pearls.
The village sends eggs inland. Fishermen leave a clay fish at the cape for good catches.
Founded as a fishing station to feed the mound country, then grew into a village. The Mazurath ruin on the next headland is older than the village.
The boat-wright is building a ship for a stranger who paid in old Velothi bronze. The headland ruin has started to glow after dark.
Reed houses on stilts on a low rise above a sandy cape, nets and fish-racks on every pole, a stone breakwater of piled clay, salt wind.
A cape village south of Seafalls, the confederacy's southern coastal outlier. No UESP page for Khiar.
About nine Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel; fishermen, net-makers and an old boat-wright.
A steady fishing village. Its boats go out at dawn and sell to Seafalls; its people dislike the Skeith smugglers' habit of landing at the cape.
Ancestor ghosts within, crabs and hackwings on the beach, and a sinkhole in the courtyard that goes down to the sea cave beneath.
Once a watch-hold that signalled the Velothi's boats. Now a landmark for blockade-runners and a source of ash-glass shards that wash up on the beach below.
Velothi ancestor shrine niches line the inner hall. The ghosts of the hold's household remain at their posts.

Cantemiric Velothi built along the eastern seaboard between Archon and Thorn and died in the Knahaten Flu (2E 560). Kornakim's position on a seaward point suggests a watch-hold over the sea lanes, which is our reading, not canon.

A signal brazier at the top of the tower still holds a spell-lit fire that has never been put out. A smuggler's cache is hidden in the sea cave beneath the hall, left behind by a crew that did not come back.
Dark Velothi stonework in low rounded courses with a broken watch-tower at the seaward end, sand drifting into the courtyard, sea-grass growing through the floor, surf loud against the headland.
A ruined Velothi coastal hold on the headland at the bight's seaward edge. UESP has no page for Kornakim; the map names it and the Cantemiric Velothi are canon for this coast.
The ruin has no residents. It is known to the Skeith smugglers as a landmark and to the Arorha clay-men as a place not to dig.
Roofless but standing. A smuggler's lantern sometimes burns on the headland, though the smugglers do not go inside.
The town itself is safe: its elders hold watch and its ring of water keeps predators out. Beyond the channel lie Ultherus swamp with its dragon's-tongue, Tumnatu hunters and deep-water predators.

It makes tuned chimes, metal-woven rope and shallow-draft sail-and-paddle boats, and trades them up the channels to Helstrom, Truowa and Blackrose for tin, copper, sap and dragon's-tongue gathered in the swamp.
Sithis and the Hist beside a quiet regard for Z'en, the Kothringi god of toil, and Dibella, kept at a small chime-hung shrine. The town's tree-minder tends a village tree where eggs are laid.

A Kothringi town until the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560 emptied it. Argonians, immune to the flu, moved into the empty houses and kept the old name because it belonged to the place. Over the centuries they added Kothringi habits that the Hist did not forbid. The 4E 48 nativists called them half-foreign.
A Kothringi cairn bead-trove under the oldest footings; a chime that rings with no wind; the guild elders' dispute over who may tune the Hist-shrine chime; a boatwright who needs rare Ultherus herbs.

Stilt houses on stone footings, a Kothringi habit; chimes of tin and copper hung from every eave; a market square on the ring of ground; boats moored three deep in the surrounding channel. The air hums with metal.

Korydon is a market town of about two dozen households on a ring of dry ground surrounded by water, the chief of the Kothringi-named towns of the Ultherus country. The name is a Kothringi one, kept by the Argonians who moved in; no source describes the place itself.
About 22 residents, nearly all Argonian with a few mixed families. Chime-smiths, rope-weavers, boat-wrights, a tin broker and the elders; a few families keep a stone cairn for the old Kothringi dead.

In 4E 201 Korydon is the most orderly town in the interior, run by a council of guild elders, cold toward the Archwardens and warm toward Gideon. Its chimes ring from every eave and mark the hours, the water level and the weather.
The dead are said to play the hall at night, and its columns are toppling one by one. Mine-Burner watchers shoot at anyone carrying off chimes.
A hall of music and festival. Today its columns' bronze chime-fittings are prised off for scrap, and a few chimes of fine Kothringi tuning are carried away as curiosities.
Music was the Kothringi's prayer to Dibella and Kynareth, and the columns were tuned so that the wind would sing for both. Mine-Burner tribesmen do not enter the hall, out of respect.

Kyrenos was a music-hall of the Kothringi, a long building whose columns held rows of chimes tuned in a scale. The hall fell silent when the Flu of 2E 560 killed its players, and the Mine-Burner tribes later passed it by when they burned the mines.
A tuned set of chimes that sounds only at dusk, a Mine-Burner who guards the hall, or a Chime-Keeper claim to the stones.
A long hall of tall stone columns open to the sky, each with an iron arm at the top where the chimes once hung. A few chimes still turn in the wind and the floor is covered in drifted leaves.
A ruin of the Kothringi, the silver-skinned humans of the Blackwood who died of the Knahaten Flu in 2E 560. It is a long music-hall whose columns once held rows of chimes.
The hall is uninhabited. The Mine-Burner watchers sometimes shelter in the porch. The occasional bard from Gideon makes the walk to hear the columns sing.
The hall is unheld. It stands on dry ground on the north edge of the Banujha Basin, and Mine-Burner watchers from the nearby posts know it as a place where the wind still sounds the chimes.
Restless dead rise from the oldest cairns at night, and Sul-Xan diggers work the south side. At D3 the diggers are the greater danger by day.
Once a craft town of glass beads and moonstone. Treasure-diggers now work it, as do the Sul-Xan raiders who come for the cairns.
The Kothringi honoured Z'en, Dibella, Mara and Kynareth and their cairns still hold bead strings. Naka-Desh chimes hang in a single thorn tree beside the largest cairn.

Meliton was a Kothringi town in the western hills that the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560 left empty, part of a homeland that once held many such towns. Its Kothringi name is on the map; the dead were laid in the cairns outside it.
A cairn with a humming doll the Naka-Desh will not discuss, and a Sul-Xan trench a Hutan-Aru elder wants filled.
Rings of stone footings on a hill, cairns heaped with glass beads and a chime-hung thorn tree at the centre. Hutan-Aru's smoke shows to the north.
A Kothringi ruin on the map at (-14,-71); named by us in the style of Kothringi towns such as Korydon and Toklea. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08); the Kothringi do.
The ruin has no residents. The Naka-Desh come on foot from the west in the dry months, and Hutan-Aru hunters leave them alone.
Cairns, footings and two standing walls on a hill-shoulder above Hutan-Aru, visited each year by the Naka-Desh who hang chimes in memory of their friends.
The planking is rotten and the slip drops away into deep water. Crocodiles lie below the quay in the shade of the boat-house.
A boatyard on the river trade between Gideon and the interior. Now it is a source of ship-timber and iron fittings, and the one place where the old Kothringi boat design can still be seen.
The Kothringi hung a Kynareth wind-chime from the quay's end to ask for fair wind, and the Naka-Desh still cut a small notch on the mooring stone for a safe journey. Nothing grander is kept.

Pelaxis was the Kothringi river quay and boat-house on the channel east of Gideon, where shallow-draft sail-and-paddle boats were built and repaired. When the Flu emptied it in 2E 560, the last boat was left half-planked on the slip.
A boat-builder's tools, a sunken boat with something aboard, or smugglers using the quay.
A stone quay with mooring posts sunk in the bank, a long boat-house with its roof half gone and a launching slip with a half-built hull still on it. Weed hangs from the quay edge.
A ruin of the Kothringi, the silver-skinned humans of the Blackwood who died of the Knahaten Flu in 2E 560. It is a river quay and a boat-house for shallow-draft Kothringi sail-and-paddle boats.
The quay is uninhabited. Naka-Desh fishers sleep under the boat-house roof in bad weather. Boatwrights from Gideon visit now and then to look at the Kothringi hull design.
The quay is unheld. A few Naka-Desh river-folk beach their boats against the old mooring stones, and diggers from Gideon come to see the abandoned slip.
Rain-soaked roof beams can drop without warning. Bog-wolves den in the back room and the Paatru will challenge strangers using the hearth.
A merchant-family's hall, once rich in goods carried up from the coast. Today it holds nothing but scavenged stone, though the rumour of a sealed strongroom keeps diggers coming.
The family honoured Kynareth for the winds that carried their ships, and the horn on the lintel is set above a wind-chime hook. The Paatru, who are not of that faith, leave a bone charm at the door.

Dorianth was the longhouse of a seafaring Kothringi family, the sort who sailed the coast and traded up the Nha Enasa channels. The leviathan-horn on its lintel was the family's mark, and no one of the family survived the Flu of 2E 560.
The horn itself, a family tomb or a haunting that follows the hall's old boat-song.
A long hall of pale stone with a carved leviathan horn over its doorway, a hearth at the end and a collapsed roof-beam across the middle. Reeds grow through the floor flags.

A ruin of the Kothringi, the silver-skinned humans of the Blackwood who died of the Knahaten Flu in 2E 560. It is a hall with a leviathan-horn carved on its lintel, the longhouse of a seafaring family.
The hall is uninhabited. Paatru hunters from the camps to the east use the hall's hearth during the rains. A Gideon scholar comes now and then to copy the lintel.
No one holds it. Its lintel stone is the one thing that draws visitors: Paatru and Naka-Desh both know it and use the hall as a shelter against the monsoon.
The dead of the terrace stir at night and the pool is deep with leeches. Naka-Desh watchers will shoot at a looter who disturbs the graves.
The terrace was the Kothringi's burial ground, so it never traded. Now it draws grave-robbers after the burial goods. The Naka-Desh keep it as a place of memory.

Each grave is marked with a stone and a chime-post, and the Kothringi hung tin and copper chimes there to speak to the dead. The Naka-Desh, friends of the Kothringi in life, keep the ring of posts in repair.

Mnemosa is a burial terrace of the Kothringi on the high ground of Nha Enasa, east of Gideon. The terrace was filled at the height of the Flu in 2E 560, so the stones carry far more names than the settlement ever had.
A burial offering a descendant wants returned, a dig that disturbed the dead, or a Naka-Desh riddle carved on the stones.
Stepped terraces of grave-stones set in a ring of weathered chime-posts, with the posts hung with green-crusted tin and copper. Reeds have taken the lowest step and a shallow pool sits in the middle.
A ruin of the Kothringi, the silver-skinned humans of the Blackwood who died of the Knahaten Flu in 2E 560. It is a terrace of burial stones with a ring of chime-posts.
The terrace is uninhabited. Naka-Desh come in pairs at the turn of the year to tend the chime-posts. Now and then a grave-robber from Gideon is found in the reeds.

No one holds it. The Naka-Desh treat it as a place to be visited, not lived in and paddle up from the channels to renew their chimes. Diggers who rob the terraces are driven off if the river-folk catch them.
Restless dead at the four cairns, and Sul-Xan raiders who dig from the stream side. At D3 the raiders come in the dark of the moon.
It was a craft town with beadwork and a pottery lane. Treasure-diggers and Cyrodilic relic-buyers from Nahk-Zeel Station now visit it.
The Kothringi's four powers are marked by four small cairns at the town's centre, each with a different colour of glass. Naka-Desh chimes hang from one tin frame.
Aithros was a Kothringi town in the far western hills, emptied by the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560 and never resettled. It lies a day south-west of Hutan-Veel, close to the Cyrodiil border.
A pottery heap with unbroken Kothringi bowls that a Nahk-Zeel buyer pays well for, and a raider who left his tools in the trench.
Stone footings in a loose ring around four coloured cairns, with a tin chime-frame and a pottery heap by the stream. The border road is a day to the north.
The map shows a Kothringi ruin at (-23,-76), close to the Cyrodiil border. We named it in the style of Kothringi towns such as Korydon and Toklea. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
The ruin has no residents. Naka-Desh come in small parties and Hixinoag villagers cut wood on the slope below without crossing it.
Footings, cairns and a few walls above a stream, visited in the dry months by Naka-Desh chime-hangers from the border road.

Mangrove crocodiles and mudcrabs lie in the channel at the landing, and the footing around the altar gives way under a heavy boot. Gideon's diggers say that ghost lights at dusk draw the careless into the pools.
It was a place of offerings, not of trade. Now the leaf-carved stone is prised out and carried to Gideon, and small gold and silver votives are still turned up in the root-mud.

The altar slab is Dibella's, and the leaf-and-wave carving on it is the Kothringi sign of her. Gideon's Nibenese bring flowers and wine to it, and the Naka-Desh hang tin chimes in the mangroves above.

Calyphe was a Dibella shrine of the Kothringi at the western end of the mangrove country, a few miles from the Gideon road. When the Knahaten Flu emptied the Blackwood in 2E 560 its keepers died untended, and the mangroves have grown through the floor since.
A buried offering-vault, a chime-keeper who guards the roots, or a Gideon digger hunting a Dibella relic.
Leaf-carved grey stone sunk to the lintels in black mud, with mangrove roots arched over the altar and the broken pillars. Chimes tick in the branches over it.
A ruin of the Kothringi, the silver-skinned humans of the Blackwood who died of the Knahaten Flu in 2E 560. It is a Dibella shrine of leaf-carved stone half sunk in mangrove roots.
The shrine is uninhabited. A Nibenese shrine-seeker from Gideon may leave an offering at the altar slab. The diggers keep a camp on the dry hummock beside it.
The shrine is unheld. Diggers from Gideon reach it by flat-bottomed boat through the mangrove channels, and Naka-Desh boatmen tie a chime to the roots at the landing on their way past.
Restless dead of the knights walk the barracks at night, and wild boars and bog-wolves den in the roofless nave. The tomb steps are slick and the cellar floor is rotten.
Knights' hall, once paid for from the Gideon garrison's wages and its levies of grain. Today it yields dressed stone for Gideon's builders and the odd corroded blade or buckle.
The knights took Kynareth and Mara as their patrons, as many Kothringi did, and the hall's end wall carries a worn wave-and-wind carving. A Gideon soldier will leave a coin on it for luck.

Eurydike was a hall of Kothringi knights who took the Empire's pay as part of Gideon's garrison in the Third Era. After the Flu of 2E 560 the old hall stood empty, and its barracks block fell in during the Oblivion Crisis storms.
A forgotten knight's seal, a grave that someone has re-opened, or a dispute over a silver-skinned mummy.
A long low hall of grey-white stone with its roof gone, a row of broken columns down the middle and a tumbled barracks wing at the back. A rusted shield-hook still hangs from one wall.
A ruin of the Kothringi, the silver-skinned humans of the Blackwood who died of the Knahaten Flu in 2E 560. It is a hall of Kothringi knights who served in Gideon's Imperial garrison.
The hall is uninhabited. Off-duty guards from Gideon sometimes camp in its doorway and tell the hall's story to newcomers. Treasure-hunters come for the knights' tombs.
Nothing holds it. It lies within a day's walk of Gideon, so the garrison's patrols and the diggers both know it, and caravans on the Gideon road use its broken gable as a marker.
Shoals, sea-drakes.
A light fee on passing ships.
A Sithis token on the stairs.
An Imperial light rebuilt by the Archwardens.
A false light by wreckers, a missing logbook.
A stone tower on a rock with a stilt keeper's house, rimed with sea salt.
A lighthouse on the south coast at the edge of the Sea of Mists.
A keeper's family of four.
Kept by a keeper family.

The town centre is D1: guarded by the council's men, with ripper eels in the canals and cutpurses in Pusbottom. The drowned Imperial quarter and the Hist's roots are D3, with sea-drakes in the deep water beyond.
Lighterage, bay trade, salvage from the drowned quarter, and rice from Hereguard-style plantations nearby. Pusbottom, repopulated as a slum, supplies the criminal trade of the coast.

The third Hist is walled but open, tended by two minders at once, and no faction may hold exclusive access. A sunken shrine to Xhon-Mehl the Fisher, the Ancestral Organ Lord of Lilmoth, is known to divers.

Founded by the Lilmothiit, ruled by Priest-Kings, taken by the Empire, then wrested back by the An-Xileel before 4E 48. Its second Hist went mad and summoned Umbriel in 4E 48, and the Slaughter at Lilmoth destroyed the city. The site was resettled within generations because the harbour has no rival nearby.

The name of the drowned quarter, which locals will not say to strangers. The third Hist and the rule written around it. Pusbottom's criminal quarter and the lapsed docks-only law. Salvage from the drowned villas, and the sunken shrine of Xhon-Mehl.

Ninety percent of the fabric is Argonian stilts and platforms that climb into the air, wired together by walkways, over a drowned layer of Imperial villas. Old Imperial walls survive in places; mould, vines, big bamboo, sleeping palms and harmless drifting shines mark the drowned quarter.

A merchant port on the southern point of the Althii islands, built over shallow water so large ships anchor out and lighter their goods in. It is the biggest town on the south coast and the market for the delta villages and estates of the Althii islands.

About four in five are Argonians, with a working foreign dock population of Bretons, Khajiit and Imperial-descended traders. Elders, including retired Shadowscales, settle disputes. Tree-minders rotate through the Hist's post so that no one holds it alone.

Rebuilt but not restored: smaller, lower and wholly Argonian in its fabric. The merchant council sets tariffs and pays guards. It is hostile to the successor state, which was the party that killed it, and the old law keeping unlicensed foreigners on the docks lapses in places and is enforced in others.
Sinkholes under the turf, snakes in the burrow roofs and the shades of the plague dead at the third dome. A stranger is likelier to be lost than attacked.
The den housed about a family and the small trades it kept: dye roots, fox-fur work and bead-dyeing. It now draws antiquaries and burrow-robbers from Natai.
Fox-kite tokens hang in a ring of three burrows facing south, spirit tokens set for the dead who fled. Some are fresh, left by people who do not say who they are.
Kit Mounds was one of the fox-folk dens near the inland edge of the washes before the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560, and its last families fled toward Blackrose and left it empty.
A Blackrose antiquary wants a dated fox-kite pole from the south dome, and a Natai herb-woman says the burrows carry the voices of the flight.
Three low turf domes with doorways no taller than a seated Argonian, leaf-lined and flooded to the knee in the wet. A line of rotting fox-kite poles runs between them, pointing toward Mudmoth.
A Lilmothiit ruin: a cluster of turf domes near the south.
There are no Lilmothiit left to live here. The nearest living people are Lujei hunters and Natai fishermen, who avoid the mounds, and a Blackrose scholar who comes in the dry months.
The domes are overgrown with sedge and wet-season water stands in the lower burrows. Scholars from Blackrose have mapped it twice and left pegs in the turf.
Thorn tangles that hold a person like a net, venomous snakes in the burrow roofs and plague-dead who rise on the crown at dusk. The brambles are the worst of it.
The den kept bramble-fruit presses and fox-pelt work, and it now draws delta antiquaries and fruit-pickers from Delta Ferry in late summer.
A cluster of spirit stones faces the lake, each with a small notch for a fox-tail charm. Delta Ferry boatmen add a thread for luck on the crossing.
Brushmound was a Lilmothiit den between Khariton and the delta ferry that its families left for Blackrose during the Knahaten Flu of 2E 560. Bramble overran the mound afterward.
A Delta Ferry boatman needs the thorn cut back from a buried ferry cache, and a Blackrose scholar asks for rubbings of the notched stones.
A thorn-wrapped mound of turf with three burrow mouths and a bramble canopy so thick that the roofs look like a single hill. A ferry track skirts it on the east.
A Lilmothiit ruin: a bramble-covered den north-east of Ka-Asei.
No living Lilmothiit remain; Delta Ferry boatmen and Khariton scavengers cross the mound and a patient scholar from Blackrose has dug a test pit.
Bramble hides the mound's three doorways and the burrows are shallow with standing water. Delta Ferry traders sometimes camp on its dry crown.
D3: the dome roofs are cracked and fall without warning, and fishermen report the dead walking the midden at night. Crabs and carrion-birds hold the beach below.
Ashiit was a coastal den of nomadic fox-folk who traded shells and salted fish with the Argonian villages. Now treasure-hunters and the odd scholar come for its grave-goods.
The den's graves are lined with shell and bone, which suggests care for ancestors by the shore. The Lilmothiit's actual beliefs went unrecorded, so the rest is guesswork.
One of the coastal dens held until the flu of 2E 560; it was abandoned at once.
A fox-tail charm in a child's tomb; a carved bone flute.
Low turf-and-leaf domes, cracked and weed-grown, with a midden of shells.
Ashiit Den is a cluster of low turf-and-leaf domes, cracked and weed-grown, above a midden of shells. Vine covers it and Argonians keep away.
Ashiit has no residents, though fishermen swear they hear kits' voices on still nights. Beachcombers and a few treasure-hunters visit in the dry months and do not stay.
Ashiit Den stands on the south-western shore of the southern island, half collapsed and swallowed by vine. Argonians who pass along the coast avoid it as a place of the old sickness.
D3: tunnels collapse under the dune sand, and the smugglers' door is guarded. At night the shifting sand sounds like footsteps.
Kitsa was a small burrow of kits and elders who gleaned the southern shore for eggs, shells and wreck-wood. Now only smugglers and the occasional scholar seek it, for hidden space and for bones.
Tiny shell charms hang in the tunnel niches, and the walls show kit-stories scratched in ash. Their meaning is lost, though they read as a hearth-faith of ancestors and small guardian beasts.
A den of kits and elders, overbuilt and silted over the centuries.
A kit's story scratched on the walls; a smuggler's door added to the tunnel.
Domes half buried in dune sand, and tunnels in the dunes.
Kitsa Burrow is a set of domes half buried in dune sand, with a door that smugglers have cut into its tunnel.
Kitsa Burrow has no residents. Smugglers have cut a door into the tunnel. They alone use it.
Kitsa Burrow lies at the southern tip of the island, its domes half buried in dune sand and its tunnels drifting full. Passing Argonians keep to the water side of the dunes.
D3: the crown is hollow and island farmers report undead guarding the chieftain's tomb. Predators and bats nest in the lower galleries.

It was the meeting-ground where the island's dens traded and settled disputes, and the chieftain's household lived on the crown. Treasure-hunters now come for the burial hoard and are rarely seen again.
The ring of posts and the central mound suggest a gathering-place for the dead, with a chieftain's burial under the crown. How the foxfolk honoured it went unrecorded.
Once the meeting-ground of the island's fox-folk; last used in 2E.
A chieftain's burial hoard; a fox-bone talisman.
A large turf mound crowned with a fallen leaf-roof and ringed by fallen posts.
Reknaa-iit is a large turf mound crowned with a fallen leaf-roof and ringed by fallen posts. It was the meeting-ground of the island's fox-folk and was last used in the Second Era.
The mound has no residents. No village stands near it. Island farmers like Wattle-Pool's couple see lights there some nights and stay indoors.
Reknaa-iit stands at the centre of the southern island, the largest den-mound on the isle and half fallen in. Argonians who cross the island give its ring of fallen posts a wide berth.
D3: crocodilians and bats hold the tunnels, and Argonians nearby report undead stirring beyond them. Collapsing mound-roofs are a danger even in daylight.
Rushiit was a den of foragers living on the northern island's wetland game and reed. Treasure-hunters and scholars come now, but crocodilians turn most of them back at the door.
The Lilmothiit's beliefs are unrecorded, though the surviving charms show care for the dead and for fox-spirits. The tunnels are too fouled by predators to show more.
A den abandoned at the flu; its tunnels were taken by crocodilians and bats.
A scholar's missing notebook; a crocodile with a golden ring in its nest.
Mounds of turf and leaf, the entrance gnawed wide by predators.
Rushiit Den is a set of turf-and-leaf mounds whose entrance predators have gnawed wide. Crocodilians and bats hold the tunnels.
Rushiit has no residents. The predators have driven off even beachcombers. A scholar's party went in some seasons back and did not return.
Rushiit Den lies in the heart of the northern island, its mounds gnawed open and now a lair for marsh predators. Argonians in the area say the place is wrong and keep their children from it.
D3: undead in the tomb-rooms and smugglers in the lower hall, with cracked domes overhead. The shore path from Fort Reedmoth is the only easy approach.
Tailfall was a den of fishers, whose kits' tales survive in Argonian stories. Now smugglers and treasure-hunters use it, and scholars come to copy its carvings.
A ring of tails carved into the doorposts shows an ancestor cult built around the fox-tail, and a kit-fable on a lintel records a founding story. The dead are laid facing the shore.
A den of fishers, whose kits' tales survive in Argonian stories.
A kit-fable carved on a lintel; a hideout used by smugglers.
Domes overlooking the shore, a ring of tails carved in the doorposts.
Tailfall Mound is a set of domes overlooking the shore, with a ring of tails carved in its doorposts. Smugglers hide in the lower rooms.
Tailfall has no residents, but smugglers hide in the lower rooms and watch the strait. Reedmoth's soldiers pretend not to know.
Tailfall Mound looks out over the north-eastern shore of the northern island, close to Fort Reedmoth. Argonians who pass avoid its domes, and the garrison does not patrol it.
Flooded tunnels with no dry exit, snakes in the fallen roof and plague-dead in the lower burrow. A person in the hollow can be trapped by rising water.
The den kept a small reed-dye trade and a few hides. It now draws reed-cutters from Mir-Xal and treasure-hunters after fox-kite relics.
Faded fox-kite cloth hangs in the dry roots of a leaning tree at the den's edge, and the Bucalos hunter ties a thread to it for a safe return.

Tailhollow was a fox-folk den at the western edge of the washes, abandoned when its families fled the Knahaten Flu in the 2E 560s and walked inland toward Blackrose. A hollow where the roof fell in gave it its name.
A Mir-Xal reed-cutter has found a sealed clay jar in the hollow that he will not open, and the Bucalos hunter asks that his blind be left alone.
A roofless turf hollow with its tunnel mouths half under water and a ring of black stumps around it. Fox-kite poles lie fallen across the mud.
A Lilmothiit ruin: a flooded den in the west washes.
Tailhollow has no residents. Mir-Xal reed-cutters work the edges and an old Bucalos hunter keeps a blind in the hollow.
The den is waterlogged. The roof has fallen in and the burrows are open to the sky. Mir-Xal watermen use it as a landmark on the western channel.
Collapse and swamp predators.
Once a camp; now it offers fox-kite fabric and bone-charms.
Fox-spirit charms of orange paper hang in the dome.
The Lilmothiit founded Lilmoth and Blackrose and held the southern coast; the Flu finished them around 2E 560.
A fox-folk charm, a hidden kit-cache or a scholar seeking Lilmothiit lore.
A low grass-covered dome with a door, a hearth ring and faded orange paper.
A dome den of the Lilmothiit, turf and leaf-woven, left to the weather.
Uninhabited; the den was nomadic and left little.
The den is uninhabited; scholars and diggers come rarely.
D1: the shore is close to Thorn's patrols, though crocodiles take swimmers at the bank.
Logs and sawn planks floated to Thorn; the camp buys food and rope from Guxal.
The crews tie a rag to the camp's biggest stump for the felled trees' Hist and spit on the ground before the first cut.
It grew out of the Archein concession timber camps that fed Thorn's building; the field-owners kept it when the Archeins fell.
A crew boss who says a raft went missing with a client's marked logs, and a stand of timber the crews refuse to cut because of what is carved in the roots.
A bunkhouse and drying sheds on pilings, log rafts moored along a raw earth bank, stumps and sawdust everywhere.
A small timber camp on the inlet's southern shore, west of Thorn, unlabelled on the map as [Logging Camp]. Its name, Cutbank Camp, is ours.
Five or six: a gang boss, a cook and sawyers hired out of Thorn's riverbank villages, Argonian and Dunmer.
A handful of crews cut and raft timber for Thorn's builders and for the garrison at Fort Thornmoth.
Swamp predators and Mine-Burner anger when fees are late.
Red mangrove timber and bark sold to Soulrest.
Sithis, with a Bosmer shipwright's Nine charm over the door.
Timber concessions were destroyed in 3E 427; this camp is a small rebuild under licence from the city.
A late fee, a lost log-raft or a body found in the timber.
Log huts, a skid-road, piled red logs and a landing on the channel.
A logging camp of a few huts and a log-landing, licensed by Soulrest's merchant council.
Soulrest Argonians, a Khajiit tallyman and a clerk.
Five loggers and a clerk work a stand of red mangrove; the Mine-Burners tolerate it for a fee.
Predators and falling timber.
Timber for Soulrest.
A small Sithis token on the felling-post.
A continuation of the Third Era concession's timber trade.
A missing logger; illegal cutting.
A clearing with a bunk house, a log yard and a haul track.
A timber camp in the cape's forest.
Five Argonian loggers.
Under licence to Soulrest.
D4: lamias, undead knights and keystone-fed wards.
Once the Ayleid cult centre and keystone workshop; now a source of Ayleid relics, keystone shards and tombs for scavengers.
The Ten Ancestors; a shrine to Azura stands outside; Argonians remember the keystones as a theft of their dead.

Built after 1E 198 over subjugated Argonians. The Liege Lord bound his knights; the Enchanter turned the binding on him and had the knights kill him. In 2E 582 Dominion soldiers, lamia and ancient Ayleid warriors held it.
A keystone that still holds a soul; the Azura shrine outside and its keeper; a looter band missing since the monsoon.
A hilltop amphitheatre with a ring of ruined seats, an inner bailey and tomb wings below; pale stone and dead trees.
Loriasel is a ruined Ayleid citadel and amphitheatre built by the Barsaebics for the Ten Ancestors on a hill over the Venomous Fens.
None live here; lamias and undead; a guarded visitor's track from Jal-Veesa.

The ghost-knights were freed in 2E 582; the Enchanter's works and the keystones remain. Argonians put the amphitheatre to uses that the Ayleids never envisioned. The Veesa-Teeleel guard the ruin from looters.
Gar and crocodilians in the channel; bandits on the track; the washes beyond are wild.
Fish, eels, reeds, the ferry fare and pole-boat hire.

Lujei's tree-minder keeps the hatching records for the ferry families and carries the dead out by boat to the drowned Blackrose tree, a short pole across the lake. The elders pay a share of the crossing tolls to the island core as the price of that burial right.
A fishing village that grew into the island's west landing after the late-3E rebellion, when the city could no longer keep a bridge there.
A missing ferryman, a toll quarrel with the island core, a night crossing with someone's sealed chest.
Stilt houses on a muddy shore, a fish-drying rack frame, a lantern post at the landing, a tarred pole-boat yard.
A lakeshore village on the west bank, with Lujei Ferry just to its west, facing Blackrose across the channel.
Argonian fisher families, a few ex-prisoners' descendants.
Its elders pay the island core for protection and keep the ferry crew, who report to them.
Gar and crocodiles in the channel; night crossings are by lantern only.
Fares per head and per cart, with a charge for livestock.
A small Sithis-token tied to the landing post for crossing luck.
Run since the road was cut in the Third Era; the Imperial bridge fell in the late-3E rebellion and was not rebuilt.
A passenger who must not be seen, or a raft cable that has been cut.
A plank landing, a cable and winch, a lantern pole, a thatched shelter on stilts.
A ferry landing on the channel: a cable raft, a landing hut and a waiting shelter.
Argonian ferry families.
A crew of two families keep the raft for Lujei's elders and the island core.
Storm squalls on the open lake; deep-water predators near the landing; the shoal causeway drowns at high water.
Eels, fish, piloting fees and the lantern toll from boats crossing between Julo and Yalugo.
Sithis and the lake itself; a stone cairn on the high point is where the island's dead are laid.
Nothing is recorded. The island's stone footings are read as work by incomers after 4E 48; before them the island was a bare reed bank.
A lantern signal has been answered from open water; the old boy-pilot knows a hidden passage across the lake; eel pots keep catching something that is not eel.
Low reed-and-stone houses on a hump of silt, eel pots drying on poles, a lantern post at the south tip, and flat water on every side.
Luntoc is a small island hamlet in the lake, built in the stone-footed Stormhold manner; it serves as a pilot station for the shoals. The name has no UESP page.
About five residents, one extended Argonian fishing family and a boy who pilots strangers.
Five people keep eel traps, a lantern for night boats and a causeway of stones across a shoal that surfaces at low water.
Quiet by day. Lake eels and flood surge, and the odd raid from a hungry Tumnatu party or a Naga band off the north road.
Red-clay pottery and dye, fish and eels. Pots go by canoe to Truowa and Aroxhu; salt and tin come back.
Hist and Sithis; the mound's small tree is tended by a tree-minder who also keeps the eggs of the three neighbouring camps.
Nothing is recorded. The mound-building habit and the Tumnatu camp to the west imply a village founded as a lake landing for Aroxhu's pottery trade, in the settled period after 4E 48.
The kiln-fired clay will not set since the mound flooded; a pot-dye recipe is wanted at Aroxhu; the ferryman has seen lights on the lake at night.
Low reed houses on a raised red-clay mound, drying racks of pots and dyed cloth, a kiln-smoke haze and canoes drawn up on the lake shore.
Marzai is a village of about ten on a raised mound of red clay where the lake meets the eastern shore, a western outlier of the Clay-Mound People of Aroxhu. The name has no UESP page.
About ten residents of the Oxhu-Teeleel people: potters, fishers, a ferryman and an elder-woman who keeps the mound's tally of floods.
It sends two elders to the Aroxhu council and keeps cool peace with its Tumnatu neighbours across the water, trading eggs and smoked fish for clay-fired pots.
Rockfall inside, and an old tunnel behind the north wall. D2 outside; the road to Oxayo is watched from Fort Chalkmoth.
The pit yields building stone, cut in blocks and floated down the river to Tsonac.
A cairn of cut chips marks the gallery mouth, one chip for each season the gallery has stood. The crew ask the Hist of Oxayo's tree for firm rock.

Xanuc Diggings has cut building stone from the wall of Chixathe Mesa since Imperial times, when Oxayo's carters first hauled it out; the Archwardens kept it working afterward. It lies between Oxayo and Fort Chalkmoth.
The north gallery has broken through into an older tunnel that the crew cannot explain. The foreman wants a missing hand found.
A raw cut in the mesa wall above Oxayo with grey spoil heaps down the slope and a timbered entrance. The ox-cart track winds down beside it.
The map shows an unlabelled mine symbol in the wall of Chixathe Mesa, between Oxayo and Fort Chalkmoth. We named it Xanuc Diggings; UESP has no page for it, and the symbol is Project Tamriel's.
Four quarrymen, a foreman and a cart-driver, all Argonian, living in Oxayo and walking up each morning.
A crew works one gallery and a cutting face, with an ox-cart track down the mesa side to Oxayo.
A rockfall risk inside; D1 outside because the road is watched.
The pit yields chalk and limestone, burned to lime for mortar and saltrice-pan lining.
Lime-white handprints mark the pit's inside wall, one for each hand lost to the kilns. The crew ask the Noota Nara tree for a dry season.
Chalkmoth Pit is the chalk and limestone working that Fort Chalkmoth was sited to guard, cut since Imperial times for lime. It lies on the mesa shoulder between the fort and Noota Nara.
A kiln-master wants a lost shipment of mortar-lime traced, and an old chalk face has opened onto a sealed room.
A white-scarred pit in the mesa with a lime kiln and smoke above it, and a cart track running to Noota Nara.

The map shows an unlabelled mine symbol on the mesa shoulder between Fort Chalkmoth and Noota Nara. We named it Chalkmoth Pit for the fort that guards it; UESP has no page for it, and the symbol is Project Tamriel's.
A kiln-master, four diggers and a carter, Argonian, drawn from Noota Nara and the fort's dependants.
A crew works one chalk face and a burning kiln, and the white dust shows from the fort's wall.
Rockfall inside and a long drop at the cutting edge. D2 outside because the Ayiin road is watched.
The pit yields dressed building stone sold to Thorn's builders.
A cairn at the gallery mouth is kept by the Ayiin crew, who ask the Hist of their village tree to keep the flank sound. Thorn's clerk ignores it.

Kalaxo Cut has taken stone from the east flank of the mesa above Ayiin since Imperial times, when the Thorn builders first quarried it; the tribes of Ayiin kept it working. Its blocks go west to Thorn.
A block order for Thorn has gone missing on the track, and the crew say they hear tapping behind the north wall.
A sheer cut in the mesa's east flank above Ayiin, with square blocks stacked beside a timbered entrance and a steep cart track.
The map shows an unlabelled mine symbol on the mesa's east flank above Ayiin. We named it Kalaxo Cut; UESP has no page for it, and the symbol is Project Tamriel's.
Four quarrymen, a foreman and a cart-driver, Argonian, from Ayiin, with a Thorn clerk who comes to count the blocks.
A crew works one gallery and a cutting face, hauling blocks down to the Ayiin road in ox-carts.
Cave-ins in the older shaft, brine pools with rotting water, and mudcrabs that nest in the spoil heap.
Rock-salt for curing: blocks go to Thorn, ground salt to Arorha for fish. The salt is cheap but its trade is steady.
The workers carry small hatching-stones from their home villages and leave a pinch of salt at the mine mouth for those buried underground.
Imperial-era bonded labour first cut the salt-bed for the East Empire Company's saltrice and fish trade; the shafts were kept running by Thorn's field-owners after the Company left.

The old shaft was sealed after a collapse that killed bonded labourers; one of their descendants wants the bodies recovered and the overseer refuses. Something has been cutting a new gallery at night.
A cut face of grey-white rock streaked with rust, a timber headframe, wooden carts and stacked salt blocks under reed roofs. The air smells of brine and wet stone.
A small rock-salt mine in the rise between Thorn and the bight, worked by Thorn's field-owners' hired hands. We named it in the Warden Marches' plain Imperial style; it has no UESP page.
About five Argonians, descendants of freed labourers, plus a warden-appointed overseer from an old Archein family who keeps the ledger and the keys.
A handful of workers cut brine-hard salt blocks in two shafts and load them on carts. A warden from Fort Thornmoth checks the tally each month and takes a levy.
D2: roof-falls and what lives in the old galleries.
Raw crystal sold to Stormhold's guild halls; the pit pays a fee to the Vicecanons.
A small ancestor shrine at the adit mouth.
The crystals under Stormhold were dug by Warden Varus's prisoners in the 3E; the market remained and private diggers moved in.
A vein that sings at night; a pit-boss who wants someone to look at a gallery that was sealed.
A timber-propped adit in a hillside, a tipping-yard of spoil and a few huts.
An unlabelled mine placed by us, named for the nearby village. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08); Stormhold Crystal is a UESP page and the deposits run under the northern hills.
Argonian and Dunmer delvers; a pit-boss who knows how to read a vein.
An adit and a tipping-yard where delvers bring up raw crystal for a Stormhold buyer.
Flooding, cave-ins, predators and outlaws.
A gold mine of the Soulrest concession before 3E 427.
A crooked Hist-token on a pole at the mine mouth is the last shrine, put up by tribal raiders who burned the works in 3E 427. Rain has bleached it to bare wood.
Dug by the Empire's Soulrest concession; destroyed in 3E 427.
A buried payroll, a rich vein left unmined, and a rescue of trapped diggers.
Rusted rails, collapsed timber props, a broken sluice.
Old Goldseam is a run of rusted rails, collapsed timber props and a broken sluice, with flooded shafts and a ruined winch house. Outlaws from the Percar hills shelter in the mine mouth.
Old Goldseam has no residents. A few outlaws from the Percar hills shelter in the mine mouth, and scavengers pass between Stonecut Quarry and Zeh-Orun.
Flooded shafts and a ruined winch house.
Gas pockets, cave-ins and scavengers.
It once cut timber and gold-bearing ore together for the Imperial concession. Now Chasepoint salvagers haul its iron and charred beams away.
A half-burned miners' tally board with a Sithis scratch hangs near the portal, still in place. Chasepoint carters make the sign as they pass.
Dug under the Soulrest concession; burned in 3E 427.
A sealed gallery with the old assay records.
Black-scorched timbers and a collapsed portal.
Blackdrift is a mine of black-scorched timbers and a collapsed portal, with a scavenger camp at the portal. It cut timber and gold-bearing ore together.
Blackdrift has no residents. Salvagers from Chasepoint work its timber, and an outlaw crew sometimes uses the old overseer's shed as a lookout.
Sealed or collapsed, with a camp of scavengers at the portal.
Flooded galleries, smugglers.
It was the ninth numbered shaft of the Imperial concession on the south of the cape; now it draws salvagers for iron ties and rail, and Xal-Tarek's garrison discourages the bolder ones.
A cracked Imperial votive niche is cut into the shaft head and holds a single drowned lamp. Miners say that the ninth shaft took a toll of lives, and Xal-Tarek's men avoid the name.
Part of the Imperial concession; burned in 3E 427.
A smugglers' store hidden in the lower galleries.
A timber headframe and a wide mouth.
Ninth Shaft has a timber headframe over a wide mouth, flooded below, with smugglers storing goods above.
Ninth Shaft has no residents. Xal-Tarek's patrols check the portal on their rounds, and a few scavengers work its spoil by night.
Flooded at the bottom, with smugglers storing goods up top.
Gas, collapse and fire-scarred undead.
It was an open cut worked for ore by the Imperial concession and burned in the uprisings of 3E 427; it now draws scavengers who dig the slag for scrap and Naxan boys who find glass in the ash.
A scorched Hist-token is nailed to a charred post where the cut begins, and loggers touch it as they cross.
Dug under the concession; fired in 3E 427; the Great Burn's network lies beneath.
A forgotten vent shaft to the burn network.
A black pit with gas shimmering over it.
Ashfall Cut is a black pit with gas shimmering over it. Redtimber loggers cut through it on the way to Naxan.
Ashfall Cut is empty of residents. Redtimber loggers cut through it on the way to Naxan, and scavengers camp in the lee of the cut.
Gas vents and ash.
Safe in town; the surrounding marsh roads carry bandits and the wild washes have predators.
Tolls on the Soulrest road, carting timber and stone, and a river quay for Blackrose-bound goods.
Local Sithis shrines; its dead go to the Banujha tree.
A waystation of the Third Era timber trade; it kept its trade when the mines burned in 3E 427 and grew as a toll town.
A toll dispute, a smuggler caught with Bramman's river cargo, a message for the Banujha tribes.
Timber and reed buildings on raised ground, a toll gate on the road, a warehouse quay, red clay tracks.
A pentagon town on the road between Soulrest and the Blackrose lakes, on the only broad dry rise in the washes.
Argonians, a few Khajiit teamsters, Imperial-descended clerks.
It answers to Soulrest's merchant council, though it hears the mine-burning tribes' complaints too.
Dragon's-tongue patches are deadly to the careless; channels hide predators; Tumnatu parties pass by.
Dragon's-tongue and other swamp herbs, fish and a small guide fee for boats going south.
Sithis and a small Dibella chime, kept for travellers; the hamlet's eggs are laid at Korydon.
The name is Kothringi in style, and Argonians resettled the place after 2E 560. Its chime-post is the oldest working one in the Ultherus country.
The chime-tender has lost count of the strikes; a boat came up from Blackrose with a corpse aboard; a rare herb grows at one hummock.
Stilt houses on a hummock, a tall chime-post of tin and copper above the roofs, herb racks and boats tied to every post.
Myroleon is a hamlet of about six Chime-Keepers at the southern end of the Ultherus swamp country, on the first channels toward Blackrose. The name has no UESP page.
About six, Argonian herb-gatherers; one of them is the post's chime-tender.
In 4E 201 it keeps the chime-post for boats, gathers dragon's-tongue and sells it up to Korydon.
Paatru and Naga raiders cross the ridge; wild lizards in the pens.
Lizard-herding, hides, tin chimes traded with the Paatru and with Helstrom's levy.
Sithis and Dibella; a small cairn for the old dead.
A Kothringi-named place resettled after 2E 560; the ridge made it a lookout, and in 4E 48 refugees from the north hid here.
The Paatru camp wants a chime tuned; a Naga band is watching the pass; the old watchman saw a light on the peak.
Low stone-footed huts on a ridge shoulder, lizard pens, windchimes everywhere, wide views over the marsh.
Nacydes is a hamlet of about five on a ridge shoulder at the west of the Aunike country, among the few Chime-Keeper places that sit on drier ground. The name has no UESP page.
About five Argonians, lizard-herders and a chime-maker; they speak to the Paatru camp across the ridge by bargaining.
Five people hold the hamlet, keep lizard-steeds and trade chimes for hides. They post a watch on the nearest peak.
Sea-drakes and surf off the shore; the wreck's cargo draws scavengers.
Shellfish, salt, wreck salvage and sea fish.
The Natai tree-minder keeps a drift-tree shrine of Sithis at the tide line; the dead are carried to the Blackrose Hist by boat on a yearly trip.
Settled by Blackrose fisherfolk who followed the southern channels to the coast; it has salvaged the wreck to its east for a generation.
A wreck to dive, a salt-pan dispute, a smuggler landing that avoids Soulrest.
Low stilt houses at the tide line, salt pans, drying racks, weathered salvage timber.
A coastal village on the south shore of the washes, at the tip where the land meets the Sea of Mists.
Argonian shellfish-gatherers and salvagers.
Under the island core's nominal protection, though it is a long way off; it governs itself.
Pirates of the bay; river predators.
Fish, timber hauling, coastal boats.

Naxan's Sithis shrine is a ring of pale stones on the headland, where fishermen and loggers both pause on the way to the Topal Bay road. The families share a single egg-chest that goes to the Banujha tree once a year by Soulrest's coast road.
A shore village of the Third Era timber trade.
A boat hijack, a timber contract.
Timber stilt houses, a log landing, drying racks.
Naxan has timber stilt houses, a log landing and drying racks at the western end of the Topal Bay road. A reeve governs it for Soulrest, and the ruined fort of Wrackmoth lies on the same coast.
Argonian fishers and loggers.
Governed by a reeve for Soulrest.
Wild at night; predators on the bank; Tumnatu hunters in the reeds.
Staging fees, herbs, fish and mending. Most of the income comes from passing traffic.
Sithis; the family's eggs are laid at Korydon's tree.
Nothing is recorded. The Kothringi name implies a Kothringi site resettled by Argonians; it has been small ever since.
A wrecked boat in the reeds with unsold goods; a hidden Kothringi cairn behind the houses; the lantern has been lit from outside.
A few stilt houses beside a green waterway, hung with chimes; a lantern post; mossy moorings.
Nemeon is a small hamlet on a side waterway between Lake Ulaish and Korydon. The name has no UESP page; its form follows the Kothringi-named towns.
About six Argonians, a boat-wife, her sons and a hired herb-picker.
It stages boats going between the lake and Korydon and keeps a waystation bench and a lantern.

The mound's flooded undercroft is the danger: giant snakes lie in the drowned cellar and ward-bound dead stand at the broken arch. At D3 the ground is the safe part, and the Vandrel Farm side is the usual way in.
Once an outlying hall of the Ayleid settlement; now a source of loot for scavengers.
Ayleid shrine fragments; the Veesa-Teeleel's ward-stakes ring the mound.
Barsaebic Ayleids settled this country after 1E 198 and were beaten by the Hist, by legend. Nothing is known of this site.
A looter's map that marks a Fenlord's vault; ward-stakes pulled up one by one.
White stone arches and fallen columns half-covered with vine on a reed-ringed mound; black water in the undercroft.
An Ayleid ruin of the Barsaebics, marked on the map. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08); what it holds is ours to decide.
The ruin has no residents; a hermit scavenger sometimes lives there.
Half-flooded and avoided. The Veesa-Teeleel call it sick ground and keep their own away.
D1: the village is safe by day; the mesa edge above it is wilder.
Clay pots, spears with fire-hardened tips, fish and trade with the fort.
A Hist tree grows in the village. A dragon-spear is displayed beside it as a relic.

Before 2E 864 a dragon burned the village's walls to the ground. The villagers heated their spear-tips in the dragonfire, took the enchantment and pierced it; Dreekius carried the head to Stros M'Kai, where it hung in the Draggin Tail Inn in Port Hunding.
A spear-smith's apprentice says she can make the dragon-fire tips again if she is brought something from the fire, and the elders want the head's story told in Port Hunding.
A walled village of mounds and reed roofs, with a single burned-black post kept where the old gate stood.
Noota Nara is a village in Black Marsh and the original home of the Argonian Dreekius. UESP gives no position; our map puts it on the river below Fort Chalkmoth.
A dozen or so households of Argonians who follow the Clay-Mound customs of the east, led by a council of elders; hunters, potters and spearsmiths.
The village survives. It rebuilt its walls in timber and clay and still tells the story, with the head's loss as an old grievance.
D1: predators in the paddies, flood.
Rice, fish and a ferry across the strait to the southern island.
Hatching families go to Lilmoth or Uluo; a post-shrine on the rice dyke.
Founded by Lilmoth-coast families who drained rice ground; its boundary with Three Waters land is fixed by custom.
A boundary quarrel with Uluo; a ferry-man missing; a drained field with old bones.
Stilt houses beside paddies cut in low ground, sluice gates and a ferry pier.
A coastal village on the south shore of the northern island, between Uluo and the east coast road.
Argonians of the Lilmoth coast with some Three Waters in-laws.
Ten households farm rice, net fish and trade with both Uluo and Lilmoth.
Safe; the basin's reeds are wild.
Tin and copper chimes, metal-woven rope and shallow-draft boats.
Z'en and Dibella beside Sithis; a chime for each of the dead.
A name given by the Kothringi stayed on the place. Argonians re-settled it after the Flu and kept the name.
A chime-maker's commission, a boat race or a stolen tuning-fork.
Stone footings under stilt houses, tin and copper chimes on every eave and a long landing.
A hamlet of stilt houses with stone footings, kept by Argonians who resettled Kothringi-named places after 2E 560.
Chime-Keeper Argonians, craftsmen and traders.
About eight people make chimes, boats and rope. The hamlet is orderly. Its people treat the Archwardens' officials coldly and Gideon's traders warmly.
Safe in the village; the strait has sudden squalls and the odd sea-drake sighting.
Landing fees, lodging, boat repair, fish and a small trade in lantern oil and rope.
A small shrine to the drowned on a post in the channel; hatching families go to Lilmoth's tree.
Grew as a half-way stop on the Archon, Lilmoth, Soulrest and Tear line, where small boats rest and hand cargo across.
A boat found drifting; a boatman who owes money to both Archon and Lilmoth; cargo that was not meant to be on the lighter.
Stilt houses and platforms linked by gangways, a hostel with a long deck, boats tied three deep, and a lantern on a mast.
A village built over the water of the strait, at the narrowest crossing between the Nushara shore and the islands.
Argonians of the Lilmoth coast, with Archon and Lilmoth boatmen resting overnight.
Ten or so households keep the landing, lantern and a hostel; the village pays tariff to Lilmoth's council because most of its custom comes from there.
Bay pirates raid the landing when the council boat is away; tidal flats flood fast and drown the careless.
Fish, salt-fish and dried eel to Gideon, ferry fares to Aphon, and the harbour dues Gideon's officer collects at the landing.
Dibella and Sithis are both invoked at the boat blessing each spring; a small shrine to the drowned stands at the tide-line.
Olvani is a Project Tamriel name with no canon history. It grew from a customs landing of the Imperial-era Gideon trade into a village that survived on fishing.
A boat that never came back from Aphon, a smugglers' crate dropped at the tide-line, or a harbour dispute that reaches Gideon's court.
Stilt houses on a long mudflat, drying racks, upturned punts, grey light off the bay and a smell of brine and smoke.
A village at the mouth of Gideon's estuary on Topal Bay's eastern shore. It is Gideon's fishing port and the landing for boats to Aphon Isle and the Topal Bay coast.
Lukiul families with Cyrodiilic names and a Khajiit sailor or two who came on a bay-boat and stayed.
About twelve people haul nets on the mudflats and ferry travellers to Aphon Isle. They report smugglers to Gideon when there is a reward and say nothing when there is not.
Armed lookouts who attack strangers quickly; the coves are trapped, and the bluff caves hold crocodiles that the crew feeds.

They move moon sugar, salt, ash-glass, Dunmer wine and untaxed saltrice, and take a cut from every cargo. They are genuinely outlaw, unlike the chartered pirates of the north camp, and the two crews are rivals.
Mostly none; some Dunmer keep a Tribunal-era charm, some Argonians a village-tree token. Everyone shows the sea respect.

Argonia has three legal entries and a long coast; any unwatched beach near a customs port draws smugglers. Skeith's position between Thorn, Seafalls and Archon makes it the obvious cache for goods that avoid both customs houses.
The leader will hire a stranger to carry a cargo past Marshgate Watch. A rival pirate crew has burned a boat, and war between the two camps is close.
Lean-tos of driftwood, tarred canvas and reed roofs, boats hauled up on grey shingle, barrels hidden under nets, a smoking drying-rack.
A smuggler camp in the lee of Skeith Isle's low south-western bluffs. The name is ours; the map labels it only [Smuggler Camp]. No UESP page.

Mixed crews: Argonian boatmen of the Okuwun coast, a few Dunmer from Tear, runaway Archein families, Khajiit moon-sugar dealers. The leader is a former Archon harbour clerk who knows every customs rule.
About fourteen men and women live in lean-to huts above the tide line, with two hidden coves and a cache in the caves under the bluff. They bring in boats on the dark of the moons.
Crossbow and fire-arrow lookouts and a camp that fights as a crew; the keep above is a stronghold, the water below is full of eels.
Prize cargoes, ransom, protection fees on coast boats, and the occasional state commission to chase a rival. They sell to Archon quietly.
A rough sea-faith: each ship has a carved figurehead they swear by, and the keep's dead are left to the tide.

The Archon coast was 'riddled with pirates' in the late First Era and General Lucinia Falco sent letters of marque to them; our reading is that the tradition survived as a half-chartered fleet in 4E 201, the state's substitute for a navy.
The captain wants a rival ship's chart taken from Hollow Tide Camp. A letter of marque, genuine or forged, would let the stranger sail as a chartered privateer.
A line of hulks and stilt-houses on grey water, ropes and nets slung between, a stone jetty at the keep's foot, smoke and lanterns.
A stilt-and-hulk pirate camp in the shallows on Skeith Isle's western shore, serving Rainbreaker Keep. The name is ours; the map labels it [Pirate Camp]. No UESP page exists.
About twenty pirates, mostly Argonian boat-crews with a few Dunmer and Khajiit seamen. The pirate-captain, a one-eyed Argonian, has a letter that the Archwardens neither honour nor repudiate.
Four ships' crews share the camp. They hold the keep above as a strong room and raid shipping but leave Archon's own boats alone.
D1: crocodiles at the weir and fleshflies in the heat.
Eels, gar and reed bundles sold up river to Stormhold; weir fees from passing boats.
A small Hist-shoot shrine fed with the first catch of the season.
Reasoned: the weirs are older than the city's modern state and have been kept by the Sedge-Wardens since before the Dunmer.
Someone is pulling up the weir stakes at night; a boat of Dunmer traders asks to cross without paying.
Pale stilt huts on a mud bank, a woven fish-weir across the creek, mats and fish drying on racks.
An unlabelled outpost placed by us, named in the jade culture's reed-and-weir style. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
Veesa-Teeleel families on rotation from Jal-Veesa; a weir-warden who knows every trap.
A few stilt huts and a drying-rack yard on the bank, with a boat landing and a weir across the creek.
The Naga camp to the north hunts here; predators come to the sap-skins and the station keeps spears at each door.
Sap tapped from the Hist-tended trees on the bank goes down to Helstrom's market; the station barters it for dried fish and cloth.
There is no Hist at the station; the keepers carry hatchlings and the dead to the nearest village tree. A small totem-post at the landing, carved with a sap-drop, is touched on leaving.
A hunters' camp for Helstrom's market, grown into a permanent station once the tribes returned to the interior after 4E 48.
A sap-skin has been found slashed and replaced with a wrong one; the young tree-minder wants an egg-clutch carried to Helstrom unseen.
Four stilt huts and a drying frame of sap-skins on a firm bank, an eel-trap line across the shallows, and a canoe landing wreathed in hanging moss.

The map gives this outpost no name and UESP has none; the name is ours. Five Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom keep it, tapping sap from the trees along the bank and answering to a tree-minder in Helstrom.
About five Saxhleel sap-gatherers, a young egg-tender and a boy sent to learn the trees.
Five Saxhleel keep the station through the year, tapping sap from the trees along the bank. They report to a tree-minder in Helstrom by boat. Nothing about the station is written down.
Naga and Tumnatu parties pass here; the junction's currents drown the careless.
Hatchery eggs, fish and sap exchanged with boats going between Helstrom and the lake.
The station has no Hist of its own, so hatching and burial are done at the nearest village tree. A totem-post carved with a heron stands at the landing, and boatmen bow to it passing.
The junction's old nest-pits are read as sites that the Root-Folk kept from before the Empire; the station is the watch they keep on them.
A clutch is missing from the nest-pits; boats pass that did not come up the river; the old sap-speaker will name who took it for a price.
Tall stilt platforms over a wide river junction, nest-pits of clay lined with moss, a watch post with a lantern and a horn.
The map gives this outpost no name and UESP has none; the name is ours. Five Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom hold its stilt platforms over the junction and tend eggs in clay nest-pits.
About five egg-tenders and watchers; one is an old sap-speaker.
Five Saxhleel hold the station where the river arms spread into the delta. They tend eggs, watch the water for strangers, and send word to Helstrom's tree-minders once a month.
D2: large predators and the odd hunter-bandit.
Pelts, feathers, smoked meat; they buy salt and arrowheads.
A small root shrine at the camp's edge for the Hist's speech.
Root-Folk hunters have used the rise for generations as a place from which to watch the jungle edge.
A trapper who has seen strange lights in the Sarpa country to the south, and a bear skin worth more than the camp itself.
Stilt houses under the trees, with pelts stretched on frames and a lookout in a tall trunk.
An unlabelled outpost whose name we give: Xuvagol, in the Root-Folk's style. UESP has no page.
Saxhleel hunters and their kin, led by an old trapper who knows every path to Tsonac.
Six live there; they hunt and trade pelts at Tselan.
Squalls and storm surf; smugglers use the islet at night and the keepers pretend not to see them.
Fish, eggs and a small mooring fee for boats on the Marzai-Truowa run.
The islet has no Hist; hatchlings are rowed to the nearest village tree. A totem-post at the landing is hung with Marzai shells, and the keepers touch it before a crossing.
A lake station kept by the Root-Folk to guard their share of the lake's eastern trade.
A cask left on the platform is marked for Truowa. It has not been claimed. The egg-tender has found new eggs in an old nest.
A reed-built platform on silt with a lamp tower, an eel line and a stack of dried fish racks.
The map gives this outpost no name and UESP has none; the name is ours. Four Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom hold a reed-built platform with a lamp tower and racks of dried fish.
About four watchers and an egg-tender.
Four Saxhleel hold the islet, watching the water between Marzai and Truowa and tending eggs. They pass news of the eastern shore to a tree-minder when a boat comes by.
D2: wild country around; a Naga camp lies a short way south.
Ferry fares, a night's bed, smoked meat for the road to Helstrom.
None formal; a grave-stake row on a rise behind the house.
Reasoned: a ferry point on the hinge road since the colonial period.
The ferryman sells directions and warns against the camp to the south-west; a body washed up at the landing.
A timber landing, a rope-hauled flat barge and a long low house of stone and reed.
An unlabelled minor outpost placed by us, named in the Stormhold manner (Dunmer family name and landing). UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
A Dunmer-descended ferryman and his Argonian crew.
One family keeps a flat ferry and a roadhouse and sells directions south.
Ultherus herbs can kill the careless; predators in the open water south; Tumnatu parties.
Lodging for boatmen, dragon's-tongue and swamp herbs, fish and mending.
There is no Hist at the station; the keepers go to Korydon's tree for hatching and burial. A totem-post at the jetty is carved with a boat-prow, and the crews touch it for fair passage.
A waystation of the Root-Folk, shown in forest green on the map south of Korydon. It lets the Helstrom assembly hear of the Blackrose waters.
A herb-gatherer wants dragon's-tongue taken to Korydon before it spoils; a boat from Blackrose never put in.
Stilt huts around a boat-yard with a bell at the landing and herb racks on every rail.
The map gives this outpost no name and UESP has none; the name is ours. Five Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom keep stilt huts round a boat-yard, with a bell at the landing.
About five boatmen and herb-gatherers.
Five Saxhleel keep the waystation, feeding boat crews bound south and watching the great water. They report to the tree-minder of Korydon at each full moon.
Crocodiles, giant snakes and the Root-Folk's own traps on every path.
Hunting, eggs and sap-gathering; they sell hides and skins to Aroxhu.
The eggs are warmed to a rhythm that they say the Hist sets from afar; they hold no tree here.
The Root-Folk keep stations through the inner swamp; Tazhul was set up to tend eggs on a warm mud-bank and hunt the marsh.
Two eggs have failed to hatch and the egg-minder believes someone has cursed them. A hunter has found a Sarpa feather in a trap.
Root-hollow lodges and stilt-houses on a mud-bank, egg-racks, drying hides, marsh herons.
An unlabelled forest-green triangle on the map: a Root-Folk station on the edge of Okuwun-Rahei. We named it in Argonian style; no UESP page.
About four Saxhleel, hunters and an egg-minder; wary of strangers.
A small station with a rack of eggs and a hunters' lodge; the Root-Folk keep apart from the mounds and the Agaceph.
D1: the road is watched; jungle cats come to the well at night.
Small tolls and a share of whatever the travellers carry; it sells water and dried fish.
A tree-hollow offering box for the Hist is nailed to the post's gate.
