Imperial forts once ran a chain of waystations along the track; this is one the Archwardens kept.
Guards who have found a Tsonac stone-carver's cart abandoned a mile off, and a message left for a courier who never arrived.
A stilted watch house with a lantern pole and a stone-edged well, and a chain across the track.
A roadside post unlabelled on the map as [Outpost], set where the Tsonac track meets the bay's southern shore. Its name is ours.
Argonian guards on hire and a Dunmer messenger who also trades in dyes.
Four men from Fort Thornmoth rotate through it, checking loads and sending word along the road.
Mesa predators and the odd bandit from the Balormaak road. D2.
Hides and feathers go to Ayiin and Joxhi, and the outpost gets cloth and salt in return. A guiding fee for travellers to Balormaak is a smaller income.
A small shrine to the Hist at the settlement edge, tended by the elder; eggs go north to the tribe's tree at Helstrom.
Yuvexa is an old watch point on the southern lip of the mesa, used by Root-Folk hunters from Helstrom for generations to watch the Balormaak ruin and the Ayiin road.
A hunter has seen strange tracks near the Sarpa camp, and a trade-pouch for Ayiin was left at the gate.
Stilt houses under a few trees on the mesa's south edge, drying racks and a lookout in a trunk that faces the Velothi ruins.
An unlabelled outpost, given the name Yuvexa. UESP has no page for it.
Two Root-Folk families, one elder and a few youths, from Helstrom's hunting clans.
Five or so people live here, hunting and gathering and trading to Ayiin. A lookout post faces Vorannuhl.
Smuggler bands, tribal raiders from the Sarpa camp, and the bad road in the monsoon.
Tolls and small fines. A quarter goes to the confederacy's treasury.
None official; the spear-watch carry hatching-stones from home villages.
Built after Arorha's boatmen lost goods to coast robbers, and manned by volunteers from Renhu and Khiar.
The watch have caught a smuggler with Archwarden stamps on his bills; the leader wants someone neutral to carry him to Aroxhu.
A clay mound with a palisade of cut reeds, a round thatched watch-hut, a bar across the road, a cluster of spears in a rack.
A watchpost of the Oxhu-Teeleel on a mound above the Renhu-Seafalls road. The name is ours; no UESP page exists.
Five Argonians on rotation from Renhu and Khiar, led by a woman of Khiar who knows the road.
Five spears keep the watch, with a bar across the road and a toll box. They pass Seafalls folk and Aroxhu carts free and charge outsiders.
Fleshflies, swamp-crocodiles in the ditch, and smugglers landing by night who will fight rather than pay.
Tolls, on a scale of a few septims per cart. The post buys fish and bread from Arorha and sells nothing.
None officially. The wardens go home to their village trees to hatch and bury.

Built by the Imperial Commission as a toll and way-station for the Thorn-Archon road. It was abandoned in the Interregnum and reoccupied by the Archwardens' detachment when the frontier screen needed a customs point on the east road.
A customs bill for a cargo that never arrived is on the sergeant's desk. A warden has been taking bribes from Skeith smugglers. The sergeant wants it proven.
A square stone-and-timber blockhouse on a mud-brick plinth, a toll bar across the road, a signal pole and a few huts of reed round it.
A small garrison post where the Thorn road crosses the neck of land at the bight's northern end. We named it in the Marches' naming habit; no UESP page exists.
Six Argonian wardens of old Archein lines, in patched half-Imperial livery, led by a sergeant who keeps the paper and the post's one cutlass.
Six wardens rotate through from Fort Thornmoth. They stamp cargo bills, take a levy on clay and salt, and watch the shore for boats that avoid Thorn.
Mesa predators and a bandit now and then on the Tenmal road. D2.
Hides and reeds go to Tenmal and the pit crews; the post gets lamp oil and iron in return.
A small shrine to the Hist at the post's edge; eggs are carried north to the Helstrom tree, and the elder holds the naming.
Nuxhal is a Root-Folk hunters' post on the western part of the mesa, used for generations as a gathering station for hunts beyond Tenmal Pits.
A hunter has seen strange tracks near the Sarpa camp, and a trade-pouch for Tenmal Pits was left at the gate.
Stilt houses under a stand of trees, drying racks and a lookout built in a trunk facing Tenmal Pits' smoke.
The map shows no name for this outpost; Nuxhal is ours, and UESP has no page for it. Its stilt houses stand under a stand of trees, with a lookout built into a trunk.
Two Root-Folk families, an elder and a few youths from Helstrom.
Five or so people hunt and gather, trading with Tenmal and Tenmal Pits, the nearest settlements.
Murkwood's medusas lie to the west. The keepers never go beyond the third bend after dusk. Fellrunners also bite.
Fellrunner feathers and pelts traded to Helstrom's market; a single armband of the pale down lets a hunter cross Murkwood unseen.
No Hist grows here; the keepers go to a village tree for hatching and burial. A feather-hung totem-post stands at the bend, and the first feather of each season is given to it.
A hunters' stand using Murkwood's canon fellrunner trade (Lore:Murkwood), settled once the hunters kept their feathers here between runs.
A hunter went into Murkwood wearing a feather band and has not come back; a feather-trader will pay for a missing band recovered.
A hummock hung with drying skins and feather bundles, three stilt huts and a narrow canoe lane under overhanging roots.
The map gives this outpost no name and UESP has none; the name is ours. Four Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom keep three stilt huts on a hummock hung with drying skins and feather bundles.
About four hunters and a feather-trader.
Four Saxhleel keep the hummock, hunting along the bend and trading fellrunner feathers to passing boats. They answer to a tree-minder in Helstrom and send a share of every sale.
Mesa predators, and a dark cave nearby that the wardens forbid their children to enter. D2.
Reed, feathers and hides go to Ranvos Landing and Tenmal Pits, and the post gets lamp oil and salt back.
A small shrine to the Hist at the post's edge; eggs go west to the Jal-Veesa tree, and the post's elder keeps the name-cords.
Reeka-Veesa is a Sedge-Warden post on the mesa's west side, used for generations to watch the road between Tenmal and Ranvos Landing and to gather reed and feather.
A child of the post has slipped into the dark cave nearby that the wardens forbid. A bundle of feathers meant for Ranvos Landing was left at the gate unclaimed.
Stilt houses under a few trees, drying racks of reed and feather, and a lookout in a trunk that faces Sahlpesh Cave.
The map shows no name for this outpost; Reeka-Veesa is ours, and UESP has no page for it. Its stilt houses stand under a few trees on the mesa's west side, with drying racks of reed and feather.
Sedge-Warden families, one elder and a few youths.
Five or so people live here, hunting and gathering and answer to Jal-Veesa's wardens.
Storm squalls and deep-water predators; Tumnatu canoes pass without leave.
Eels and lake fish traded to Marzai, Julo and passing boats.
The islet has no Hist, so the keepers row to a village tree on the shore for hatching and burial. A totem-post carved with an eel stands at the landing, and the first eel of the run is given to it.
A lake station of the Root-Folk, founded to keep the lake's northern fishing open to the Helstrom country.
A canoe was found drifting with its paddles shipped. The lantern was lit although no boat had come.
An islet of silt with two reed huts, eel pots on poles and a lantern at the water's edge.
The map gives this outpost no name and UESP has none; the name is ours. Four Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom live in two reed huts, with eel pots on poles round the islet.
About four eel-trappers and a watcher.
Four Saxhleel live on the islet, trapping eels and watching the lake's north shallows. A tree-minder in Helstrom hears their news at the autumn eel-run.
D1: highway wildlife and the odd thief.
A toll on goods leaving the city, a lamp-oil trade and a few stalls.
A grave-stake for the post's dead and a cross-marked stone from the Dunmer period.
Reasoned: a post where the road leaves the mounds, taking tolls since the colonial period.
A cart with a sealed crate that the clerk is told to let through; a night guard who has seen lights on the northern road.
A low stone toll-house with a lamp post and a wooden bar across a causeway.
An unlabelled outpost placed by us, named for its position at the head of the northern causeway. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
A reeve, two Argonian guards and a clerk on market days.
A small stone hut and a bar across the road, with a shed for the reeve and room for a cart.
Watchers with bows cover the channel, and the toll chain trips unwary boats. Crocodiles use the same channel.
Watching, fishing and a small toll on boats heading to Soulrest.
The post keeps a clutch hearth, but their Hist lies near Soulrest, so hatching and burial are a journey inland. A fang charm hangs over the landing.

Banu-Veeth Post is a Mine-Burner watch post at the south of the Banujha Basin, built to cover the water-way toward Soulrest. The tribes who burned the Imperial mines in 3E 427 set the first watch here.
A toll dispute, a coastal stranger to question, or a message for Jarecai.
A stilt watch-post on the water with a lookout platform and a long boat-landing, with a toll chain across the channel. A heap of salt sacks sits under a lean-to.
Banu-Veeth Post is a stilt watch-post with a lookout platform, a long boat-landing and a toll chain across the channel. Six Mine-Burner Argonians hold it.
Six Mine-Burner Argonians: three watchers, a ferryman, a cook and a boy who runs messages to the basin. They are hostile to anyone from the coast.
A few Mine-Burner tribesmen hold the post year-round, watching for boats from Soulrest and the coast. They stop every boat and take a toll of salt or iron.
Crocodiles lie below the weir where the offal goes in, and the log walk is slick. At D1 the camp is safe; the creek downstream toward Mirasel is not.
Eels and gar sold to Jal-Veesa and Stormhold.
A Hist-shoot post with the first catch.
Reasoned: the weirs date back to before the Dunmer.
Someone has been taking from the traps at night.
Pale stilt huts on a mud bank and a woven weir across the creek.

Reed-Sill Weir is the weir-wardens' camp on the creek north-east of Gandranen, one of the Veesa-Teeleel traps that feed Jal-Veesa. We placed and named it in the jade style for an unlabelled outpost symbol; UESP has no page for it (searched 2026-11-08).
Veesa-Teeleel families on rotation from Jal-Veesa.
Six or so wardens live here in stilt huts around a log weir with a landing, running the eel and fish traps that supply Jal-Veesa's market.
D2: far from help; wildlife and the odd thief.
A small toll and a stall of lamp oil and dried fish.
A grave-stake for the post's dead.
Reasoned: a post on the long road from Stormhold to the western frontier.
A reeve who wants word sent to Stormhold; a guard who saw lights at Loriasel.
A low stone hut and a gate across a causeway.
An unlabelled outpost placed by us, named in the Stormhold manner. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
A reeve and two guards.
A small stone hut and a gate across the road.
Meddling with a totem draws dangerous beasts; Paatru raiders from the west camp.
Tolls and trade with river traders from the Gideon country who come openly.
A rune-carved totem marks the ground by the landing. The Hutan-Tzel say that meddling with one draws dangerous beasts, and the keepers wipe it clean and speak to it at dawn.
The Hutan-Tzel keep fortified outposts along the Panther River, per the tribe's canon (Online, via tribes.md).
A totem has been moved and the beasts have come; the rune-carver can read the stolen one.
A fenced bank with a palisade of reed, rune-carved totems and a ferry.
The map gives this outpost no name and UESP has none; the name is ours. Six Hutan-Tzel keep a fenced bank with a reed palisade, rune-carved totems and a ferry.
About six Hutan-Tzel watchers and a rune-carver.
Six Hutan-Tzel keep the bank, watching the river and taking a small toll from boats. They answer to the naheesh at their own tree, not to Helstrom and send a share of every toll.
Bow-watchers cover the channel and the signal horn calls reinforcements. Ruin-diggers who ignore the warning are shot.
Watching, fishing and a small toll on boats.
They keep a clutch hearth, but their Hist lies near Soulrest, so hatching and burial are a journey inland. They leave small offerings at the ruins' edge when passing.
Jal-Resh Post is a Mine-Burner watch post on the Banujha waters between Jarecai and Kharaxos. The post was built by the tribes to keep the two ruined cities' ground free of looters.
A watch officer needing a courier, a wrecked boat or a stranger arrested.
A stilt post at a channel bend, a lookout tower with a signal horn and a landing with two war-canoes drawn up. The ruined cities show faintly through the haze on either side.
Jal-Resh Post is a stilt post at a channel bend with a lookout tower, a signal horn and two war-canoes drawn up at the landing. Six Mine-Burner Argonians hold it.
Six Mine-Burner Argonians: three bow-watchers, a boatman, a cook and a young one learning to read tracks. They know every digger who has come this way.
A few Mine-Burner tribesmen hold the post and watch the channel for diggers heading for the ruins. They turn back anyone who cannot give a reason.
Banujha crocodiles patrol the landing, and strangers who mock the river-folk may be turned away by arrow. Mine-Burner watchers are close at hand.
Osheeja gar fishing, smoked fish and barter for salt and iron.
A chime-post at the landing recalls the Kothringi and the dead of the river. The river-folk go to their tree for hatching and burial, a boat-journey of several days.
Ukeel Station began as a net-mending landing on the Banujha, where the Naka-Desh first met the basin's Mine-Burner tribes. It has been rebuilt every few years since 4E 48 by the same few families.
A riddle for passage, a net-snag with a surprise, or a gar-hunter asking help.
A stilt platform of reed thatch above the Banujha, a fish-rack, a net-drying frame and a boat landing with a chime-post at the end. Fish scales glitter on the planks.
Ukeel Station is a reed-thatched stilt platform above the Banujha with a fish-rack, a net-drying frame and a boat landing. Five Naka-Desh keep it.
Five Naka-Desh: a net-boss, two fishers, a smoker of fish and a child who learns the river's ways. They love a riddle and give a good one in return for a gift of salt.

The station is held through the year by a handful of Naka-Desh fishers, who net osheeja gar from the Banujha and trade the catch at the water's edge. They watch strangers from the platform and ask for riddles.
Hostile to Imperial-descended visitors.
Watching, fishing.
A Banujha tree-token shrine.
Placed by the tribes after the 3E 427 uprising.
A message for the council; a wounded watcher.
A tall stilt platform with a lookout and a boat.
A watch post of the mine-burning tribes, on stilts at the water's edge.
Six Banujha tribesmen.
Manned by watchers.
D2: touching a totem draws beasts.

Hutan-Aru's people hunt and guide travellers across the river branch, and sell hides and smoked fish to Umpholo and the Meliton hill-folk. They bargain hard over bridge-tolls, which every passing caravan must pay.
Totems carved in runes only they can read.
Reasoned: the Hutan-Tzel hold a chain of river outposts and have for generations.
A bargain for passage; a totem that has been defaced.
A palisade of dark posts, a rune-carved totem, a landing.
The map shows an unlabelled outpost here. We named it in the Hutan-Tzel style. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
Hutan-Tzel guards under a local naheesh.
A palisade around a few huts, with a totem carved in runes.
D2: wildlife; Root-Folk hostile to uninvited guests.
Sap and eggs.
A young Hist tree at its centre.
Reasoned: Hist-country outposts reach outward from Helstrom.
A sapling that is dying; an invitation to the Root Talk.
Root-hollows and stilt huts under a canopy.
An unlabelled outpost placed by us, named in the Root-Folk style. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
Root-Folk, Saxhleel.
A stand of stilt huts around a Hist sapling.
The post is armed and treats strangers as suspects. Crocodiles and marsh snakes lie on both sides of the border water.
Watching and a small toll on caravans.
The post keeps a clutch hearth, but their Hist lies near Soulrest, so hatching and burial are a journey inland. Rune-marks on the gate are for the basin's spirits.

Xul-Banu Post is a Mine-Burner watch post on the basin's north-west edge, facing Nha Enasa and Gul-Tej. It stands where the basin's waters meet the Naka-Desh channels, and has been rebuilt since the Naka-Desh trade began to grow.
A courier for Jarecai, a trade dispute with Gul-Tej, or a missing patrol.
A stilt post on the basin's north-west edge, a gate-tower facing Nha Enasa and a trading float tied beside the landing. Hides and baskets lie stacked on the float.
Xul-Banu Post is a stilt post with a gate-tower and a trading float tied beside the landing. Six Mine-Burner Argonians hold it.
Six Mine-Burner Argonians: a post-captain, two watchers, a trader and two youths. They are on good terms with the Naka-Desh of Sakeepa Station.
A few Mine-Burner tribesmen hold the post and watch the border with Nha Enasa. They trade with the Naka-Desh across the water but admit travellers to the basin only with leave.
Basin crocodiles, bog-wolves on the dry ground and the Mine-Burners' suspicion of outsiders. The reeds are easy to get lost in.
They hunt and dry fish on the rack and sell it to the Mine-Burner watch posts. They send egg-gifts to Helstrom once a year.
They keep a clutch hearth in the egg-hut and carry hatchlings to a Hist when the eggs come. Their dead go back by boat to the tree they came from.

Olaxa Station is a Root-Folk stilt post in the northern reeds of the Banujha Basin, built to keep a foothold near the Mine-Burner land. It has been held since the tribes returned to the interior after 4E 48.
A clutch at risk, an intruder to turn back, or a sap-run to escort.
A stilt platform in the northern reeds with a long drying rack, an egg-hut with a thatch roof and a boat landing hidden in the grass. Smoke from the fish-rack hangs over it.
Olaxa Station is a stilt platform with a long drying rack, a thatched egg-hut and a landing hidden in the grass. Four Saxhleel hold it.
Four Root-Folk: an egg-tender, two hunters and a rack-keeper. They are watchful of the Mine-Burner tribes, who think of the basin as theirs.
Four Saxhleel keep the post and trade quietly with the basin tribes. They tend a clutch of eggs in the egg-hut and say little to anyone.
Crocodiles and snakes lurk under the landing. Unfamiliar boats are watched, and a hostile one is turned away by arrow.
Gar fishing and a small ferry for Gul-Tej's boats.
A chime-post at the landing recalls the Kothringi, who were friends of the river-folk. For hatching and burial they travel to the Naka-Desh tree upriver.

Sakeepa Station is at a bend of the Nha Enasa channel east of Gideon, where river-folk meet the trade from Gul-Tej. It is older than the Archwardens' rule and has been rebuilt many times by the same few families.
A trade in gar-leather, a Paatru dispute or a Kothringi ruin the river-folk watch.
A reed-thatched platform on stilts at the channel's edge, a long boat-landing, a fish-rack and a chime-post with a signal lamp. Poled barges lie moored beneath.
Sakeepa Station is a reed-thatched platform on stilts at a bend of the Nha Enasa channel, with a long boat-landing and poled barges moored beneath. Five Naka-Desh keep it.
Five Naka-Desh: a trader, a ferryman, two net-menders and a young one learning the channels. They speak with Gul-Tej's merchants in riddles and keep tallies on knotted cords.
A few Naka-Desh keep the station through the year and ferry goods to and from Gul-Tej. They exchange news with every boat and are said to know who has gone up and down the channel.
Watchers with bows cover the road. Bandits sometimes test the post at night, and bog-wolves cross the causeway at dusk.
Watching and a small toll on the Soulrest road.
They keep a clutch hearth, but their Hist lies near Soulrest, so hatching and burial are a journey inland. A fang-charm is nailed over the toll gate.
Deshaa Post is a Mine-Burner watch post at the basin's south-west edge, covering the road toward Soulrest and Chasepoint. It was built after 4E 48 to give the tribes a say in who uses that road.
A road-warden needs a witness, a smuggler's crate or a Soulrest agent.
A stilt post at the basin's edge where the road turns toward the coast, with a toll gate, a lookout and a wagon yard. The road runs in a raised causeway beside it.
Deshaa Post is a stilt post with a toll gate, a lookout and a wagon yard beside a raised causeway. Six Mine-Burner Argonians hold it.
Six Mine-Burner Argonians: a toll-keeper, three watchers, a smith who mends axles and a boy with a horn. They know the carters of the road by name.
A few Mine-Burner tribesmen hold the post, watching the road and taking toll from carts. They are known on the road for fair, hard bargaining.
Naga raiders from the south-west camp and swamp predators; the watch is the city's first warning of anyone coming up from the south.
Eggs, fish and a small toll for rafts passing between the south fork and Helstrom.
The rise has no Hist; hatchlings are carried the short way to Helstrom's own tree. A small totem-post with a lamp-niche stands on the crest, and the keepers speak to it at dusk.
A watch has been kept here since the Third Era settlements on Helstrom's approaches. It is now a Root-Folk station.
A signal went up at night with no visitor in sight; an egg-tender claims the Hist spoke to her in the mud.
Stilt huts around a clay nest-pit on a low rise, a signal pole and a rope bridge to the next hummock.
The map gives this outpost no name and UESP has none; the name is ours. Five Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom keep stilt huts round a clay nest-pit, with a signal pole on the crest.
About five egg-tenders and watchers.
Five Saxhleel keep a night watch on the rise and tend a clutch of eggs. They light a lamp for travellers on the south road and report each dawn to a tree-minder in Helstrom.
Reed snakes and crocodiles near the landing. A Paatru hunter who takes offence is dangerous, and so is the open north reach beyond the lamp.
Gar fishing and barter.
A chime-post at the landing recalls the Kothringi. The nearby Paatru camps follow another Hist, and the two peoples avoid talk of it.
Nahk-Zeel Station sits at the northern edge of Nha Enasa, where the channels thin out toward Gul-Tej. It was built to watch for Paatru hunting parties and to pass their goods on to river trade.
A message to Gul-Tej, a lost net or a riddle contest with a stranger.
A reed platform on stilts at the channel's northern edge, with a lamp-post, a fish-rack and a boat landing. Hides hang drying on a frame beside the landing.
Nahk-Zeel Station is a reed platform on stilts with a lamp-post, a fish-rack and a boat landing. Five Naka-Desh keep a lamp lit there for boats.
Five Naka-Desh: a salt-trader, two fishers, a lamp-keeper and a girl who runs messages to the Paatru camps. They are friendly to hunters and wary of anyone who comes with a blade drawn.
A few Naka-Desh river-folk hold it and trade with the Paatru camps nearby, giving salt and iron for hides. They keep a lamp lit at night so boats can find the landing.
D2: beasts called by a disturbed totem.

Hutan-Veel earns its living on the far-west border road: guiding, selling meat to Nahk-Zeel Station and bargaining at the palisade gate with Cyrodilic traders. The outpost lives on a toll paid in salt.
Rune-carved totems.
Reasoned: another link in the chain.
A traveller who disappeared from the camp's far side.
A dark palisade and a landing.
An unlabelled outpost named by us. UESP has no page (searched 2026-11-08).
Hutan-Tzel guards.
A palisade with a rune totem.
They let pass a stranger who trades a good riddle.
Osheeja gar fishing.
They hold to their own Hist's roots. They love riddles.
Kept since the Naka-Desh spread south.
A riddle for passage; a message for Gideon.
A small hut group on a river bank, with weirs.
A river station of the Naka-Desh near Naxan.
Five Naka-Desh, wide-webbed, riddle-lovers.
A hut group and fishing weir.
The reeds hide crocodiles and snakes, and the keepers shoot at anyone who touches the sapling. Few outsiders can find the post.
They hunt the reeds for birds and eels, and send sap and egg-gifts to Helstrom. Little leaves the station except by the tree-minders' own boat.
The Hist sapling at the post's heart is sacred, and its whispers guide the keepers' choices. They hatch eggs under it and bury their dead in the reed-beds beside it.

Sarth-Hul Station is a stilt post deep in Nha Enasa's reeds, founded by the Root-Folk of Helstrom to tend a Hist sapling away from the great forest. The sapling was carried here as a cutting after 4E 48.
An egg to protect, a Hist whisper to follow, or a hunter lost in the reeds.
A stilt platform in the reed-beds, with a drying rack, an egg-hut and a young Hist sapling with a ring of stones round it. The reeds are tall enough to hide the whole post.
Sarth-Hul Station is a stilt platform in the reed-beds with an egg-hut and a young Hist sapling ringed with stones. Four Saxhleel hold it.
Four Root-Folk: a sapling-tender, two hunters and an egg-sitter. They speak the root-talk of the great trees, and hold that visitors who lie to them are seen by the Hist.
Four Saxhleel hold the post. They hunt and tend the sapling, and send word to the Helstrom tree-minders by boat each season.
Mangrove crocodiles, snakes and mudcrabs. The channels shift, and strangers can lose themselves quickly.
Gar fishing and mangrove-bark gathering.
A chime-post at the landing recalls the Kothringi dead who lie in the mangroves nearby. The river-folk make the long trip to their tree for hatching and burial.
Teth-Kasa Station is the western-most post of the Naka-Desh, set among the mangrove channels south of Gideon. It was founded after 4E 48 to give the river-folk a foothold on the delta trade.
A boat-hand needed, a riddle for passage, or a smuggler's cache in the mangroves.
A platform on stilts among mangrove roots, a rope-walk, a fish-rack and a hidden boat landing. Reed bundles and coils of rope are piled under the thatch.
Teth-Kasa Station is a platform on stilts among mangrove roots, with a rope-walk and a hidden landing. Five Naka-Desh keep it out of sight of the sea.
Five Naka-Desh: a rope-maker, two fishers, a pilot who guides boats through the mangroves and a boy who cuts reed. They are cautious with strangers from the coast.
A few Naka-Desh hold it and sell fish and reed rope to Gideon's boats. The mangroves hide it from the sea, and only people who know the channels find it.
D2: far from the guards; crocodiles in the channels and the odd Naga raider.
Reed, cut and bundled, carried to Jal-Veesa and Stormhold.
A Hist-shoot on a post at the camp's centre.
Reasoned: reed beds on the northern plain have been cut seasonally for as long as there have been mats to sell.
Cutters report a stranger who is paying for reed to be burned; a child has gone missing near the old Imperial ruin to the south.
Reed-thatched lean-tos on a mud bank, bundled reed stacked like haystacks, flat boats pulled up.

Sedge-Kal Camp is a seasonal reed-cutters' camp on the swamp north of Jal-Veesa, two cells from Stormhold, where Veesa-Teeleel crews cut sedge in the cool months for Stormhold's mat-makers. We placed and named it in the jade style for an unlabelled outpost symbol; UESP has no page for it (searched 2026-11-08).
Veesa-Teeleel cutters and their families, with a watcher from Jal-Veesa.
A cluster of lean-to huts and boat landings, occupied from the dry season's start until the reed is bound.
Deep swamp predators and Naga hunters; the hummock is the only dry ground for hours.
Hides, herbs and guide fees for those crossing the marsh toward Nacydes and the ridge.
There is no Hist on the hummock; the keepers walk the long route to the nearest village tree for hatching and burial. A totem-post at the path-head is hung with hunters' bone-charms.
A hunters' camp that became permanent because the marsh to the south-west has no other dry ground.
A guide lost a party at the last crossing; the post's fire was lit three nights running without a keeper.
A single hummock with two huts, a firepit and a signal post, with open reed all round.
The map gives this outpost no name and UESP has none; the name is ours. Four Saxhleel of the Root-Folk of Helstrom hold two huts, a firepit and a signal post, with open reed on every side.
About four hunters and a guide.
Four Saxhleel hold the hummock, hunting in the marsh and feeding the hunters who pass to Nacydes. They send a message to a tree-minder by boat once a season.
Crocodiles and water-snakes gather under the log boom. At D1 the camp is safe; the Nenria marsh south of it is not.
Eels and gar sold up river.
A Hist-shoot post.
Reasoned: weirs of the Sedge-Wardens.
Strangers asking the way to Gandranen.
Pale stilt huts and a woven weir.

Teel-Fen Weir is the weir-wardens' camp on the creek north-east of Gandranen, closer to Jal-Veesa than Reed-Sill, with traps for eel and carp. We placed and named it in the jade style for an unlabelled outpost symbol; UESP has no page for it (searched 2026-11-08).
Veesa-Teeleel families.
Five wardens and their families live on a small stilt platform at the weir, with a landing and a drying rack of fish. They hand off the catch to Urvyn Farm's cart every other day.
Totem rules; Naga parties from the south-west camp; Murkwood's medusas just across the bend.
Messages, tolls and guide fees between Helstrom's Root-Folk and the Gideon country.
A rune-carved totem stands at the Murkwood edge of the post, and the keepers leave a bowl of river water at its foot. They say it keeps the wood's beasts from the landing.
The Hutan-Tzel sit between Helstrom and the Gideon country and act as go-betweens (cultures.json).
A messenger came with a letter and no body; the naheesh wants a bargain brokered with the Root-Folk.
A palisade of reed on the bank, totem posts with runes only the tribe reads, and a long canoe shed.
The map gives this outpost no name and UESP has none; the name is ours. Six Hutan-Tzel keep a reed palisade on the bank, totem posts and a long canoe shed.
About six Hutan-Tzel and their naheesh's messenger.
Six Hutan-Tzel keep the post on the Murkwood edge and carry messages between Helstrom and the west. They house the go-betweens overnight and answer to their own naheesh.
The lilmothiit den lies close by, and so do bog-wolves and marsh snakes. The abandoned village's floors are rotten.
They hunt along the basin edge and tend a clutch of eggs. They also trade with the lilmothiit for cloth, giving fish in return.
The post has a clutch hearth but no Hist of its own; its keepers carry hatchlings to a village tree. They leave a share of the first catch at the village's old shrine.

Zul-Meeka Station is on the south-east edge of the Banujha Basin, near a lilmothiit den and an abandoned village. The Root-Folk established the post to watch the village ground and its returning families.
A hunter guarding a clutch, a Mine-Burner dispute or a missing sap-gatherer.
A stilt platform on the basin's dry south-east edge, an egg-hut, a lookout post and a boat landing. The abandoned village's roofs show through the reeds nearby.
Zul-Meeka Station is a stilt platform on dry ground with an egg-hut and a lookout post. Four Saxhleel hold it.
Four Root-Folk: two hunters, an egg-tender and a lookout who tracks the lilmothiit. They are quick to tell strangers which paths avoid the den.
Four Saxhleel hold the post and keep an eye on the lilmothiit den and the abandoned village. They have an uneasy peace with the lilmothiit who live nearby.
D3: wraiths of the flu-dead and crocodiles at the quay.
Once a river quay and market; now it holds old Velothi goods and boat fittings for the taking.
The Velothi followed Mephala by their own tradition; Guxal's people call the ground sick and bury their eggs far from it.
One of the Dunmer dissident settlements of the east coast, killed by the Knahaten Flu in 2E 560-603 and never reoccupied.
A Thorn ferryman wants his father's boat found, last seen tied to the old quay. A sealed cellar door has Velothi marks.
Curved Dunmer stonework with root-split walls, a stone quay going under water, moss and bright fungus.
A Cantemiric Velothi ruin on the water's edge. UESP has no page for it; the Velothi settlement of this coast is canon.
Empty of living folk; hunters and river-poachers pass by day.
A drowned quay, fallen towers and a market square with a tree growing through it; Guxal's people hunt round it but do not enter.
D1: the risk is Sarpa raiders to the south-west.
Stone from Xanuc Diggings, river fish and tool-mending.
A cairn replaces a tree; the elder passes dreams to Tsonac's tree-minder.
Founded over an old foundation as Tsonac's people spread south onto the mesa.
A horn blown at night for no reason anyone can name, and a cache of Sarpa feathers found in the quarry.
Stone houses with reed roofs on a riverbank, a signal horn on a pole, mesa cliffs beyond.
A Stone-Sleeper hamlet on the river at the mesa's north-west. UESP has no page; name and people are ours.
Stone-Sleeper families, quarry hands and a watch-elder with a horn.
Eight live there; they quarry the Xanuc Diggings and watch for Sarpa raiders.
Steep cliffs, loose rock and nesting hackwings, plus a pirate lookout who will shoot at strangers.
Nothing is made here. It serves as the lookout for both camps and the beacon-stone for boats on the Okuwun coast.
Sailors leave a pebble on the cairn for luck; the Argonians say the stone is a Hist's old bone, which is a story only.
Nothing is recorded of it. Seamen of every age have used it as a landmark, and the Imperial keep at the shore may have been built to watch it.
A smuggler's cache is hidden under the cairn; its map is on the wreck of the Stormwidow. A shaman's bones are said to lie in a cave on the north face.
A dark grey-green tooth of rock with sea-birds nesting in its cracks, thin salt-grass on the lower slopes, wind-bent shrubs.
A bare grey-green peak of dark, sea-worn rock at the island's centre, named by us for its look. It is not on UESP's list; the Arnesian island's dark green-grey terrain is canon.
No residents. A lookout from Marque Landing climbs it in the day.
It serves as a seamark. A rough cairn stands at the top and a goat-path climbs the south face. The pirates keep a lookout post on it in clear weather.
Raiders, falls, ridge cats.
Nothing is made here; it is a post.
A small chime hangs at the top for the wind's blessing.
A lookout kept by the people of Nacydes, who post a watch here when raiders move.
The sentry saw a light in the Paatru camp that is not a fire; a lost scout's pack lies in a crevice.
A rocky summit with a hut and a chime, with wide views over reed and mere.
The map marks Nacydes Watch only as a peak; UESP has no page for it, and the name is ours. A hut and a small chime stand on its rocky summit, where Nacydes posts a sentry when raiders move.
The peak has no residents; a sentry sits in the hut when needed.
Nacydes keeps a watch on the summit when the Paatru or the Naga stir.
Falls, ridge cats and Naga parties on the summit path.
Nothing is made here; the watchfire basket is the only work.
The watchfire is a small offering to the Hist.
A lookout for the Chime-Keepers of Tydeos, whose watchfire burns on its top.
The summit holds a Kothringi cairn bead-cache; a stranger was found dead beside the fire.
A bare rock summit above the marsh with a fire-basket, a few stunted trees and a view of lakes.
The map marks Aunike Crown only as a peak; UESP has no page for it, and the name is ours. Tydeos' watchfire-keeper climbs its bare rock summit each dusk to tend a fire-basket.
The peak has no residents; hunters pass.
Tydeos' watchfire-keeper climbs it each dusk; otherwise it is empty.
Gas, collapse, fire-undead.
Sulphur and alchemical reagents.
Argonians avoid it as a place of Sithis's anger.
The Great Burn (1E 2828) spread by an underground peat network from Stormhold to Soulrest.
A vent shaft to the burn network, reagent harvest.
Black ground, white ash, dead snags and gas vents.
A named landmark: the scar where the Great Burn's underground network reached the cape.
None; sulphur-gatherers and scavengers.
Still dead ground; smoke hangs low in damp weather.
Rockfalls, bandits on the road.
It sells cut stone to Soulrest's builders and road-menders and pays a fee to the merchant council for the licence. Carts leave twice a week for Chasepoint and the port.
The crew keeps a small Sithis niche in the cutting shed and a rock chip is left on its ledge for each season without a death.
Opened in the Third Era for Soulrest's buildings.
A stone contract; a find in the strata.
A terraced cut and a stone sled track.
Stonecut Quarry is a terraced cut with a stone sled track beside the Percar road. Its grey blocks go to Soulrest's harbour works and the coast road.
A crew of five Argonian quarrymen.
A crew of five works the Percar road face under a Soulrest licence, cutting grey blocks for the harbour works and the coast road.
Rockfalls, bandits.
It sends red facing stone by barge to Soulrest's coast wall and its warehouses, and the licence fee goes to the merchant council. Redbank blocks are prized for their colour.
The crew keeps a Sithis shrine in a niche cut into the face itself, and the foreman marks the first block of each season with a red mark for it.
Opened for Soulrest's red stone.
A rival crew's sabotage.
A red-stained cut and a sled track.
Redbank Quarry is a red-stained cut with a sled track and a short track to the shore. Its blocks are prized for their colour.
A crew of four Argonian quarrymen.
A crew of four works the red-stone face on the south side of the cape, under a Soulrest licence, with a short track to the shore.
Pirates, a locked strong room, trapped stairs and flooded lower cells where the tide enters.
A strong room for prize cargoes and ransom. Captives are kept for ransom or sold to buyers on the Okuwun coast.
An Imperial shrine to Akatosh in the chapel was left standing and is now stacked with crates; the pirates swear by their figureheads.

Probably built in the late First Era when the Empire policed the Archon coast, to watch and break the pirate trade; the Third Empire kept it as a signal tower until the secession of 4E 6, when the garrison left.
A captive in the cells knows where the Resolute Crest's chest lies. The quartermaster keeps a book of every prize and every bribe taken from wardens.
A squat square keep of grey stone with a signal tower, weather-pitted, a sea-wall and a stone jetty, hung with fishing nets and ships' lanterns.
A stone keep on a rise by the shore of Skeith Isle, built by the Empire and now held by pirates. The name is the map's; there is no UESP page and its Imperial origin is read from its symbol and name.
Twelve of the Marque Landing pirates live here under the quartermaster, with up to a dozen captives in the cells at a time.
Pirates took it in the last twenty years. They hold the upper hall as their moot-room and the lower vault as a strong room; the undercroft, once the garrison's cells, is the pirates' prison.
Coastal crocodiles, fleshflies and nighttime smuggler landings on the inlet.
Estuary fish, eels and rice; the guesthouse earns from travellers on the Seafalls road.
The village sends eggs inland to Aroxhu; the elder's family keeps a tide-chart carved on a clay tablet, which half the village thinks is a prayer.
People of Inoja settled it as a late daughter-village when the mounds filled. Its position on the road makes it the stopping place for Seafalls-bound carts.
A boat sold to a stranger has turned up in Skeith's camp with the elder's name burned into the keel. A signal light has been seen on the bluff at night.
Reed-thatched stilt houses on three low mounds by a muddy inlet, nets draped over poles, boats at a clay landing, gulls overhead.
A village between the inlet and the road to Seafalls, with a view of Skeith Isle on clear days. No UESP page for Renhu.
About twelve Argonians of the Oxhu-Teeleel, farmers and netters; a few Seafalls pilots lodge here.
A tidy village with a small guesthouse and good fish. The elders watch for Skeith smugglers who sometimes buy their boats.
Fish, rice, laundry and labour for the fort; boat hire for the Archon crossing.
Hatching at Lilmoth; the fort families keep Imperial habits.
Grew beside the Imperial fort; the villagers kept their houses when the Archwardens re-garrisoned it.
A soldier's debt; a fisherman's catch of something strange; a message to Archon.
Stilt houses on a low rise by the road, fish racks, a landing and the fort's tower visible to the east.
A village on the north shore of the northern island, by the road from Uluo to Fort Reedmoth.
Argonians of the Lilmoth coast, some married to fort families of Archein descent.
Ten households trade with the fort, the ferry-men and passing boats.
Sea-drakes, pirates on the Sea of Mists, flooded creeks.
Landing fees, salt, shellfish, coastal freight.
A tide-line Sithis shrine; hatchlings go inland.
A Third Era timber landing that outlived the mines.
A smuggler boat at night; a lost salt shipment.
A wooden jetty, drying racks, low stilt houses, a salt pan.
A village on the south coast, below Mir-Xal.
Argonian boatmen, a few Khajiit coasters.
Under the Soulrest merchant council; its reeve collects landing fees.
Surf and spray on wet rocks, rope-bridge falls, sea-drakes in the bay, and Skeith pirate boats in the dark.

The portage, which charges cargo-carriers by weight; piloting; pearl-shell and sea-salt; and a trade in drift-wood and wreck-salvage. Seafalls is the transfer point on the north-east link between Thorn, Branchmont and Archon.

They hold that the sea keeps the memories that the Hist let fall. They leave painted shells and knotted cords at the falls, keep death-dancers for burials, and nest on the shoals. Hatching and naming mean a long journey inland.
The Spray-Folk came here from the Archon shore, beyond any Hist tree. Under the East Empire Company they ran the portage for Company boats; since 4E 6 the portage is theirs alone.
The pilot-elder needs a successor and has chosen a hatchling who cannot swim. A ship has come in with a cargo that does not match its bills, and the Archwardens want it quietly seized.
White falls dropping into a sea-pool, stilt houses and nest-platforms on the cliff and shoals, rope-bridges over the spray, salt-crusted decks, the lighthouse beyond the point, gulls and surf.

A coastal village at the falls where a river reaches the Padomaic, the reason cargo changes boats here. Canon names Seafalls as Archon's neighbour to the north-north-east and the settlement register calls it a falls-and-portage settlement; UESP has no page of its own.
About fourteen Argonians of the Spray-Folk: pilots, portage-men and net-menders. The pilot-elder, an old woman who has taken a hundred ships through the surf, is the village's voice.
A small, self-contained village. Their pilots take ships into Archon and off the Thorn road. The Archwardens charge them nothing because no other crew will do the job.
Wind on the gallery, slippery rocks and the shoals; pirates sometimes douse the light to wreck a ship.
Light-fees from the pilots of Seafalls, a share of salvage from every wreck on the shoals.
The keeper keeps a clay lamp for the lost dead and lights it with the beacon.
Built by the East Empire Company for its Archon-Thorn run; kept alight by the Spray-Folk since the Company left.
Someone has doused the light twice and a ship was lost. The keeper's hatchling saw a boat from Skeith Isle on the first night.
A white-lime tower of stone on the point, a gallery with a great brass lamp, a keeper's hut and a boat-slip, surf below.
A tall beacon house on the point south-east of the falls, guarding ships from the shoals. The tower and its keepers are ours; there is no UESP page.
Three Argonians, a keeper and his two hatchlings; one of them is a trained watcher with a long glass.
Lit every night by the keeper, who burns fish-oil bought from Archon and sells directions to the lost.
Mud-crabs, tidal flats that drown the careless, and the occasional patrol from the fort; D2.
Shellfish, dried fish and salt, sold toward Truowa; rice and tools come back by raft.
Sithis and the Hist as the tribe holds them; the sea-edge families add a prayer to the tide at each net-laying.
Founded by Three Waters families seeking clams and cockles on the western mudflats, then drawn into Truowa's trade when the city grew.
A trader needing safe passage between the fort and Truowa; a shell midden older than the hamlet with Velothi beads in it.
Pole houses over grey mudflats, shell middens like low white hills, nets spread to dry on frames, and salt pans.
A coastal hamlet at the far west of the Nushara waters, nearest to Truowa and the fort that watches the water-road.
Three Waters Argonians with some Truowa-bound rice traders; the families are kin to Tapauo and Uluo.
Eight raft-families net, gather shellfish and sell to Truowa's lighters; they pay the garrison at Fort Gysilla the toll and nothing more.
Sea-drakes, drowning and sharp timbers.
Cargo of salt, cloth and lamps.
Natai holds a drowned-sailor rite for the wreck's lost.
Wrecked on the shoals in a storm some years back.
A locked captain's chest, a smuggler's cache and a lost logbook.
A broken hull on a sand bar, ribs rising through green water.
A wreck off the south shore.
No residents.
Natai salvagers dive it by turns.
D3: sea-drakes, a shaft of cold current and a collapsed hatch.
It once let a salvage master carry out dives into the spires; now it is itself salvage.
Divers tap the sphere three times for luck.
Built by a salvage master of Lilmoth to reach the deep spires without a bell and lowered by a barge. Its cable parted in a storm and it was lost. The master died of grief.
The pilot's logbook; a map of the spires; a lock that opens to a salvage master's key.
A brass ball with portholes and rivets, a broken cable trailing, wreathed in kelp and light.
A sunken diving vessel, a brass bathysphere, resting on the sea floor near Echo Deep.
No residents. Divers report the ghost of its pilot tapping at the glass.
It lies on its side half buried in silt, its ports cracked and its glass still glowing.
D1: crabs, a tide that traps the careless, sinking decks.
It once carried cargo for the Archon trade; now people strip timber, nails and brass.
Sailors leave bits of cord on the stern post for the drowned.
Wrecked on the sandbar some years before 4E 201 when her pilot missed the channel; the crew survived.
A sealed strongbox in the hold; the pilot's logbook that shows who bribed him.
A grey broken hull with the masts down, barnacled, gulls on the rail, half buried in white sand.
A wrecked trading ship on the shore a short walk from Archon.
No residents; beachcombers from Archon come at low tide and a hermit crab-catcher camps near.
The hull lies on its side half sunk in sand, stripped of cargo and rigging by locals and tide.
Drowned dead in the hold, slaughterfish and a current that pulls toward the split in the hull. The depth is a short swim from shore.
Dunmer relic-collectors and ledger-hunters pay for the captain's logbook; Thorn's Archwardens would pay more to bury it.
Thorn's coast Argonians do not pray at the Silt Bride, for she carried their kin in chains. They leave a painted shell on the nearest shore for the captives, and spit on the water over the hull.

A Dres-chartered slaver of the kind that sailed from Thorn after the Arnesian War and into Helseth's ban, sunk in a storm with captives aboard. Slavers were still active in Arnesia late in the Third Era.
The logbook names the Dunmer families who bought captives from Thorn; some of them still trade there. The Thorn Vicecanon wants it, as do the families it names.
A black-oaked hull furred with weed, rusted shackles trailing from the hatch, fish in the cabin windows.

The Silt Bride lies on her side on the shelf off Thorn, a short swim from shore. She was a Dres-chartered slaver of the Arnesian trade. The ship and its name are AGENT_INVENTED; there is no UESP page for it.
The wreck has no residents. The slaver's crew drowned in the hold with their captives. Shackled dead are seen moving in the cabin at low tide.
The brig lies on her side in the shelf off Thorn, hull split amidships, the stern cabin intact.
Slaughterfish in the shallows and drowned dead in the hold; the lower deck is narrow and the water is cold.
A strongbox of Company coin and ship's papers is the draw. Salvagers from Ysan and Arorha have picked at the hull but not reached the hold.
Local Argonians leave a knotted cord on the nearest shore for sailors lost at sea, as the Spray-Folk do at Seafalls.
One of the Company's last saltrice runs from Thorn to Archon before the province closed, sunk in a squall with the harvest aboard.
The ship's papers name a Dunmer consignee in Thorn who never paid for the harvest. A diver can bring them up.
A listing timber hull on grey silt, barnacled ribs, rotten sacks heaped in the hold, ropes drifting in the green light.
A sunken saltrice freighter on the seabed of the bight, a short swim from the shore near Ysan. The ship and its name are AGENT_INVENTED; no UESP page exists for a wreck here.
The wreck has no residents. The crew drowned with the ship and remain aboard as drowned dead.
Barnacled and half-buried in silt. The hull is intact enough to enter; the cargo has long since turned to black sludge.
Slaughterfish and a drowned dead captain who guards the strongbox; the water is shallow but the shoal bottom is jagged.
Her cargo, moon-sugar casks gone to rot and a strongbox of Skeith coin, is the draw; Skeith crews dive for it and do not tell the wardens.
Skeith smugglers drop a coin in the water above the Brindle Gull before a night run, for luck against the wardens. Arorha's fishers leave a knotted cord on the shore for the crew.
A fast sloop running untaxed goods from Skeith Isle to the Arorha shore; she ran onto the Kornakim shoals in a squall within the last twenty years.
The sloop's logbook shows the route and a landing the wardens do not know about, and the Skeith smugglers would kill to keep it secret.
A small clinker hull with a painted gull on the bow, soft with weed, with spars and lines floating above it.

The Brindle Gull was a fast sloop on the Skeith Isle run to the Arorha shore. She rests upright in shallow green water on the Kornakim shoals. The ship and its name are AGENT_INVENTED; there is no UESP page for it.
The wreck has no residents. The smuggler crew went down off the Kornakim shoals. The captain remains on guard over the strongbox.
The hull rests upright in shallow green water, mast broken at the step, the deckhouse hatch still shut.
Rotten decks, crabs in the hold and a rising tide; the camps will fight anyone they catch at the wreck.
Timber, copper sheathing and cordage are stripped for the camps. The captain's strongbox is the real prize.
None; the pirates say the figurehead is bad luck and have turned it to face the sea.
A chartered privateer of the Archon coast, driven ashore in a gale and abandoned by her crew, who joined the Marque Landing camp.
The captain's strongbox holds a map to the cairn on the Grey Tooth. Both camps search for it and neither has found it.
A listing hull half-buried in grey sand, ribs open to the sky, ropes and sails rotting, a figurehead of a veiled woman.
A beached ship on the south-west shore of Skeith Isle, partly above the tide line. The ship and her name are AGENT_INVENTED; no UESP page.
The wreck has no residents. Scavengers from both camps sneak in at the ebb.
Her upper hull is picked clean; the lower hold is full of sand and sea-water at high tide and rarely entered.
Deep water, cold currents, drowned Imperial marines, sea-drakes and the pressure itself; this is a dive for the well-prepared.
A chest of Akaviri tribute and the ship's brass sell for a fortune to a collector at Archon. The depth is the barrier. A diver must be skilled to reach it.
Divers who reach the Resolute Crest salute the ensign before touching the chest, which is an old Imperial custom. Skeith's crews tie a knotted cord at their camp for the Navy dead.
Uriel Septim V's Far East Fleet sailed the Padomaic against Akavir in the 3E 270s; this ship went down on the return run, long before the province left the Empire.
A dying marine's letter of command is in the captain's cabin, naming a stash on Skeith Isle. A collector at Archon wants the chest.
A tall black-oaked hull ringed with weed, a bronze figurehead of a crest worn smooth, ballistae on a sunken deck, shoals of fish.

The Resolute Crest sailed in Uriel Septim V's Far East Fleet and went down on the return from Akavir in the 3E 270s. She rests upright on the deep shelf east of Skeith Isle. The ship and its name are AGENT_INVENTED; there is no UESP page for it.
The wreck has no residents. The marines of the Far East Fleet went down with the ship. Their drowned dead still stand watch on the quarterdeck.
The great hull rests on the deep shelf east of Skeith Isle, upright, weedgrown, the quarterdeck still above the silt.
Sea-drakes, drowning.
Cargo of cloth and lamp oil.
A sailors' rite at the nearest harbour.
Wrecked in a storm.
A captain's chest and a smuggler's cache.
A dark hull in blue water.
A wreck on the sea floor.
None.
Visited by Soulrest salvagers.
Drowning in the beam-tangle, bay sharks and shoals of stinging jellyfish. The sand-bar shifts in storms.
Its hold still carries Cyrodilic wine casks and iron bars, a cargo the salvagers have brought up in small lots.
A Nibenese sailor's Dibella charm of shell and copper lies on the deck, tied to the stern post by a drowned hand.
The Grey Heron was a merchantman bound for Gideon that struck the sand-bar off its estuary in a winter gale. It sank in Topal Bay with most of its cargo, in the years after the Empire's fleet left.
A sealed cargo, a drowned captain's log or a diving contract.
A broken hull lying on the sand under green water, with weed-hung ribs and a stern post still standing. Shoals of small fish move among the beams.
A merchantman that sank off Gideon's estuary.
A pair of salvage boats from Gideon visit in the summer. Local fishers mark the spot with a float.
Salvage divers from Gideon work the wreck in calm weather and haul up what the sea has left. Some of the cargo is still in the hold, out of reach under the beams.
Drowning in the cleft, sharks that rest in the shade and razor-edged rocks that tear a diver's rope.
Its hold had contraband: moon sugar, skooma flasks and bolts of Valenwood silk, some of it still in oilcloth.
A sailor's charm of knotted rope lies on the deck, and a tin cup of offering-coins is wedged below the helm.
The Sallow Anne was a smuggler's sloop that ran onto the rocks off Aphon Isle while fleeing a patrol. It was lost in the years after the Empire's fleet left. Its crew went unclaimed.
A smuggler's strongbox, a rival crew or a chart.
A narrow hull jammed into a rock cleft, with its mast snapped short and a net of kelp over the open deck. Silver fish flicker in the shadow beneath.
A smuggler's sloop wrecked on the rocks off Aphon.
Aphon fishers dive on it for what they can sell. A smuggler from the bay comes by now and then to search.
Divers from Aphon and Soulrest visit the wreck in calm weather, and smugglers search for its hidden cargo. Smugglers say the captain's strongbox was never found.
Slaughterfish, crocodilian ambushers in the reeds, and getting lost in the beds; no bandits.
Thatch, mat-reed and eel traps sold at Uluo; they buy salt, iron hooks and cloth.
Reed-cutters leave the first bundle of each season on a stump for the Hist; otherwise they go to Uluo for hatching and burial.
Settled by Three Waters reed-cutters who followed the best beds; the hamlet moves its houses a few poles each generation as the reeds shift.
A cutter who found something metal in the mud of the bed; a trapper's request to clear a nest of ripper eels.
Low reed-thatch houses on stilts above hummocks, tall drying racks of pale reed, and eel traps hung like baskets over the water.
A small hamlet on a ridge of firm ground in the reed beds south of Inoio, off the road and reached by punt.
Three Waters Argonians; a reed-master leads and answers to Uluo's elder.
Six households cut, dry and bundle reed in season and trap eels in the off-season. The hamlet is quiet and few outsiders come.
D1: a guarded crossing; fleshflies in clouds, crocodiles in the river, the odd smuggler.
Road trade to Gideon and Leyawiin, tolls, a market of smugglers and herb-sellers, and a ferry for when the bridge is under water.
Dibella shrine in the old customs house, as in Gideon; no Hist, a foreign foundation. Argonian residents go home to a village tree to hatch and bury.
The Empire built the post, bridge and customs house to tax the Blackwood Road. The Legion left and Imperial presence ends in canon by 4E 48; the families who served the post stayed on.
A smuggler who wants the bridge swamped on the night he crosses; the customs ledgers; Gideon's refusal to honour the successor state's seals.
A long white bridge over a black river; a stone customs house with weathered Imperial seals; mud-and-timber houses on stilts and a few Cyrodiilic gables; fleshfly-chewed guards.

Slough Point was an Imperial census-and-excise post with a Commission-built white bridge over a black tidal river, its guards chewed by fleshflies. UESP's Blackwood page lists it as an Imperial town in Blackwood, close to the Black Marsh border; the map puts it inside Black Marsh, beside Fort Rustmoth, which is how we place it. UESP has no page of its own.
Lukiul Argonians and Nibenese-descended families of the Gideon frontier; Khajiit and Imperial traders pass through; the garrison are Archwarden soldiers.

A village around the old customs house and the bridge. The tide still swamps the bridge for days at a time and shuts the crossing, as the Argonian Account describes. The toll is kept by the garrison of Fort Rustmoth next door.

Inside the gates guards keep order; threats are theft, smugglers' feuds and a visitor carrying the wrong cargo. The landward burn-scar is gas and dead timber; the inland tribes are hostile to coast officials.

Southern Sea trade, salvage from wrecks off the cape, and Bramman's river, the concealed channel from Topal Bay to the Blackrose lakes. Gold and timber are no longer exported at scale; the old workings behind the city are derelict.

Sithis and the Hist through the interior tribes' trees; Imperial-descended families keep the Nine in small shrines; Khajiit sailors keep the moons. A Brotherhood of Seth presence is canon and stays hidden.

Argonians lived here since the wraxu birds were alive. Red Bramman ran pirates from a mangrove river nearby in 1E; the Great Burn (1E 2828) reached its edge; the tribes burned its plantations and mines in 3E 427, ending gold and timber exports. The Empire left after the 4E 48 catastrophe.

A faction contest for the council, a hidden mangrove landing to find, derelict Imperial mines to enter, the hatching-ground leverage that the Banujha tribes hold over the city, and control of smuggling through Bramman's river.

A port behind its gates: stone Imperial quarter at the peninsula's neck, timber and stilt wharves below, mangrove creeks to the south, xanmeers etched with wraxu, and burn-scarred dead ground and gas vents on its landward edge.

The southwest coast port on a peninsula wrapping Topal Bay, capital of Black Marsh in the Third Era. In 4E 201 it is an administrative city with nothing left to administer, and the most mixed and contested city in the province.
About 60% Argonian, a large Khajiit share among seafarers, Imperial-descended administrators' families, Bosmer and other maritime minorities. A few dozen named residents at Skyrim's scale.

A merchant council, the ex-Imperial civil apparatus with no sovereign, the mangrove-river interests and the interior mine-burning tribes contest the city, the unexplained 'struggle for regional hegemony' of canon. The government quarter is half empty and repurposed. The city has no Hist, so its Argonians hatch, name and bury inland in Banujha country.
D2: storms, sea-drakes beyond the reef, and wreckers on the shore.
Tolls on anchorage; provisions from Karketa.
No Hist; the garrison hatches and buries at Lilmoth.
An Imperial coast fort; no Imperial presence remained after 4E 48 and the successor state took it over.
A beacon that fails on a stormy night; a ship's captain who claims he paid the toll.
A squat stone keep with a beacon tower, a landing below and the sea open to the south.
A coastal fort at the south-west tip of the island, standing watch over the sea road to Lilmoth.
Argonian garrison of Archein-line officers, with fishermen from Karketa as neighbours.
Eight garrison men keep a beacon, inspect ships and pay little attention to Lilmoth's politics.

D0 inside the walls, where guards keep order. Outside the gate are crocodile-infested ravines and sunken marsh; below the city the Silyanorn tunnels and a sunken Ayleid ruin are an outlaws' refuge (D3).

River traffic to Morrowind and to Alten Corimont down the northern trunk road, the customs on that traffic, and the Stormhold Crystals dug in the tunnels below. Sedge mats, dried fish and reed goods arrive daily from Jal-Veesa and the weirs; the guild halls sit in the repurposed Ayleid compound.

The Hist tree stands in the town square in the middle of a pond, ringed by ancient pillars and a low stone wall, public and defended. Dunmer households keep their ancestors and a quiet Tribunal-shaped habit; the grave-stake tradition of the Argonians and the Ayleid-compound mortuary sit side by side.

Barsaebic Ayleids founded Silyanorn here after 1E 198; the Hist later conquered them, by legend. The Dunmer used the site as the foothold of their slave trade, adding stone roads, light posts and bridges, and the city invented the Vicecanon office to try slavers. It was the Pact's capital of Black Marsh in 2E, held a prison under Warden Quintus Varus in the late 3E, and was overrun but lightly damaged by Umbriel's undead in 4E 48.

The Silyanorn undercity holds crystal tunnels and a lost book of wisdom about the natural energies of Black Marsh. The Conclave of Baal keeps its Vaults of Gemin. The old quarrel between the Argonian west quarter and the Dunmer is a further hook, and so are the Vicecanons' courts.

A city on a mountainside: Dunmer ornate stone, stone roads, light posts and long wooden bridges over ravines, with large Argonian mud huts on the mounds between, and a waterfall running down through the old Ayleid compound.

The city of the Valley of Storms region and the likeliest first sight of the province for a newcomer. (full TEXT: "Stormhold is the largest settlement of Shadowfen, a major city of Black Marsh, sited near the banks of the river that forms the border with Morrowind. The city of the Valley of Storms region and the likeliest first sight of the province for a newcomer.")

Argonians beside the largest and oldest Dunmer minority in Argonia, descended from a colonial population, about a fifth of the city. The western quarter was where the Argonians who worked for the Dunmer lived, and the memory is still live. Outsiders are met with pragmatism: this is the city that has always had to live with them. Several Vicecanons sit at once, one for each people.

The waterfall, the ravine-severed mounds, the Hist in its pond and the Silyanorn substructure all survived 4E 48. The rest has been rebuilt in the 153 years since. The damage that remains is in the population. The Vicecanons keep the river customs and the frontier screen's offices here.
D3: drowning on the spiral stair, cold in the lower galleries, and the octopus's grip. Sealed doors have caught divers who took too long.
Once a temple-tower of the old age, it is now a salvage ground of bronze, vakka stones and bone, close enough for a day's dive from Lilmoth. Bell Station takes the state's share.
Divers say it was a place of Sithis and the water-spirits and pray before entering. The Hist-glyph on its sealed door suggests the Hist once spoke here.

An Argonian-built tower of the old age before the sea took the land: Murkmire is said to have been swallowed by the Southern Sea, and the Padomaic took most of the Hist's first domain. It lies closest to Lilmoth's drowned quarter.
A salvage master's marked chest; a sealed door with a Hist glyph.
A broken spire furred with weed, round windows and a staircase spiralling down.
A drowned spire standing on the sea floor, reached by diving. It lies closest to Lilmoth's drowned quarter.
A hermit octopus has taken a gallery. Divers say a dead priest walks the stair on moonless tides.
Teku-Sul Spire lies closest to Lilmoth's drowned quarter, silted and furred with kelp and coral. Bell Station's divers visit it often because it is the nearest, and have stripped the upper floors.
D3: slaughterfish in the flooded hall and the cold near Echo Deep's edge. Trapped galleries have killed salvagers who lost their line.
It was a temple-tower of the old age; now a salvage ground of bronze, vakka stones and bone, half cleared by Bell Station. The remaining rooms are the hard ones, down by the deep edge.
Divers say the tower belonged to Sithis and the water-spirits, and they pray before entering. The curling stone arms are read as an offering to the deep.

An Argonian-built tower of the old age before the sea took the land: Murkmire is said to have been swallowed by the Southern Sea, and the Padomaic took most of the Hist's first domain. It stands near Echo Deep and is partly salvaged.
A diver trapped in a gallery; a salvage chest.
A tall spire with curling stone arms and a flooded inner hall.
A drowned spire standing on the sea floor, reached by diving. It stands near Echo Deep and is partly salvaged.
A school of slaughterfish and their hunters live there. Divers avoid it and tell of a diver still trapped in one gallery.
Haxtil-Meht Spire stands near Echo Deep, partly salvaged and furred with weed. Bell Station's divers work it in short shifts, because slaughterfish school in its flooded hall.
D4: sea-drakes nest in the galleries and attack at once, and the cold and depth near Echo Deep wear a diver down. A leaning stair can drop away under weight.
A temple-tower of the old age and now a sea-drake's lair, it is a salvage ground of bronze and bone that few can reach. The hoard in the nest is what draws the bravest.
Argonian divers say it was a place of Sithis and the water-spirits, and they pray before entering. The sea-drakes are read as the water-spirits' answer.

An Argonian-built tower of the old age before the sea took the land: Murkmire is said to have been swallowed by the Southern Sea, and the Padomaic took most of the Hist's first domain. It stands near Echo Deep and is a sea-drake's lair.
A sea-drake's hoard; a dead diver's kit.
A leaning spire, dark with weed, the sea-drakes' nests in its upper galleries.
A drowned spire standing on the sea floor, reached by diving. It stands near Echo Deep and is a sea-drake's lair.
Sea-drakes live there and defend the nests. A dead diver's kit lies at the foot of the stair.
Zeshul-Tha Spire leans on the sea floor near Echo Deep, dark with weed and nested by sea-drakes in its upper galleries. Bell Station's divers rarely enter and never alone.
D3: dreugh scouts, cold and silt that clouds the water in a moment. A carved prize in a dreugh's grip is bait.
A temple-tower of the old age; now a salvage ground of bronze, vakka stones and bone, contested with dreugh. Bell Station divers work it only in numbers.
Argonian divers say it belonged to Sithis and the water-spirits and pray before going down. The dreugh's coral wrap marks it as theirs now.

An Argonian-built tower of the old age before the sea took the land: Murkmire is said to have been swallowed by the Southern Sea, and the Padomaic took most of the Hist's first domain. It stands north of Bell Station and hosts dreugh.
A dreugh's carved prize; a diving-bell chain.
A spire half sunk in silt, its top wrapped in coral.
A drowned spire standing on the sea floor, reached by diving. It stands north of Bell Station and hosts dreugh.
Dreugh scouts live there, keep carved prizes and watch the water. The station's crews tell of a diving-bell chain that was cut from below.
Naxiil-Ru Spire stands north of Bell Station, half sunk in silt and capped with coral. Dreugh scouts hold it, and Bell Station's crews give them the room.
D3: eels at the foot, deep cold and the distance from Bell Station if a line fails. The lamp on the sand is a marker for the dead salvager's grave.
A temple-tower of the old age; now a salvage ground, though the summit shrine is left untouched by custom. The sand plain around it yields bone and bronze.
A summit shrine of ancestors still bears offerings, and divers pray there before entering. The old faith is still practised at this spire.

An Argonian-built tower of the old age before the sea took the land: Murkmire is said to have been swallowed by the Southern Sea, and the Padomaic took most of the Hist's first domain. It stands the furthest north-east.
An ancestor shrine with offerings; a salvager's lamp.
A lone spire on a sand plain, with a shrine on its summit.
A drowned spire standing on the sea floor, reached by diving. It stands the furthest north-east.
Eels live at the foot of the spire. A dead salvager's lamp still burns on the sand. Divers who come leave offerings at the shrine.
Okhu-Thteel Spire is the furthest north-east, a lone tower on a sand plain with a shrine on its summit. Bell Station's crews visit rarely, as the sail from the station is long.
D3: drowning in the lower gallery where the crew died, and cold at depth. Their cache is trapped by the same fall that killed them.
A temple-tower of the old age that the station has worked since its founding; the first bell hung from its platform. Little of value remains above the grave.
Divers touch the platform's bell-cord before going down and pray to Sithis and the water-spirits. The crew's grave is kept free of salvage by the station's own custom.

An Argonian-built tower of the old age before the sea took the land: Murkmire is said to have been swallowed by the Southern Sea, and the Padomaic took most of the Hist's first domain. It stands beside Bell Station.
A failed crew's cache; the station's first bell.
A spire next to Bell Station's anchor chains, a platform of old salvage.
A drowned spire standing on the sea floor, reached by diving. It stands beside Bell Station.
Nothing lives there, but a failed salvage crew lies in its lower gallery. The station keeps their cache sealed and does not speak their names.
Va-Seeth Spire stands beside Bell Station's anchor chains, with a platform of old salvage built around its foot. It is the station's own spire and the easiest to reach.
D4: the ghost, the cold of the deep edge, and a current that pulls divers off the tower. Divers must not touch the sealed door.
A temple-tower of the old age, kept sealed and unworked; the door's guard turns all salvagers back. Its bronze is mapped but untouched.
Argonian divers say it was a place of Sithis and the water-spirits, and the ghost is thought to be its last priest. They pray before approaching and do not linger.

An Argonian-built tower of the old age before the sea took the land: Murkmire is said to have been swallowed by the Southern Sea, and the Padomaic took most of the Hist's first domain. It is the outermost spire in deep water.
A sealed door and a ghost who guards it.
A tall pale spire on the edge of the deep, bright in the water.
A drowned spire standing on the sea floor, reached by diving. It is the outermost spire in deep water.
A drowned sea-priest's ghost keeps the sealed door. Divers who have seen it describe a figure bright in the water.
Thul-Kesh Spire is the outermost in deep water, tall and pale on the edge of the deep. Bell Station's divers rarely go, as the water is cold and the light poor.
D1: wildlife and flooded causeways; crocodiles take the odd goat.
Saltrice, marsh greens and eels carried to Stormhold's market; a ferry stage on the river branch below the village.
A small Hist-shoot shrine at the causeway head; Dunmer ancestor stones in the farmyards.
No canon history. Reasoned: the causeway farmsteads grew up under the Dunmer colonial period, when Stormhold needed food from raised ground, and kept their stone footings after the Dunmer left.
A causeway washed out in the monsoon and a family cut off; a feud between the Argonian and Dunmer farm-holders over a water-right.
Low stone-footed houses with mud-plaster walls and reed roofs on raised platforms; stone causeways between the mounds and drying frames in the yards.
Surkina is a village in the Stormhold manner, a few miles south-east of the city. UESP has no page for it (searched 2026-11-08); it is a Project Tamriel name.
Mixed Argonian and Dunmer farm families; a headman who is also the Vicecanon's reeve.
A dozen households of Argonians and Dunmer on stone mounds, linked to Stormhold by a causeway that floods in the monsoon.
Waterfowl-hunting predators, slaughterfish, floods; D2 outside the hamlet.
Saltrice, the main food crop of the bayou, with surplus sold to Archon and Lilmoth by raft.
Planting and harvest are marked by chanting to the Hist; the first sheaf is set on the water.
The tribe's rice grounds are older than the town; Tapauo's founders moved up the channel to find fresh silt.
A blight that spreads from a raft of seed bought from an outsider; a wager over who may plant the last bed.
Rafts of rice-bed in neat rows beside stilt storehouses, with drying racks, sacks and a long landing of poles.
A hamlet of rice-growers between two channels, a half-day's raft north of Uluo.
Three Waters Argonians; a rice-warden decides when to plant and what the elder is owed.
Eight households plant, tend and harvest, loading rice onto rafts for Uluo and the Archon market.
Feather-serpents, undead of the old assault and deep water around the halls.
Once a tribal stronghold; now salvage for passers-by and an Argonian grave-place.

Nothing is worshipped at Tarak Shan now. Amalaja's minder leaves a reed offering at the old gate for the defenders whom the Third Legion killed. People in the washes hold that the water here is a grave.
Stormed by the Empire in the time of Tiber Septim (2E 857 to 861), where the soldier Attrebus was wounded; abandoned since, with a feather-serpent legend attached.
A pile of Imperial arms from the storming; a feather-serpent's den; a Legion banner.
A ring of tiered halls on water, broken, covered in lichen.
Tarak Shan is a ring of broken tiered halls on the water, covered in lichen, with a flooded stockade and a sunken landing. A feather-serpent legend clings to it.
Tarak Shan is uninhabited. Scavengers come by boat for Legion brass and the occasional skull. Hunters from Amalaja will not stay a night.
Collapsed stilt halls, a flooded stockade, a sunken landing.
Marsh predators and delta bandits at night.
Rice and reed, fish traps, ferry connection to Delta Ferry.
A newly regrown Hist at Lilmoth serves them; they carry their dead to its tender.
A delta farming village rebuilt after the 4E 48 catastrophe that emptied Murkmire.
A paddy blight, a landlord's feud and a chance to carry rice to Blackrose.
Paddies in shallow terraces, stilt houses with rice stores, a boardwalk road.
A village in the farmed land east of Blackrose, within Lilmoth's trade.
Argonian farmers and their households.
Part of Lilmoth's trade network and hostile to the Archwardens.
D1: road-side wildlife; D2 in the pits.
Wayhouse trade on the road east, river landing fees and Stormhold Crystals dug in the nearby pits.
A Hist-shoot shrine and Dunmer ancestor stones; the villagers avoid the old shrine ground on the hill.
No canon history. The name echoes Ten-Maur-Wolk, a Boethiah-worshipping Dunmer settlement after 1E 700 turned slave camp; if the villagers descend from that ground, they would not say so.
A pit-boss who has found a vein that hums; a traveller who arrived by river and has not left his room.
Stone-footed stilt houses along the bank, a landing of timber stages, a long wayhouse with a stone chimney.

Tenmal is a village in the Stormhold manner on the road east of the city. UESP has no page for it (searched 2026-11-08); the name is close to Ten-Maur-Wolk (Tenmar Wall), the road hinge that canon names as a neighbour of Stormhold, and may be a village that grew along the same road.
Argonian and Dunmer families of the river road; a ferryman and a pit-boss.
A river-side village with a landing and a wayhouse, and a crystal pit above it worked by a few households.
Inside the walls it is D0 by law, but purse-cutters and bribed guards are the real risk. At the door the paddies and the coast road are D1; the saltrice workers bear grudges against the field-owners.

Saltrice, the crop the East Empire Company once exported, is the city's wealth, with the Tear road, border tolls and smuggling beside it. Timber and stone come in from the Arnesian jungle to the west; Tsonac sells to Thorn and buys its rice.

A field-edge tree outside the walls serves the Hist; the Dunmer minority keeps the old Temple saints, among them Roris, the trader whose death began the Arnesian War. The Nine have a few shrines in the old Imperial quarter.

The Barsaebic Ayleids founded it. House Dres raided it in the mid-First Era and rose to a Great House on the slaves taken; Dres ruled it in the Second Era until Heita-Meen, once a slave in its saltrice fields, killed Councilor Glathis Dres in 2E 572. In the Third Era it was a city-state under King Tibus and rival to Archon, and the Arnesian War of 3E 396 was fought on its border.

A disputed saltrice field with two deeds, a smuggling ring that passes goods through Fort Thornmoth, a Dunmer family hunting a runaway slave's descendants, and the ruins at Kharraluhl and Bala Karag that scavengers sell from in the market.

A walled city of Ayleid-founded stone under Dunmer and Imperial rebuilding, with Argonian timber and reed quarters round it, set on flat grassland that runs to green saltrice paddies in every direction. Thorn Palace, the Mages Guild, the Conclave of Riana and the Conclave of the One are its named places.

Thorn is one of the eight major cities of Black Marsh, in the grassland of Thornmarsh in the north-east, with Morrowind and the road to Tear to its north. Its epithet is the Jewel of the East: as deadly as it is beautiful, a city where vagabonds eye purses and the guards turn a blind eye.

About three in four are Argonian, with a large Dunmer minority of mixed families whose ancestors stood on both sides of the coffles, and a few Imperial-descended traders. Vicecanons (one to three, chosen locally), field-owners, toll-clerks, saltrice gangs and smugglers make up the people who matter.

In 4E 201 Thorn is intact and the most prosperous place in the north-east. With Dres gone the saltrice fields passed to whoever stood in them: freed labourers' descendants and the ex-Archein families who managed them.
